questions.title: Deadlock Storm Under Load: Root Cause and Prevention
questions.prompt: Your OLTP system is throwing an increasing number of deadlock errors (1205) during peak hours, and the on-call team's current fix is just to retry the failed transaction. As the architect, walk through: what a deadlock actually is at the lock-manager level, why SQL Server resolves it by picking a victim, and the concrete, durable design changes you'd make to drive the deadlock rate toward zero rather than just making retries cheaper.
questions.modelAnswer: A deadlock is a circular wait: Transaction A holds a lock Transaction B needs, while B simultaneously holds a lock A needs, so neither can ever proceed without intervention. SQL Server's lock monitor periodically scans for exactly this cycle and, once found, picks a 'victim' to roll back automatically, based on which transaction is cheaper to undo (or an explicit DEADLOCK_PRIORITY setting), raising error 1205 to the victim's caller. Retrying the rolled-back transaction only treats the symptom -- it does nothing to reduce how often the cycle forms in the first place. The durable fixes are architectural: (1) enforce a consistent access order to tables across every code path that touches them, since the single most common real-world cause is two transactions locking the same two tables in opposite order; (2) keep transactions as short as possible, moving validation and unrelated reads outside the BEGIN/COMMIT boundary so locks are held for the minimum necessary time; (3) review indexing so transactions acquire narrow row/page locks instead of escalating to page or table locks on large scans, which dramatically widens the blast radius of any single transaction; (4) consider READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT isolation, which removes most reader/writer blocking entirely via row versioning, at the cost of additional tempdb version-store overhead; (5) for cases where natural ordering genuinely can't be enforced, use sp_getapplock to serialize access explicitly. Before declaring any fix complete, capture an actual deadlock graph (via Extended Events' xml_deadlock_report) to confirm the real access pattern rather than guessing from symptoms.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the team, respectfully, that retrying is a band-aid, not a fix -- it just hides the real cost of the problem. First I'd pull an actual deadlock graph, not just the error count, because I want to see exactly which two statements and which two resources are colliding before I propose anything. Nine times out of ten it comes down to two code paths touching the same tables in opposite order, so step one is standardizing access order across every stored procedure that touches those tables. Step two is auditing transaction length -- anything that's validating data or doing unrelated reads inside the BEGIN/COMMIT boundary comes out. Then I look at whether lock escalation is widening the blast radius because of missing indexes, and only after that do I bring up snapshot isolation as a structural option, being upfront that it moves the cost into tempdb rather than eliminating it. I'd present this as 'here's the mechanism, here's the evidence, here's what actually gets the rate toward zero' rather than just 'add a try/catch and retry.'
commonMistakes: Treats retry logic as the fix instead of eliminating the cause
Doesn't look at actual access order across stored procedures
Ignores lock escalation thresholds on large updates
Assumes deadlocks are a bug SQL Server should prevent rather than a resolvable mutual-wait
Never captures an actual deadlock graph (XML) before proposing a fix
keyPoints: Defines deadlock as a circular wait on locks, not a generic error
Explains SQL Server's victim-selection mechanism
Identifies inconsistent access order as the most common root cause
Proposes shortening transactions and reviewing indexing to reduce lock footprint
Considers snapshot isolation as an architectural lever, with its tradeoff (tempdb/version store)
Recommends instrumentation (deadlock graph / extended events) before declaring a fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains deadlock mechanics and victim selection
Identifies root-cause patterns (access order, long transactions, lock escalation)
Proposes durable architectural fixes, not just retry logic
Addresses tradeoffs of snapshot isolation or other mitigations

questions.title: Reporting Queries Are Blocking the Nightly Order Pipeline
questions.prompt: Business users running ad-hoc reports against the live OLTP database during business hours are intermittently blocking order-entry transactions, and vice versa. Compare the architectural options -- read-committed snapshot isolation, a reporting replica, and query hints like NOLOCK -- and recommend what you'd actually implement, including what you give up.
questions.modelAnswer: Under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level, readers take shared locks and writers take exclusive locks, so reports and order-entry transactions genuinely contend for the same locks on the same rows, causing exactly this symptom. NOLOCK (or READ UNCOMMITTED) removes that blocking by skipping locking entirely, but it allows dirty reads, can double-count or miss rows during a page split, and is unacceptable for anything a finance or operations team relies on for correctness -- I would not recommend it as a general answer here. READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT (RCSI), enabled at the database level, gives readers a transactionally consistent versioned snapshot from tempdb's version store instead of taking shared locks, so reporting reads stop blocking writers and vice versa, with zero application code changes for ordinary SELECTs -- the cost is additional tempdb space and I/O for the version store, and a small per-row overhead on writers. A reporting replica (an Always On readable secondary, log shipping, or replication) solves a different, broader problem: it isolates the reporting workload's CPU and I/O consumption from the OLTP instance entirely, not just lock contention, at the cost of replication lag and additional infrastructure to maintain. My recommendation: enable RCSI first as the fast, low-risk fix for the specific symptom described (lock contention), and treat a readable secondary as the real architectural answer once the reporting workload itself starts consuming OLTP compute/I/O capacity, not just locks. The two aren't mutually exclusive -- a mature design often has both.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd separate this into two different problems that look the same from the outside: lock contention, and resource contention. For the immediate symptom -- reports and order entry fighting over row locks -- I'd recommend turning on read-committed snapshot isolation. It lets readers work off a versioned snapshot instead of taking shared locks, so the blocking just stops, and it needs no code changes. I'd be upfront that it's not free -- it adds load to tempdb's version store -- but that's a much safer tradeoff than reaching for NOLOCK, which I'd actually argue against here, because dirty reads on order data are a real correctness risk, not just a theoretical one. If the real issue turns out to be that reporting is also eating CPU and I/O the OLTP system needs, that's a different conversation -- that's when I'd bring in a readable secondary, because RCSI doesn't give you more hardware, it just removes lock contention. I'd frame it to the client as 'quick structural fix now, workload separation as the next step if reporting keeps growing.'
commonMistakes: Recommends NOLOCK as a general-purpose fix without flagging dirty-read risk
Doesn't distinguish lock contention from resource (CPU/IO) contention
Treats RCSI as free, ignoring tempdb version-store cost
Proposes a replica without acknowledging replication lag implications for 'real-time' reports
keyPoints: Explains why READ COMMITTED causes reader/writer blocking
Evaluates NOLOCK and correctly rejects it for anything requiring correctness
Explains RCSI's row-versioning mechanism and its tempdb cost
Recommends a readable secondary/replica as the durable architecture for resource isolation
Distinguishes lock contention from compute contention

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the locking behavior causing the blocking
Evaluates NOLOCK and its risks accurately
Explains RCSI/snapshot isolation mechanism and cost
Recommends and justifies an appropriate architecture (replica vs RCSI)

questions.title: A Stored Procedure Is Recompiling Constantly Under Load
questions.prompt: A heavily-used stored procedure builds a large intermediate result set using a table variable, then joins it twice more inside the same procedure. Under load, you're seeing wildly inconsistent execution times and plan cache bloat. Diagnose why the table variable choice is likely the architectural root cause at this scale, and rewrite the approach.
questions.modelAnswer: Table variables historically carry no real statistics -- on many compatibility levels the optimizer assumes roughly one row regardless of actual size -- so when the intermediate set is genuinely large, the optimizer builds a plan sized for one row: an undersized memory grant and a join strategy that's wrong for the real row count. The inconsistent timing comes from actual row counts varying run to run while the cached plan was compiled against that wrong, fixed assumption, so some executions get lucky and others spill to disk or pick a bad join type. A #temp table, by contrast, gets real statistics maintained by SQL Server, letting the optimizer size the plan for the two downstream joins accurately. The tradeoff: a significant change in a temp table's row count can trigger a recompile -- but that's a feature here, not a bug, since it means the plan adapts to actual data instead of staying wrong. The fix is to replace the DECLARE @T TABLE with a CREATE TABLE #T, optionally indexed if the joins warrant it, keeping the rest of the procedure's logic unchanged.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's happening here is that the optimizer doesn't have real numbers to work with. A table variable, on most compatibility levels, gets treated as roughly one row no matter how big it actually gets, so the plan built for it is sized for the wrong workload -- that's exactly why the timing is inconsistent: the actual row count varies, but the plan doesn't adapt. My fix is to swap it for a #temp table, because SQL Server maintains real statistics on those, so the two downstream joins get a plan that's actually shaped for the data. I'll be upfront that this trades one problem for a different, much smaller one -- a temp table can trigger a recompile when its row count shifts significantly -- but I'd rather have an occasional recompile that produces a correct plan than a stable plan that's confidently wrong every time.
questions.example:
-- Before: table variable, optimizer assumes ~1 row
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetRegionalSalesSummary
AS
BEGIN
    DECLARE @ActiveOrders TABLE (OrderID INT, CustomerID INT, Amount MONEY);
    INSERT INTO @ActiveOrders
    SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, Amount FROM dbo.Orders WHERE Status = 'Active';

    SELECT c.Region, SUM(a.Amount)
    FROM @ActiveOrders a
    JOIN dbo.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = a.CustomerID
    GROUP BY c.Region;
END
GO

-- After: temp table, real statistics, optionally indexed
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetRegionalSalesSummary
AS
BEGIN
    CREATE TABLE #ActiveOrders (OrderID INT, CustomerID INT, Amount MONEY);
    CREATE INDEX IX_ActiveOrders_CustomerID ON #ActiveOrders (CustomerID);

    INSERT INTO #ActiveOrders
    SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, Amount FROM dbo.Orders WHERE Status = 'Active';

    SELECT c.Region, SUM(a.Amount)
    FROM #ActiveOrders a
    JOIN dbo.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = a.CustomerID
    GROUP BY c.Region;
END
GO
commonMistakes: Treats 'table variables are always faster' as a universal rule
Doesn't connect inconsistent timing to missing statistics on a large table variable
Recommends a CTE instead, missing that a CTE is re-evaluated/inlined and doesn't solve the cardinality problem either
Adds an index to the table variable via inline constraint without recognizing its limits
Ignores the recompile tradeoff when switching to a temp table
keyPoints: Explains the statistics difference between table variables and temp tables
Connects missing statistics to bad cardinality estimation and inconsistent plans at scale
Chooses #temp table over table variable or CTE for this specific large, multiply-joined scenario
Provides a correct before/after rewrite
Acknowledges the recompile tradeoff as acceptable here

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses missing statistics as the root cause
Chooses the right replacement structure with justification
Provides correct, working SQL example
Acknowledges tradeoffs (recompilation) honestly

questions.title: Parameter Sniffing: One Cached Plan, Two Very Different Row Counts
questions.prompt: A stored procedure filters orders by @CustomerID. For a customer with a handful of orders it returns in milliseconds; for your biggest customer with several million rows, the exact same procedure call times out. Nothing about the query changed. Explain what's actually happening at the plan-cache level, and lay out the durable fixes you'd choose between, including the tradeoffs of each.
questions.modelAnswer: This is parameter sniffing: when a stored procedure compiles, SQL Server peeks at the actual parameter value supplied on that first call and builds one cached execution plan optimized for that value's estimated row count, then reuses that same plan for every subsequent call regardless of what parameter comes in next. If the plan was compiled against a small customer, the optimizer chose a plan shaped for a small result set -- likely nested loops with a lookup -- and that same plan is catastrophic against a customer with millions of rows, where a hash or merge join with a full scan would have been far cheaper. The symptom isn't random; it's entirely a function of which value happened to compile the plan, which is why it looks like it 'used to work.' Durable fixes, in order of how I'd actually choose: (1) OPTION (RECOMPILE) on the statement forces a fresh, value-specific plan on every execution -- correct for every call, but pays the compilation cost every single time, which is wasteful for a high-frequency procedure; (2) OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR @CustomerID UNKNOWN) tells the optimizer to use the average-distribution estimate instead of sniffing any single value, which avoids the worst-case outlier plan but may make the common case slightly less optimal; (3) WITH RECOMPILE at the procedure level has the same cost profile as per-statement recompile but applies to the whole procedure; (4) query store plan forcing lets you pin a known-good plan once you've identified one that performs acceptably across the real distribution of parameter values, which is a strong operational fix but needs monitoring since data growth can eventually make the forced plan wrong too; (5) splitting the procedure into two paths (a small-customer branch and a large-customer branch, chosen by an IF before the query even runs) avoids a single plan ever having to serve both distributions, at the cost of more code to maintain. I'd pick based on call frequency and skew: for a rarely-called heavy procedure, RECOMPILE is cheap enough; for a hot-path procedure called thousands of times a minute, OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN or query store plan forcing is usually the right call, because paying a full recompile on every call would itself become the bottleneck.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it the same way I'd explain it to the team that paged me: the procedure didn't change, the data behind one parameter value did, and the plan cache is still serving a plan that was shaped for a tiny customer. SQL Server only looks at the parameter value once, on the first compile, and then it's locked in until something invalidates that plan. So the fix isn't 'optimize the query' -- the query's fine -- it's deciding how we want the optimizer to handle that skew going forward. For something called rarely, I'd just slap OPTION (RECOMPILE) on it and move on, because paying for a fresh plan every call is cheap compared to how rarely it runs. For something hot, I don't want to recompile constantly, so I'd reach for OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN first, which tells the optimizer to plan for the average case instead of gambling on whichever value shows up first -- and if I need something more surgical, I'll go find a known-good plan and force it through Query Store, which I'll then keep an eye on, because a forced plan isn't a fix I set once and forget; the data keeps growing underneath it.
commonMistakes: Describes the symptom (it's slow for one customer) without naming the plan-cache mechanism causing it
Jumps straight to adding an index without addressing that a single cached plan is the root cause
Recommends OPTION (RECOMPILE) everywhere without weighing its per-call compilation cost on hot paths
Doesn't mention Query Store plan forcing as an operational option
Treats the fix as permanent without noting that data growth can make a forced or optimized-for plan wrong again later
keyPoints: Correctly explains that one parameter value's estimate shapes the cached plan for all future calls
Distinguishes RECOMPILE (per-call cost, always-correct plan) from OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN (average-case plan, no per-call cost)
Mentions Query Store plan forcing as a monitored, surgical fix
Considers call frequency and data skew when choosing between the options
Notes that any chosen fix needs to be revisited as data distribution changes over time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the parameter-sniffing / plan-cache mechanism
Presents multiple durable fixes (RECOMPILE, OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN, Query Store forcing, branching)
Weighs the real tradeoffs (per-call cost vs. plan quality) rather than naming one fix blindly
Chooses between fixes based on call frequency / skew, not a one-size-fits-all answer

questions.title: Cutting a $40K/Month Databricks Compute Bill Without Hurting SLAs
questions.prompt: Finance flags that Databricks compute spend has grown to roughly $40,000/month, and asks you, as the platform lead, to cut it meaningfully within a quarter without missing any existing SLA. A quick audit shows: most nightly ETL jobs run on long-lived all-purpose clusters that stay up all day 'just in case,' autoscaling is disabled almost everywhere, and a few ad hoc analyst notebooks are attached to the same large cluster as production jobs. Walk through where you'd cut first, what you would NOT touch, and how you'd verify savings didn't come at the cost of reliability.
questions.modelAnswer: The highest-impact, lowest-risk cut is moving scheduled ETL jobs off all-purpose clusters onto job clusters: an all-purpose cluster that stays up all day bills continuously regardless of utilization, while a job cluster spins up for the run and terminates on completion, so cost becomes proportional to actual compute time rather than wall-clock uptime -- this is almost always the single biggest lever in an audit like this one. Second, enable autoscaling with min/max bounds informed by historical load (not arbitrary defaults), so clusters stop paying for idle headroom sized for a worst-case that rarely occurs. Third, separate the ad hoc analyst notebooks onto their own interactive cluster with an auto-termination policy (e.g., terminate after 30-60 minutes idle), since sharing a cluster with production jobs means a runaway exploratory query can inflate the sizing production actually needs, or contend with it directly. Spot/preemptible instances are worth evaluating for fault-tolerant batch workloads where a preempted worker just gets replaced and retried, but I would explicitly exclude anything SLA-critical or stateful -- the fraud-alerting continuous pipeline's cluster, for example, should stay on-demand, because preemption risk there is a business risk, not a reliability inconvenience, and correctness/latency guarantees are not the place to shave compute cost. To verify savings are real and not masking a reliability regression, I'd tag every cluster by team/job for cost attribution, compare before/after DBU and cloud spend per workload, and specifically watch SLA-miss rate and job duration for two to three weeks post-change, since a change that looks fine under one week's load might not hold under a spike.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk finance through this as 'there's one obvious lever and three smaller ones, plus a line I won't cross.' The obvious lever: these ETL jobs don't need an all-purpose cluster sitting up all day, they need a job cluster that exists for the run and disappears -- that alone is usually most of the savings in a situation like this. The smaller levers are autoscaling with real bounds instead of none, and getting the analysts off the production cluster so their queries stop driving its sizing. The line I won't cross is the fraud-alerting pipeline's cluster -- I'd tell finance directly that's not a cost-cutting candidate, because a preempted spot instance there isn't an inconvenience, it's a missed fraud alert. And I wouldn't declare victory off one good week -- I'd watch SLA-miss rate for a few weeks before telling anyone the savings are safe.
commonMistakes: Suggests shrinking or spot-pricing a cluster backing an SLA-critical or stateful streaming workload
Treats autoscaling as a free win without setting sensible min/max bounds, causing scale-up thrashing
Doesn't separate ad hoc analyst workloads from production job clusters
Declares savings based on one day of lower cost without watching for SLA regressions over several weeks
Misses that all-purpose-vs-job-cluster billing is usually the single biggest lever available
keyPoints: Identifies all-purpose-vs-job-cluster mismatch as the primary cost driver
Enables autoscaling with bounds informed by historical load, not arbitrary defaults
Isolates ad hoc/analyst workloads from production clusters
Uses spot/preemptible instances selectively, excluding SLA-critical or stateful workloads
Verifies savings against SLA-miss rate over a meaningful window, not a single day

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies the highest-impact cost lever (job vs all-purpose clusters)
Correctly scopes where autoscaling/spot should and should not be used
Addresses workload isolation (ad hoc vs production)
Proposes a sound verification method against SLA risk

questions.title: RA3 Nodes and Managed Storage: What Actually Changed From DC2
questions.prompt: A client still running a DC2 Redshift cluster asks why you'd recommend migrating to RA3 nodes, beyond 'it's newer.' Explain what managed storage actually changes about how Redshift separates compute from storage, why that makes RA3 cheaper to scale for most workloads, and the one scenario where a DC2-style dense-compute design can still be the right call.
questions.modelAnswer: DC2 nodes are dense-compute: local SSD storage lives on the compute node itself, so scaling storage means scaling compute whether or not you need more of it, and resizing is a comparatively heavy operation. RA3 decouples the two: each node has high-performance local SSD used as a cache, but the durable copy of every block lives in a managed storage layer on S3, so storage scales independently and automatically, and compute nodes can be resized or paused without moving the actual data wholesale. This matters for cost because most real warehouses have an uneven storage-to-compute ratio over time -- data volume keeps growing while query concurrency doesn't grow at the same rate -- and RA3 lets you pay for the compute you need and the storage you actually hold, rather than over-provisioning compute just to get enough attached disk. RA3 also enables Redshift Spectrum and data sharing cleanly, since the managed storage layer is what those features read from underneath. The one case where I'd still consider a DC2-style dense-compute design is a workload that is genuinely both small in total data volume and extremely latency-sensitive on local I/O with a stable, low-growth footprint -- small enough that managed storage's slight indirection doesn't pay for itself and the simplicity of fully local storage is a real advantage. In practice today, new Redshift clusters should default to RA3 (or Redshift Serverless) unless there's a specific, measured reason not to, since AWS has been pushing DC2 toward end-of-life for new provisioning.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the client it's not just 'newer,' it's a different storage model. On DC2, your data lives on the compute node's own disk, so if you need more storage you're paying for more compute whether you wanted it or not, and resizing is a bigger operation. RA3 splits that apart -- compute nodes keep a fast local cache, but the real data sits in managed storage on S3, so storage and compute scale independently. For almost every client I've worked with, data grows faster than query concurrency does, so that split directly turns into lower cost over time. It also unlocks Spectrum and data sharing cleanly, since those both read off the same managed storage layer. The only time I'd keep someone on a dense-compute design is a genuinely small, stable, latency-sensitive workload where the extra simplicity of fully local disk is worth more than the flexibility -- and even then I'd want real numbers before making that case, not just instinct.
commonMistakes: Explains RA3 as simply 'faster hardware' rather than the storage/compute decoupling
Doesn't connect managed storage to why Spectrum and data sharing require RA3
Claims DC2 is categorically obsolete with no legitimate remaining use case
Ignores that resizing/scaling operations behave differently between the two node families
keyPoints: Explains managed storage as decoupling compute scaling from storage scaling
Connects the decoupling to typical cost savings as data grows faster than concurrency
Notes RA3's managed storage layer underpins Spectrum and data sharing
Identifies a legitimate, narrow scenario where dense compute can still make sense

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the managed storage vs. dense compute distinction
Connects the distinction to real cost/scaling behavior

questions.title: Redshift Spectrum vs. Data Sharing: Two Different Answers to 'Query Data Outside This Cluster'
questions.prompt: Two engineers on your team disagree: one wants to use Redshift Spectrum so the BI cluster can query raw files sitting in the data lake; the other wants to use Redshift data sharing so the BI cluster can query live tables that live inside a separate ML team's cluster. Explain why these solve genuinely different problems, and where someone would misuse one in place of the other.
questions.modelAnswer: Spectrum extends a Redshift cluster's query engine out to files that are not inside any Redshift cluster at all -- Parquet, ORC, or text files sitting in S3, typically cataloged via the Glue Data Catalog -- so a query can join native Redshift tables with external, lake-resident data without ever loading that data into the cluster. It is the right tool when the data's source of truth is the data lake, not a Redshift cluster, and you want to avoid duplicating or pre-loading it. Data sharing solves a different problem: it lets one Redshift cluster (or Redshift Serverless endpoint) grant another live, read-only, zero-copy access to specific databases, schemas, or tables that already live in managed storage inside the first cluster, without the usual step of exporting, copying, or re-ETLing the data into the consumer cluster. It is the right tool when the data's source of truth genuinely is another Redshift cluster, and you want a second workload (BI, ML, a different team's compute) to read it live without duplicating storage or waiting on a batch copy. The misuse pattern in each direction: using Spectrum to read what is actually another Redshift cluster's live table (by first exporting it to S3 as a workaround) adds unnecessary latency, staleness, and operational overhead that data sharing would eliminate directly; using data sharing to try to expose raw lake files is a non-starter, because the sharing feature operates on Redshift-resident objects, not on external Spectrum tables, treats them inconsistently, and isn't designed for governing lake-wide file access the way Lake Formation and Spectrum's external schema model already do. I'd tell the team: Spectrum answers 'how do I query the lake from Redshift,' data sharing answers 'how do I query another Redshift cluster's live data without copying it' -- they are complementary, and a mature multi-cluster architecture typically uses both for different edges of the same graph.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it for the team as two different boundaries being crossed. Spectrum crosses the boundary between Redshift's query engine and the data lake -- it's for when the real data lives as files in S3, cataloged in Glue, and you want to query it without loading it in. Data sharing crosses the boundary between two Redshift clusters -- it's for when the real data already lives inside another cluster's managed storage, and you want a second cluster to read it live, with no copy, no batch job, no staleness beyond normal consistency. The mistake I'd flag immediately is if anyone proposes exporting the ML team's live tables to S3 just so the BI cluster can Spectrum-query them -- that's solving a data-sharing problem with a Spectrum-shaped hammer, and it buys you staleness and extra pipeline maintenance you don't need when data sharing does exactly this natively. I'd tell both engineers they're both right about a different half of the architecture, not that one of them is wrong.
commonMistakes: Treats Spectrum and data sharing as interchangeable 'query data elsewhere' features
Proposes exporting a live Redshift table to S3 just to Spectrum-query it instead of using data sharing directly
Assumes data sharing can expose raw lake files the way Spectrum does
Doesn't identify where the actual source of truth for the data lives before recommending either feature
keyPoints: Explains Spectrum as querying lake files from inside Redshift via an external schema/Glue Catalog
Explains data sharing as zero-copy, live cross-cluster access to Redshift-resident data
Identifies the correct feature based on where the data's source of truth actually lives
Flags the misuse pattern of exporting live cluster data to S3 just to Spectrum-query it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what Spectrum does and when it's appropriate
Correctly explains what data sharing does and when it's appropriate
Identifies the misuse pattern in each direction
Frames the two as complementary rather than competing

questions.title: Lake Formation, Organizations, and SCPs: Where Each Layer of a Multi-Account Platform Actually Enforces Control
questions.prompt: A new platform architect on your team says 'we don't need Lake Formation, our Service Control Policies already lock down what each account can do.' Explain why that statement conflates two different layers of control, and where in a multi-account AWS data platform each of AWS Organizations/SCPs, cross-account IAM roles, and Lake Formation actually does its job.
questions.modelAnswer: SCPs, attached at the AWS Organizations level, are account-wide guardrails: they define the maximum permissions any principal in an account can ever have, regardless of what IAM policy is attached to them -- for example, denying any API call outside approved regions, or blocking the ability to disable CloudTrail. They operate above IAM and cannot grant access themselves, only restrict it; they have no concept of a table, a column, or a row. Cross-account IAM roles and resource policies are the next layer down: they decide whether a principal in Account B can assume a role or call an API against a resource in Account A at all -- a coarse, account- and resource-ARN-level boundary. Neither of those layers has any idea what a 'table' or a 'database' is in the sense a data lake cares about; they stop at the AWS resource (a bucket, a role, an API action). Lake Formation sits on top of both and adds the layer that's actually missing: fine-grained, catalog-aware permissions -- grant this specific IAM principal or cross-account consumer SELECT on these specific columns of this specific table, without having to carve the data into separate S3 prefixes with separate bucket policies to achieve the same effect. So the new architect's statement is wrong in a specific, costly way: SCPs can stop someone from calling an API they shouldn't, but they cannot grant a data scientist in a consuming account read access to three columns of a shared customer table while hiding a PII column from them -- only Lake Formation's column/row-level grants do that cleanly, without duplicating data or writing ad hoc bucket-policy logic that becomes unmaintainable past a handful of tables. A correct multi-account data platform uses all three layers together: SCPs as the account-wide ceiling, cross-account IAM/resource policies as the account-to-account door, and Lake Formation as the fine-grained, catalog-level lock on what's actually visible once you're through that door.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct that gently but directly, because it's a common and costly misunderstanding. SCPs answer the question 'what is this account even allowed to do, no matter what IAM says' -- they're a ceiling, not a grant, and they have zero concept of tables or columns. Cross-account IAM roles answer 'can a principal in another account get into this account's resources at all.' Neither of those gets you to 'can this specific analyst see these three columns of this table but not that PII column over there' -- that's a data-catalog-level permission, and SCPs and account-level IAM simply don't operate at that granularity. That's exactly the gap Lake Formation fills. I'd tell the architect: keep the SCPs, they're doing real work as your outer guardrail, but if we try to implement column-level and row-level data governance using only SCPs and bucket policies, we'll end up hand-rolling dozens of S3 prefixes and policies that Lake Formation already solves natively, and that hand-rolled version will be harder to audit and harder to change six months from now.
commonMistakes: Treats SCPs as capable of fine-grained, table/column-level data permissions
Confuses account-level guardrails with catalog-level data governance
Proposes replacing Lake Formation with ad hoc S3 prefix/bucket-policy separation at the column level
Doesn't explain that SCPs only restrict, never grant, permissions
keyPoints: Explains SCPs as an account-wide ceiling with no concept of tables/columns
Explains cross-account IAM/resource policies as the account-to-account access door
Explains Lake Formation as the fine-grained, catalog-aware permission layer on top of both
Shows how all three layers work together rather than one replacing another

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the role and limits of SCPs
Correctly explains cross-account IAM/resource policy's role
Correctly explains what Lake Formation adds and why it's needed
Frames the layers as complementary, not redundant

questions.title: EMR Serverless vs. an EMR Cluster on EC2: Picking the Right One for a New Spark Workload
questions.prompt: A team is standing up a new nightly Spark job and asks whether to run it on EMR Serverless or a traditional EMR cluster on EC2. Explain the actual architectural difference between the two, not just 'serverless is easier,' and give a decision rule based on workload shape.
questions.modelAnswer: An EMR cluster on EC2 gives you a persistent (or job-scoped transient) set of EC2 instances you provision, size, and configure yourself -- instance types, core/task node counts, bootstrap actions, and cluster-level configuration are all under your control, which matters when a workload needs a specific instance family, custom AMI, non-Spark frameworks (Hive, Presto, HBase) in the same cluster, or very fine-grained tuning of YARN/Spark configuration. EMR Serverless removes the cluster entirely: you submit a Spark or Hive job to an 'application' and AWS provisions and scales the underlying workers automatically per job, billing per vCPU-second and GB-second of actual usage with no idle cluster to manage, pause, or forget to terminate. The real decision rule isn't 'easier vs. harder,' it's workload shape and predictability: a workload with spiky, infrequent, or highly variable resource needs (a nightly job that sometimes processes 10GB and sometimes 10TB) benefits from Serverless because you're not paying for a cluster sized for the worst case sitting idle the rest of the time, and there's no risk of someone forgetting to terminate it. A workload that's large, steady-state, long-running, or needs non-Spark/Hive engines, deep YARN-level tuning, custom bootstrap scripts, or very specific instance types (e.g., GPU instances for a particular ML step) is usually better on a traditional EMR cluster, because Serverless intentionally trades some configurability for operational simplicity. I'd also flag that Serverless has a cold-start cost on the first job submission to a new application and some ceiling on configuration flexibility, so a latency-sensitive workload needs that evaluated explicitly, not assumed away.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on framing this as 'serverless is just easier' and instead ask what the workload actually looks like. If this nightly job's data volume swings wildly night to night, or it's new and nobody's sure yet how big it'll get, I'd put it on EMR Serverless, because you're not stuck sizing a cluster for a worst case that might not even be representative, and there's zero risk of someone leaving a cluster running over the weekend. If instead this job needs a specific instance type, deep YARN tuning, or needs to coexist with Hive or Presto workloads on the same cluster, I'd go with a traditional EMR cluster, because Serverless deliberately gives up some of that configurability in exchange for not having to manage infrastructure. I'd also flag the cold-start behavior on Serverless so nobody's surprised if the very first run of the day is a bit slower than subsequent ones.
commonMistakes: Frames the choice purely as 'serverless is easier' without discussing workload shape
Doesn't mention Serverless's configuration/tuning tradeoffs vs. a traditional cluster
Ignores non-Spark engine requirements (Hive, Presto, HBase) as a reason to stay on EC2-based EMR
Doesn't account for cold-start latency when recommending Serverless for a latency-sensitive job
keyPoints: Explains the architectural difference: self-managed cluster vs. per-job auto-provisioned workers
Gives a decision rule based on workload variability and predictability, not ease of use alone
Identifies cases (custom instance types, non-Spark engines, deep tuning) favoring a traditional cluster
Notes Serverless's cold-start and configurability tradeoffs honestly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the architectural distinction between the two
Gives a sound, workload-shape-based decision rule
Identifies legitimate cases favoring a traditional EMR cluster
Notes real tradeoffs (cold start, configurability) honestly

questions.title: Kinesis Shards: Why Resharding Doesn't Happen Automatically and What You're Actually Changing
questions.prompt: A teammate assumed Kinesis Data Streams autoscales the way Lambda does, and is confused why their stream is throttling under higher load. Explain shard-level throughput limits, why resharding is a manual (or explicitly automated) operation rather than transparent autoscaling, and what actually happens to hash-key ranges and consumers during a reshard.
questions.modelAnswer: Each Kinesis shard has fixed throughput limits -- 1MB/sec or 1000 records/sec in, 2MB/sec out -- and those limits are per shard, not per stream, so a stream's total capacity is simply the number of shards multiplied by those per-shard limits. Unlike Lambda concurrency, which AWS scales transparently within account limits, a provisioned Kinesis stream's shard count does not change by itself under load; On-Demand mode will autoscale, but a provisioned-mode stream throttling under load means it's stuck at a fixed shard count until something explicitly reshards it, whether that's a manual UpdateShardCount call, a scheduled scaling policy, or switching the stream to On-Demand mode. Resharding itself isn't just adding capacity -- it's changing the partition of the hash-key space: a split takes one shard's hash-key range and divides it into two child shards' ranges, while a merge combines two adjacent shards' ranges into one. Existing records already in the parent shard(s) remain there and age out per the retention period, while new records are routed to the new child shards based on their partition key's hash; consumers using the Kinesis Client Library handle this transparently by discovering the new shard lineage and following parent-to-child relationships so no records are skipped or duplicated, but a hand-rolled consumer that doesn't walk that lineage can miss the transition. The deeper trap for anyone coming from Lambda's mental model: resharding doesn't happen in response to current throttling automatically in provisioned mode, so a traffic spike causes real, visible failures (ProvisionedThroughputExceededException) before anyone manually or programmatically reshards -- it's capacity planning, not elastic autoscaling, unless you've specifically adopted On-Demand mode or wired up Application Auto Scaling for Kinesis.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by correcting the mental model directly: Kinesis in provisioned mode is not like Lambda, it doesn't quietly grow to meet load. Each shard has a hard throughput ceiling, and if you're throttling, you're simply out of shards for the traffic you're sending. Getting more capacity means an explicit reshard -- either a manual UpdateShardCount call, a scheduled policy, or moving the stream to On-Demand mode, which does autoscale for you. I'd also flag that resharding isn't just 'add more' -- a split actually divides one shard's hash-key range into two, so if anyone wrote a custom consumer instead of using the Kinesis Client Library, they need to make sure it correctly follows the parent-to-child shard lineage after a reshard, or they'll quietly miss or duplicate records during the transition. For this specific throttling issue, my first move is to check whether they're on provisioned or on-demand, and if provisioned, just reshard or move to on-demand rather than waiting for something that was never going to happen on its own.
commonMistakes: Assumes provisioned-mode Kinesis autoscales shard count the way Lambda scales concurrency
Doesn't explain that throughput limits are per-shard, not per-stream
Describes resharding as just 'adding capacity' without explaining the hash-key range split/merge mechanics
Doesn't address what happens to a custom (non-KCL) consumer during a reshard
keyPoints: Explains per-shard throughput limits and how total stream capacity derives from them
Clarifies that provisioned-mode Kinesis does not autoscale like Lambda; On-Demand mode does
Explains the hash-key range split/merge mechanics of resharding
Addresses how KCL-based vs. custom consumers handle the shard lineage transition

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains per-shard throughput limits
Correctly contrasts provisioned vs. on-demand scaling behavior
Explains the hash-key range mechanics of a reshard accurately
Addresses consumer-side handling of the shard lineage transition

questions.title: Kinesis Data Analytics / Managed Flink: What It Actually Adds Over Consuming the Stream Yourself
questions.prompt: A teammate asks why they'd use Kinesis Data Analytics (Managed Service for Apache Flink) instead of just writing a Lambda function triggered off the stream to do the same aggregation. Explain what capability gap Managed Flink actually fills for real-time analytics, and when the Lambda approach is genuinely sufficient instead.
questions.modelAnswer: A Lambda function triggered off a Kinesis stream processes each incoming batch of records statelessly (or with whatever state it manually persists to an external store), which works well for per-record or per-batch transformations, enrichment, and routing, but it does not natively give you windowed, stateful streaming computation -- a 5-minute tumbling-window sum, a sliding-window average, or a session window keyed by user, each correctly handling late or out-of-order records and maintaining running state across many batches, is not something Lambda's invocation model is built for; you'd end up hand-rolling state management against something like DynamoDB and re-implementing windowing and watermark logic yourself, which is exactly the class of problem stream-processing engines exist to solve correctly. Managed Service for Apache Flink runs real Flink (or lets you write SQL against the stream) with built-in windowing, event-time semantics, watermarks for out-of-order data, and durable, checkpointed state, managed by AWS so you don't operate the Flink cluster yourself -- that's the actual capability gap it closes: genuine stateful, time-windowed streaming analytics with correctness guarantees under out-of-order and late-arriving data, not just 'processing records as they arrive.' The Lambda approach is genuinely sufficient when the use case is actually stateless or only needs trivial, short-lived state: filtering, enrichment, format conversion, fan-out routing to multiple destinations, or triggering a downstream action per event -- anything where you don't need a correct notion of 'this window's aggregate' across time. I'd recommend Managed Flink specifically when the business ask involves words like 'rolling average,' 'last 5 minutes,' or 'session,' and Lambda (or Firehose with a transform) for everything else, since standing up Flink for a problem that didn't need windowing is unnecessary operational and cost overhead.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask what the aggregation actually needs to remember. If it's stateless -- reshape this record, filter that one, fan it out to three places -- Lambda off the stream is the right, simple answer and reaching for Flink would be overkill. But the moment the ask is something like 'rolling 5-minute average' or 'detect when a user does X and then Y within 2 minutes,' that's genuinely stateful, windowed computation, and Lambda's invocation model doesn't give you correct windowing or event-time handling out of the box -- you'd be reinventing watermarks and checkpointed state badly, by hand, against DynamoDB. That's exactly what Managed Flink is built to do correctly and durably, without us operating a Flink cluster ourselves. So my answer isn't 'always use Flink' or 'always use Lambda' -- it's: does this need a real window and real state over time? If yes, Flink. If no, Lambda is simpler and cheaper.
commonMistakes: Recommends Managed Flink for simple stateless transformations where Lambda is sufficient
Doesn't name the specific capability gap (windowing, event-time, checkpointed state) Lambda lacks
Assumes Lambda can trivially replicate windowed aggregation without acknowledging the hand-rolled state management involved
Treats the choice as about throughput rather than about statefulness/windowing semantics
keyPoints: Identifies windowed, stateful, event-time-aware processing as Managed Flink's real value
Explains why Lambda's model struggles with correct windowing/out-of-order handling
Gives a clear decision rule based on whether the use case needs state over time
Avoids recommending Flink for workloads that are genuinely stateless

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the capability gap Managed Flink closes
Explains why Lambda alone struggles with windowed/stateful aggregation
Gives a clear, correct decision rule for when each is appropriate
Avoids over-recommending Flink for simple stateless cases

questions.title: Step Functions Standard vs. Express: Choosing the Right Workflow Type for a Platform-Wide Orchestrator
questions.prompt: You're designing a single Step Functions-based orchestrator that triggers Glue jobs, Lambda functions, and EMR steps across many teams' pipelines. Explain the practical difference between Standard and Express workflows, and which you'd choose for this platform-wide orchestrator versus a short, high-volume per-event enrichment workflow.
questions.modelAnswer: Standard workflows are built for durability and long-running execution: they can run for up to a year, every state transition is logged and individually priced, execution history is retained and fully queryable after the fact (useful for auditing exactly what happened and when in a complex multi-step pipeline), and they guarantee exactly-once execution semantics for each state. Express workflows are built for high-volume, short-duration execution: they run for at most five minutes, are priced by number of invocations and duration rather than per-state-transition, and provide at-least-once semantics, meaning a state could in rare cases execute more than once, which matters if any step isn't idempotent. For the platform-wide orchestrator described -- triggering Glue jobs (which can run for tens of minutes to hours) and EMR steps across many teams, where you want full execution history for debugging 'why did Team B's pipeline fail last Tuesday at 2am' and exactly-once guarantees matter because retrying a Glue job inappropriately could duplicate loaded data -- Standard is clearly the right choice: the cost-per-transition pricing is a non-issue for this volume and duration profile, and the durability/history guarantees are exactly what a shared, cross-team orchestration backbone needs. For a short, high-volume per-event enrichment workflow (e.g., invoked once per incoming record or API call, completing in seconds, run potentially millions of times a day), Express is the right choice, because Standard's per-transition pricing would be far more expensive at that invocation volume, and the five-minute runtime ceiling and at-least-once semantics are both acceptable given the workflow's short, largely idempotent nature. Choosing Standard for the high-volume case or Express for the long-running case are both real mistakes I'd flag in a review: the first burns unnecessary cost, the second simply won't work once any step exceeds five minutes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd pick Standard for the platform-wide orchestrator without much hesitation, because what that workflow actually needs is durability and a trustworthy audit trail -- these are Glue jobs and EMR steps that can run for a long time, and when something breaks at 2am, I want full execution history I can actually query, plus the exactly-once guarantee so a retry doesn't double-load data. Standard's per-transition pricing isn't a concern at this volume. For a different kind of workflow -- something short and invoked a huge number of times per day, like per-event enrichment -- I'd flip to Express, because Standard's per-transition cost would add up fast at that invocation volume, and a five-minute ceiling with at-least-once semantics is a totally acceptable tradeoff for something quick and largely idempotent. The mistake I'd call out in either direction: putting a long-running Glue/EMR pipeline on Express would just break once a step runs past five minutes, and putting a tiny, high-volume enrichment workflow on Standard would work fine functionally but quietly cost a lot more than it needs to.
commonMistakes: Doesn't mention the five-minute execution ceiling as a hard constraint for Express
Doesn't address exactly-once (Standard) vs. at-least-once (Express) semantics and their implications for idempotency
Picks Express for the long-running multi-team orchestrator, ignoring the runtime ceiling
Picks Standard for the high-volume short workflow without considering the cost implications of per-transition pricing at scale
keyPoints: Correctly explains Standard's durability, execution history, and exactly-once semantics
Correctly explains Express's short duration ceiling, at-least-once semantics, and volume-based pricing
Recommends Standard for the long-running, cross-team orchestrator with sound reasoning
Recommends Express for the short, high-volume workflow with sound reasoning

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the Standard vs. Express distinction
Correctly recommends Standard for the orchestrator scenario with justification
Correctly recommends Express for the high-volume scenario with justification
Flags the concrete failure/cost mode of choosing the wrong type

questions.title: Glue Job Bookmarks Across Thousands of Jobs: Where the Model Breaks Down at Scale
questions.prompt: Job bookmarks work cleanly for a handful of Glue jobs reading from S3 or JDBC sources. Explain exactly what state a bookmark tracks, and describe two specific ways the bookmark model breaks down once an organization has thousands of Glue jobs sharing sources, transformation logic, or schedules -- and how you'd design around each.
questions.modelAnswer: A Glue job bookmark persists, per job (not per source), the state of what's already been processed -- for an S3 source, the set of files/objects (and their timestamps) already read; for a JDBC source, the maximum value of a specified bookmark column already extracted -- so that the next run of that same job only processes new data, provided the job calls job.init() and job.commit() correctly and the transformation context stays consistent. At thousands-of-jobs scale, two specific failure modes show up repeatedly. First, bookmark state is tied to the job's own identity and transformation context, so renaming a job, significantly restructuring its script (changing the DynamicFrame's underlying transformation context signature), or splitting one job into two accidentally orphans the existing bookmark state -- the new/renamed job starts from scratch and reprocesses everything, which at scale means a sudden, expensive full-reprocess across one slice of the platform with no error raised to warn anyone; the fix is operational discipline -- treat job identity and transformation-context-affecting script changes as a breaking change requiring an explicit bookmark reset-and-backfill plan, documented and reviewed, rather than an incidental refactor. Second, when many jobs read from the same shared source (a common upstream table or S3 prefix) with their own independent bookmarks, there's no cross-job coordination -- each job tracks its own 'already processed' state independently, so a source-side change (a backfill, a reprocessing of old files with updated timestamps, a schema change) can cause inconsistent bookmark behavior across jobs: some jobs correctly skip the backfilled data as 'already seen,' others might pick it up depending on subtle timing, and there's no single place to see 'which jobs have bookmarked past this point and which haven't' without checking each job individually; the fix is to maintain an explicit, centralized processing-state table (e.g., in DynamoDB or a Glue job run metadata catalog) alongside bookmarks for anything shared across many jobs, so cross-job consistency is explicit and auditable rather than inferred from thousands of independent, opaque bookmark states.
questions.professionalAnswer: A bookmark is really just 'what did this specific job already see,' tracked per job -- for S3 that's processed file/object state, for JDBC it's the max value of a column you pick. At small scale that's invisible and just works. At thousands-of-jobs scale, two things bite people. First: bookmark state is attached to the job's identity and its transformation context, so an innocent-looking rename or script refactor can silently orphan the bookmark and trigger a full reprocess nobody budgeted for -- I treat any job rename or structural script change as something that needs an explicit bookmark plan, not a casual Tuesday refactor. Second: when a hundred jobs all read the same upstream source independently, their bookmarks have zero awareness of each other, so a backfill on that source can leave some jobs correctly skipping it and others not, with no single dashboard telling you who's where. For anything shared at that scale, I stop trusting bookmarks alone and add an explicit, centralized processing-state table so cross-job consistency is something I can actually query and audit, not something I'm inferring from a pile of independent bookmark states.
commonMistakes: Doesn't explain that bookmark state is per-job and tied to transformation context/job identity
Doesn't identify job renames or script refactors as a bookmark-orphaning risk
Assumes bookmarks naturally coordinate across many jobs sharing a source
Proposes disabling bookmarks platform-wide instead of designing explicit coordination for shared sources
keyPoints: Correctly explains what state a bookmark actually tracks and how it's keyed
Identifies job identity/script-refactor risk to bookmark continuity, with a mitigation
Identifies lack of cross-job coordination on shared sources, with a mitigation (centralized state table)
Proposes concrete, scale-appropriate designs rather than abstract warnings

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains bookmark state and keying
Identifies the job-identity/refactor failure mode with a sound fix
Identifies the cross-job coordination failure mode with a sound fix
Solutions are concrete and scale-appropriate

questions.title: Glue Data Quality Rules vs. Hand-Written Validation Logic
questions.prompt: A team currently validates incoming data with hand-written PySpark assertions scattered across their Glue ETL scripts. Explain what AWS Glue Data Quality (and its DQDL rule language) adds structurally over that approach, and one limitation you'd flag before recommending a full migration.
questions.modelAnswer: Hand-written PySpark assertions scattered through transformation scripts have a structural problem independent of whether the checks themselves are correct: the rules are invisible outside the code, not centrally reviewable, not reusable across jobs, and failures typically either crash the job (if raised as an exception) or get silently logged in a way nobody is actually watching, with no standard way to see quality trends over time across many jobs. Glue Data Quality externalizes this: rules are declared in DQDL (Data Quality Definition Language), a readable, structured rule syntax that's attached to a dataset/ruleset rather than buried inside transformation logic, which means the same ruleset can be reused across jobs reading the same table, reviewed by someone who isn't a PySpark engineer, and run as an explicit step whose pass/fail and specific rule-level results are captured as structured output (including a data quality score) that can feed a dashboard, trigger an alert, or gate a downstream step via the job's control flow -- rather than being an implicit side effect of custom code. This is a real structural improvement: it turns data quality from 'code review has to catch broken validation logic buried in a 500-line script' into 'read the ruleset, see the pass/fail history, see which specific rule and which rows failed.' The limitation I'd flag before a full migration: DQDL's rule library, while broad, doesn't cover every arbitrarily complex, business-specific validation a hand-written assertion can express -- a rule that depends on a multi-table join, an external reference lookup, or genuinely bespoke business logic may need to stay as custom code (or be expressed as a custom DQDL rule set with analyzer-based rules where supported), so I'd plan for a hybrid state rather than promising to eliminate 100% of hand-written validation, and I'd migrate the common, reusable checks (null rates, uniqueness, value ranges, referential patterns) first since those carry the most benefit from being externalized.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest pitch to the team is: your validation logic isn't necessarily wrong, it's just invisible. It's buried in PySpark, not reviewable by anyone who isn't deep in that script, and when it fails, it either crashes the job or quietly logs something nobody's watching. Glue Data Quality's real value is making that logic a first-class, declared thing -- a DQDL ruleset attached to the dataset, reusable across every job reading that table, with structured pass/fail results and a quality score you can actually dashboard and alert on. That's the difference between 'we have validation' and 'we can see our validation.' The one thing I wouldn't oversell: some of your bespoke, multi-table business logic probably won't translate cleanly into DQDL's rule set, so I'd plan on migrating the common, high-value checks first -- nulls, uniqueness, ranges, referential patterns -- and accept that a slice of custom validation logic may need to stay as code for a while rather than promising a clean, total migration.
commonMistakes: Describes Glue Data Quality purely as 'built-in checks' without explaining the structural/visibility benefit over scattered code
Doesn't mention that results are structured and can gate downstream steps or feed dashboards
Oversells DQDL as able to express every possible validation rule a hand-written script can
Recommends a wholesale migration with no acknowledgment of a hybrid transition period
keyPoints: Identifies the structural problem with scattered hand-written validation (invisibility, non-reusability)
Explains DQDL rulesets as externalized, reusable, reviewable, and structured in their output
Connects structured output to dashboards/alerting/control-flow gating
Honestly flags a limitation and recommends a hybrid/phased migration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the structural problem with scattered custom validation
Correctly explains what Glue Data Quality/DQDL adds
Flags a genuine, specific limitation
Proposes a sensible phased/hybrid migration approach

questions.title: DMS for a Large-Scale Heterogeneous Migration: What Full Load + CDC Actually Guarantees
questions.prompt: Leadership wants to migrate a 2TB on-prem Oracle database to Aurora PostgreSQL with 'zero data loss and minimal downtime' using DMS. Explain exactly what DMS's full-load-plus-CDC approach guarantees, what it does not handle automatically, and the one step most teams skip that causes a painful post-migration surprise.
questions.modelAnswer: DMS's standard pattern for a large, low-downtime migration is: run a full load of the existing data while simultaneously capturing ongoing changes via CDC (reading the source's transaction/redo logs) into a buffer, then apply the buffered changes after the full load completes to catch the target up to near-real-time, after which CDC continues streaming ongoing changes until a cutover is performed. This genuinely minimizes downtime -- the source stays live and serving traffic through nearly the entire migration -- and gives you a target that's continuously converging toward current, but it does not, by itself, guarantee zero data loss or full semantic equivalence: DMS replicates data and row-level changes, not everything that defines a schema's behavior. It does not automatically migrate or recreate secondary indexes beyond primary keys in every engine combination, does not translate stored procedures, triggers, views, sequences, or custom functions (the AWS Schema Conversion Tool handles some of this for schema/code conversion, separately from DMS's data replication), and heterogeneous migrations (Oracle to PostgreSQL here) involve real data type and behavior differences -- Oracle's NUMBER vs. PostgreSQL's numeric types, sequence/identity behavior, case-sensitivity differences in object names, and date/time handling edge cases -- that need explicit mapping and validation, not an assumption that DMS 'just handles it.' The step most teams skip is a rigorous data validation pass post-migration beyond row counts matching: DMS has a built-in data validation feature that can compare source and target row-by-row, but even that doesn't catch application-level semantic breakage from untranslated stored procedures or subtly different type coercion behavior, so a team needs an explicit application-level validation and regression-testing plan against the migrated target before cutover, not just 'the row counts match, ship it.' I'd set leadership's expectation precisely: DMS gets us low-downtime, converging data replication; it does not, on its own, get us a semantically identical database, and we need a separate, deliberate validation phase to actually claim zero data loss with confidence.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be careful with the phrase 'zero data loss' here, because DMS's full-load-plus-CDC pattern genuinely gets you low downtime and a target that keeps converging toward current, but it replicates rows and changes, not the whole database's behavior. Things like stored procedures, triggers, views, and sequences don't come along for free -- that's a schema/code conversion problem, which is a different tool and a different workstream from DMS's actual job. And going Oracle to PostgreSQL is heterogeneous, so there are real type and behavior differences that need explicit handling, not an assumption DMS smooths over automatically. The step I see teams skip constantly: checking that row counts match and calling it done. DMS does have a real row-by-row validation feature, and I'd turn that on, but even that won't catch an untranslated stored procedure quietly producing wrong results downstream. My actual deliverable to leadership isn't 'DMS migrated it,' it's 'DMS replicated the data with low downtime, and here's the separate validation and regression-testing plan that lets us actually claim correctness before we cut over.'
commonMistakes: Promises 'zero data loss' as an automatic property of DMS's full-load-plus-CDC pattern
Assumes DMS migrates stored procedures, triggers, views, or sequences automatically
Doesn't account for heterogeneous (cross-engine) data type/behavior differences
Treats matching row counts as sufficient validation without application-level regression testing
keyPoints: Correctly explains the full-load-plus-CDC mechanism and its low-downtime benefit
Correctly identifies what DMS does not migrate (stored procs, triggers, views, sequences)
Flags heterogeneous type/behavior differences needing explicit handling
Identifies the skipped step: rigorous validation beyond row-count matching

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the full-load-plus-CDC mechanism
Correctly identifies what DMS does not handle automatically
Addresses heterogeneous migration-specific risks
Identifies the commonly-skipped validation step with specificity
