questions.title: Savings Plans vs. Reserved Instances vs. Spot for an AWS Data Platform's Compute Spend
questions.prompt: Finance asks you to explain, in plain terms, the real tradeoffs between Compute Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, and Spot Instances for an AWS data platform running a mix of steady-state Redshift/EMR clusters and bursty batch jobs, and to recommend a blended strategy.
questions.modelAnswer: Reserved Instances are a commitment to a specific instance family/size in a specific region (or, with convertible RIs, some flexibility to change the instance type) for a 1- or 3-year term, in exchange for a meaningful discount versus on-demand -- they're the right fit when you know, with confidence, that a specific workload's instance type and size will stay steady for the commitment period, such as a Redshift cluster sized for a stable reporting workload. Compute Savings Plans are a commitment to a dollar-per-hour amount of compute usage (measured in $/hour) rather than a specific instance type, applying automatically across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda regardless of instance family, size, OS, or region, which trades a small amount of discount depth versus a matched RI for much greater flexibility as the platform's actual instance mix shifts over time -- this is usually the better default for a platform where workloads are expected to evolve, since locking into a specific RI'd instance type ahead of refactoring work is a real risk. Spot Instances offer the deepest discount (up to ~90% off on-demand) in exchange for the explicit risk of interruption with a two-minute warning, which is only appropriate for fault-tolerant, interruption-tolerant, typically stateless or checkpointed batch workloads -- a bursty EMR Spark job that can lose a worker and simply retry that task is a strong Spot candidate; a stateful streaming job or an SLA-critical Redshift query layer is not. For this platform's mix, I'd recommend: Compute Savings Plans sized to the platform's baseline, steady-state compute usage (not 100% of it -- leaving some headroom avoids overcommitting to a number that could shrink), since that baseline is real and flexible coverage is more valuable than squeezing out the last few points of discount; Spot for the bursty, fault-tolerant batch/EMR workloads specifically, with Spot Fleet diversification across instance types to reduce interruption risk; and on-demand (or RIs only if a specific workload's instance type is genuinely locked in for years) for the remainder. I would not recommend RIs as the default commitment vehicle here, specifically because this platform's workload mix is described as mixed and evolving, which is exactly the scenario Savings Plans' flexibility is designed for.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it to finance with an analogy: Reserved Instances are like pre-paying for a specific apartment for three years -- great discount, but you're locked into that exact unit. Savings Plans are like pre-paying a monthly budget for 'a place to live' that flexes across any apartment in the building -- slightly less discount, much more flexibility as your needs change. Spot is like a hotel room that might get reassigned out from under you with two minutes' notice, at a steep discount, which is fine if you don't actually care which room you're in and can just move. Given this platform has a steady baseline plus bursty batch work, my recommendation is: cover the steady baseline with Savings Plans, not RIs, because I expect the instance mix to keep evolving and I don't want to lock in a specific instance type I'll regret in a year. Put the bursty, fault-tolerant EMR/batch work on Spot, diversified across instance types so one interruption wave doesn't take out the whole job. And I'd deliberately not cover 100% of the baseline with Savings Plans -- some headroom protects us if the baseline shrinks, and on-demand coverage of that sliver is a small, acceptable cost for not overcommitting.
commonMistakes: Recommends Reserved Instances as the default for a workload mix described as evolving
Doesn't distinguish Savings Plans' flexibility (any instance family/service) from RIs' instance-type lock-in
Recommends Spot for stateful or SLA-critical workloads without flagging interruption risk
Recommends covering 100% of baseline usage with commitment-based pricing, with no headroom
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes Reserved Instances' instance-type lock-in from Savings Plans' flexible, dollar-based commitment
Correctly scopes Spot to fault-tolerant, interruption-tolerant workloads only
Recommends Savings Plans for the steady baseline given an evolving workload mix
Recommends leaving deliberate headroom rather than committing 100% of baseline usage

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains RIs vs. Savings Plans vs. Spot mechanics and tradeoffs
Correctly scopes Spot usage to appropriate workloads only
Recommends a sound blended strategy for this specific workload mix
Addresses commitment headroom/risk sensibly

questions.title: KMS Key Strategy for a Multi-Account Data Platform: Customer-Managed Keys and Cross-Account Grants
questions.prompt: A platform spanning five AWS accounts needs a consistent encryption-at-rest strategy for S3, Redshift, and Glue job outputs, with some data shared across accounts. Explain why you'd choose customer-managed KMS keys over AWS-managed keys for this platform, and how cross-account access to KMS-encrypted data is actually granted -- walk through the two-sided permission model.
questions.modelAnswer: AWS-managed keys (the aws/s3, aws/redshift default keys) are free, zero-maintenance, and fine for a single-account workload with no cross-account sharing requirement, but they come with real limits for a multi-account platform: you cannot view or modify their key policy, cannot enable cross-account grants on them, cannot control their rotation schedule precisely, and cannot use them for cross-account key sharing at all -- which immediately rules them out the moment any data needs to be shared, decrypted, or re-encrypted across accounts. Customer-managed keys (CMKs) give you a key policy you fully control, the ability to grant specific external principals (including principals in other accounts) permission to use the key for encrypt/decrypt operations, auditable CloudTrail logging of every key usage, and control over rotation and deletion -- which is the baseline requirement for any platform where Account B needs to read an object Account A encrypted. Cross-account access to KMS-encrypted data requires permission on both sides, not just one: the key's own key policy must explicitly allow the external account (or a specific role/principal in it) to use the key for the relevant actions (kms:Decrypt, kms:GenerateDataKey, etc.), AND the consuming principal in the other account needs an IAM policy in its own account granting it permission to call those same KMS actions against that specific key's ARN -- missing either side results in an access-denied error that looks identical regardless of which side is missing, which is a common debugging trap. For S3 specifically, the bucket policy or object ACL granting cross-account S3 access is a separate, additional layer on top of the KMS grant -- having S3 access without the matching KMS permission (or vice versa) still fails, since decrypting a KMS-encrypted object requires both the S3 read permission and the KMS decrypt permission to succeed. My recommendation for this platform: one or a small number of purpose-scoped CMKs per data classification tier (not one single platform-wide key, to limit blast radius and allow differentiated rotation/access policies), with explicit, reviewed key policies granting only the specific cross-account roles that genuinely need access, following least privilege rather than a broad cross-account wildcard grant.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd rule out AWS-managed keys immediately for this platform, not because they're bad, but because they simply can't do cross-account sharing -- you can't touch their key policy, so the moment any data crosses an account boundary, you're stuck. Customer-managed keys give me a key policy I control, which is what actually lets me grant another account's role permission to decrypt. The part people trip over is that cross-account KMS access needs permission granted twice -- once in the key's own policy saying 'this external role may use me,' and again in that role's own account via an IAM policy saying 'you may call KMS against this specific key ARN.' Miss either one and you get the exact same access-denied error, which makes it genuinely confusing to debug if you don't know to check both sides. And for S3 specifically, I'd remind the team that bucket-level access and KMS decrypt access are two separate locks on the same door -- having one without the other still fails. My actual design here is a small number of CMKs scoped by data sensitivity tier, each with a tightly reviewed key policy, rather than one platform-wide key everyone shares, because that keeps blast radius contained if any one key or its access list ever needs to be revoked.
commonMistakes: Recommends AWS-managed keys for a platform that needs cross-account sharing
Describes cross-account KMS access as needing permission on only one side (key policy OR IAM policy, not both)
Doesn't mention that S3 bucket/object permissions and KMS permissions are separate, both-required layers
Recommends a single platform-wide key with no scoping by data sensitivity/blast radius
keyPoints: Correctly explains why AWS-managed keys don't support cross-account sharing
Explains the two-sided cross-account KMS permission model (key policy + consumer IAM policy)
Notes S3 permissions and KMS permissions are separate, both-required layers
Recommends scoped CMKs by data classification rather than one platform-wide key

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains CMK vs. AWS-managed key tradeoffs for this scenario
Correctly explains the two-sided cross-account KMS grant model
Notes the separate S3-permission-plus-KMS-permission requirement
Recommends a sound, least-privilege key scoping strategy

questions.title: Lake Formation Fine-Grained Permissions vs. IAM Policies: Where Each One Actually Decides Access
questions.prompt: Explain, precisely, how a query against a Lake Formation-governed table is actually authorized -- what IAM decides versus what Lake Formation's own grants decide -- and why column-level and row-level filtering specifically cannot be replicated cleanly with IAM policies alone, no matter how creative the policy.
questions.modelAnswer: For a Lake Formation-governed resource, authorization is actually a layered check, not a single decision: IAM still governs whether the calling principal can invoke the relevant service API at all (e.g., can this role call glue:GetTable or athena:StartQueryExecution), but once that coarse API-level check passes, Lake Formation's own permission model takes over for what data within that table the principal is actually allowed to see -- database-level, table-level, and critically, column-level and row-level (via data filters) grants that are evaluated against the Lake Formation Data Catalog, independent of and layered on top of the IAM decision. The reason this can't be cleanly replicated with IAM alone is structural: IAM policies evaluate against resource ARNs -- a table is a resource, a column is not a distinct ARN-addressable resource in Glue/S3's model, so there is no native IAM policy statement that says 'allow access to this table except for column X.' The closest IAM-only approximation is physically separating data -- splitting a table into multiple S3 prefixes or multiple Glue tables by column sensitivity and using separate IAM/bucket policies per split -- which is not actually the same capability; it requires duplicating or restructuring the data itself, breaks the moment a new sensitive column is added without someone remembering to re-split, and still can't express row-level filtering as a rule (e.g., 'see only rows where region = your assigned region') without materializing separate per-condition datasets. Lake Formation's column and row-level grants, by contrast, are declared once against the single underlying table, enforced centrally at query time by the engines that are Lake Formation-aware (Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR with the Lake Formation integration, Glue), and require no data duplication or restructuring -- which is precisely the capability gap that makes Lake Formation necessary rather than a 'nice to have' once an organization needs per-column or per-row governance at any real scale.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it as two separate gates. IAM is the first gate, and it's coarse -- it answers 'can this role call this API at all,' like can it call Athena's query API. Lake Formation is the second gate, and it's where the real data governance lives -- database, table, column, and row-level grants, evaluated against the catalog, independent of that first IAM check. The reason you can't fake column-level security with IAM alone is that IAM policies attach to resource ARNs, and a column isn't its own ARN -- a table is. So the only IAM-native way to approximate column-level security is to physically split the data into separate tables or S3 prefixes by sensitivity, which isn't the same thing at all -- it means duplicating or restructuring real data, and it silently breaks the moment someone adds a new sensitive column and forgets to re-split it. Lake Formation just declares the column and row rule once, against the one real table, and every Lake-Formation-aware engine enforces it at query time without anyone having to duplicate anything. That's not a nice-to-have feature, that's the actual gap IAM alone cannot close.
commonMistakes: Describes Lake Formation and IAM as doing the same job redundantly rather than as layered, sequential checks
Claims IAM policies can express column-level restrictions directly on a table resource
Doesn't explain the structural reason (ARN-level granularity) IAM can't express column/row rules
Doesn't mention that physically splitting data is the only IAM-only approximation, and its real costs
keyPoints: Correctly describes the layered IAM-then-Lake-Formation authorization model
Explains why IAM's ARN-level granularity cannot express column/row-level rules
Describes the data-splitting workaround and its real costs as the only IAM-only approximation
Explains Lake Formation's grants as centrally declared once, enforced across Lake-Formation-aware engines

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the layered IAM + Lake Formation authorization model
Correctly explains the structural reason IAM can't express column/row rules
Describes the data-splitting workaround and its real costs accurately
Explains Lake Formation's centralized, non-duplicative enforcement model

questions.title: Fix a Non-SARGable, Non-Covering Query Under Load
questions.prompt:
You're handed this production query that's doing a full clustered index scan on a 40-million-row table, confirmed via SET STATISTICS IO showing logical reads in the hundreds of thousands:

SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalDue
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), OrderDate, 101) = '06/15/2013'
   AND UPPER(Status) = 'SHIPPED';

Rewrite the query to be SARGable, and write the covering index you'd create to support it, explaining your column order choice.
questions.modelAnswer: There are two non-SARGable predicates here, and both need fixing. CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), OrderDate, 101) wraps the date column in a function, forcing a scan even if an index exists; UPPER(Status) does the same to the status column. The date predicate should be rewritten as a half-open range against the raw column; the status predicate should compare against the literal in its natural case, relying on the column's collation to be case-insensitive rather than forcing a transformation on every row. For the covering index, the equality predicate (Status) should lead the key, since equality columns belong before range columns in a composite index -- this lets SQL Server seek to the exact Status value, then scan only the OrderDate range within that narrower slice -- and the remaining selected columns go into INCLUDE so the plan never needs a Key Lookup back to the clustered index.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out there are actually two separate problems stacked in that one WHERE clause, not one. The CONVERT around OrderDate and the UPPER around Status are both doing the same damage -- wrapping the column so the index can't be used no matter how well it's built. I'd rewrite the date as a range against the raw column and drop the UPPER, trusting the collation to handle case. Then for the index, I always put the equality column first -- Status -- because that lets SQL Server narrow down to an exact value before it even has to think about the date range, and I'd include the rest of the selected columns so we get a fully covering seek with no extra trip back to the clustered index.
questions.example:
-- SARGable rewrite
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalDue
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE Status = 'Shipped'
  AND OrderDate >= '2013-06-15' AND OrderDate < '2013-06-16';

-- Covering index: equality column first, then the range column, then INCLUDE the rest
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_SalesOrderHeader_Status_OrderDate
ON Sales.SalesOrderHeader (Status, OrderDate)
INCLUDE (OrderID, CustomerID, TotalDue);
commonMistakes: Only fixes one of the two non-SARGable predicates
Puts the range column before the equality column in the index key
Forgets INCLUDE columns, leaving a Key Lookup in the plan
Assumes UPPER() is needed without checking the column's collation
keyPoints: Identifies both non-SARGable predicates
Rewrites the date predicate as a range
Removes the function wrapper on Status, citing collation
Designs index key order correctly: equality before range
Makes the index covering with INCLUDE

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rewrites both non-SARGable predicates
Index design uses correct key order (equality before range)
Index is fully covering via INCLUDE
Explains reasoning, not just the syntax

questions.title: Find the Head of a Live Blocking Chain
questions.prompt: Users are reporting the application is frozen. You suspect blocking, not an outage. Write the T-SQL you'd run right now against the live server to find the head blocker -- the session that isn't waiting on anyone else but is blocking everyone downstream -- and explain what you'd do with the session ID once you have it.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests joined to sys.dm_exec_sessions, filtering for sessions that have a non-zero blocking_session_id to see everyone currently blocked, then specifically look for the blocking_session_id value that does not itself appear as a session_id with its own non-zero blocking_session_id -- that session is the head blocker, the one actually holding the lock everyone else is waiting on. Once I have it, I'd pull its current or last statement via sys.dm_exec_sql_text and check open_tran_count and last_request_start_time to understand what it's actually doing and how long it's been doing it, rather than acting blind. Only if it's clearly stuck or abnormally long-running would I consider KILLing the session, understanding that the kill itself rolls back its transaction and can take as long or longer than letting it finish. The real fix afterward is to find out why that session held locks so long -- a missing index causing a slow scan while holding a write lock, or application code that doesn't commit promptly -- because KILL is an emergency release valve, not a repeatable procedure.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I hear 'the app is frozen,' my first move is never to panic and start killing sessions -- it's to find out if this is actually blocking, and if so, where it starts. I'd run a query against dm_exec_requests joined to dm_exec_sessions, filtering for anyone currently blocked, and then specifically look for the one session that's blocking others but isn't itself waiting on anyone -- that's my head blocker. Before I touch it, I want to know what it's actually running and how long it's been running it, because killing it rolls back its transaction, and that rollback can take just as long as letting it finish. Once things are stable again, the real work starts: finding out why that session held locks that long in the first place, because if I don't fix that, I'm back here again next week.
questions.example:
SELECT 
    r.session_id,
    r.blocking_session_id,
    r.wait_type,
    r.wait_time,
    r.status,
    s.login_name,
    s.host_name,
    t.text AS running_sql
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
JOIN sys.dm_exec_sessions AS s ON s.session_id = r.session_id
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) AS t
WHERE r.session_id IN (
    SELECT blocking_session_id FROM sys.dm_exec_requests WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0
)
AND r.blocking_session_id = 0;  -- the head blocker: blocking others, blocked by no one
commonMistakes: Immediately KILLs a session without identifying the actual head blocker first
Confuses a long-running query with a blocking chain -- not every slow query is blocking others
Doesn't capture what the head blocker's own transaction was doing before acting
Treats sp_who2 output alone as sufficient without the actual SQL text or wait info
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the head-blocker query pattern using DMVs
Explains the difference between being blocked and being the source of blocking
Describes a safe escalation path (investigate before KILL)
Connects the fix back to root cause (missing index, long transaction, app behavior)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working query identifying the head blocker
Explains the DMV logic clearly
Describes a safe, sensible escalation/response procedure
Connects to durable root-cause fix, not just killing sessions

questions.title: Replace a Row-by-Row Price Update With a Set-Based Rewrite
questions.prompt: A nightly job uses a cursor to apply a different percentage increase to ListPrice per product category, reading category-specific rates from a rates table. It takes 40 minutes against 2 million products. Rewrite it as a single set-based statement.
questions.modelAnswer: The cursor's cost comes from processing one row at a time -- a fetch, a lookup, and an update per product, each with its own overhead, multiplied by two million. SQL Server's storage engine is built to process sets of rows efficiently, so the fix is to express the same logic as a single UPDATE joined to the rates table, letting the engine apply the whole operation at once instead of looping. I'd use ISNULL to handle any product whose subcategory has no matching rate, so it's left unchanged rather than silently zeroed out by a NULL multiplication. I'd check that the join column is indexed before declaring victory, and only consider batching the update (e.g., with TOP(n) in a loop) if the single statement itself causes problematic lock duration or transaction log growth at this volume -- I wouldn't reach for batching as the first move.
questions.professionalAnswer: Forty minutes for two million rows is a huge tell that something's being processed one row at a time, and sure enough, that's exactly what the cursor is doing -- a fetch, a lookup, and an update per product, over and over. My rewrite is a single UPDATE joined to the rates table, because that lets the storage engine do what it's actually built for, which is operating on a whole set at once instead of looping. The one detail I wouldn't skip is handling products whose subcategory has no matching rate -- I use a LEFT JOIN with ISNULL so those rows just stay unchanged instead of silently getting multiplied by a NULL. And I'd check the join column has an index before I call this done, because a 40-minute cursor sometimes hides a missing index underneath it too.
commonMistakes: Keeps per-row logic inside a WHILE loop over a temp table, which is just a hand-rolled cursor
Forgets to handle categories with no matching rate row (NULL rate silently zeroing the increase)
Doesn't check whether the join column is indexed before declaring victory
Jumps to batching/chunking as the first solution instead of trying the plain set-based statement first
keyPoints: Correctly diagnoses the cursor as the core bottleneck, not server hardware
Produces a correct, equivalent set-based UPDATE...FROM
Handles the no-matching-rate case correctly (ISNULL or join behavior)
Considers indexing and batching only as secondary, scale-driven refinements

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses cursor overhead as root cause
Produces a correct, working set-based rewrite
Handles edge cases (no matching rate) correctly
Discusses sensible secondary considerations (indexing, batching) without over-engineering

questions.title: Bringing a Manually Created Event Hub Under Bicep Management
questions.prompt: Six months ago, someone manually provisioned a production Event Hub namespace through the Azure Portal under time pressure. It's never been touched since, but now it needs to go through the same CI/CD-managed Bicep pipeline as everything else. Explain how you'd bring it under IaC management given Bicep/ARM doesn't have a true 'import' command like Terraform, and write the Bicep you'd use.
questions.modelAnswer: Bicep/ARM deployments are declarative and idempotent by name -- there's no separate 'import state' step like terraform import, because ARM doesn't track resource ownership the way Terraform's state file does. 'Importing' in practice means writing a Bicep resource block whose type, name, and properties exactly match the resource's CURRENT live configuration, then deploying it. Because ARM resolves a deployment by matching resource type and name, deploying a Bicep definition that matches an existing resource's current state is effectively a no-op update, and from that point forward the resource is 'under management' in the sense that the next deployment touching this Bicep file will apply diffs to it going forward. The critical risk is capturing the TRUE current configuration before writing that block -- if the manually-created Event Hub has settings (a specific capacity, a non-default retention, a particular throughput configuration) that get guessed wrong in the Bicep definition, the first deployment silently changes production instead of leaving it alone. The existing keyword resource reference is the safe way to read and confirm current properties before writing the managed resource block, rather than guessing. I'd also run a what-if deployment (az deployment group what-if) before the real apply specifically to confirm it reports zero or no-op changes, which is the actual verification that the Bicep definition genuinely matches reality.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd correct is the premise that we're looking for a terraform-import equivalent -- Bicep just doesn't work that way, since ARM doesn't keep a separate state file tracking what it owns. What actually happens is: we write a Bicep resource block that matches this Event Hub's current settings exactly, and the moment we deploy it and it comes back as a no-op, that resource is under management. The part I'd be most careful about is getting 'exactly' right -- I'd use the existing keyword first to read its real current config rather than guess at what someone set six months ago, and then I would not run this against production without a what-if deployment first. If what-if shows anything other than no changes, that's a sign my Bicep doesn't actually match reality yet, and I'd rather find that out from a dry run than from an unintended change to a live Event Hub.
commonMistakes: Assumes Bicep has a terraform import equivalent command and looks for one instead of writing a matching resource definition
Writes the Bicep resource block from assumed/default settings instead of verifying the resource's actual current configuration first
Skips a what-if deployment before the real apply, risking an unintended production change
Uses the existing keyword as if it brings the resource under management, when it's read-only and changes nothing
Doesn't account for properties that are immutable or hard to change needing to match exactly from day one
keyPoints: Explains ARM/Bicep has no stateful import; management starts by matching a resource's current live config in code
Uses the existing keyword to safely read current configuration before writing the managed definition
Verifies the match with a what-if deployment before the real apply
Flags the risk of a mismatched property causing an unintended change to production on first deploy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why Bicep has no true import and what bringing under management actually means
Correct use of the existing keyword to verify current state safely
Correctly matches the managed resource definition structure
Proposes what-if verification before the real deployment

questions.title: Write Redshift WLM Query Monitoring Rules to Stop One Team's Queries From Starving Everyone Else
questions.prompt: A shared Redshift cluster serves both a BI dashboard team and an ad hoc analyst team. Analysts occasionally submit multi-hour queries that eat the whole cluster's memory and starve the dashboards. Write the WLM configuration (queues plus a query monitoring rule) you'd use to cap and automatically act on runaway ad hoc queries without touching the BI team's queue.
questions.modelAnswer: The fix is workload isolation plus an automatic circuit breaker, not just a warning. I'd create a dedicated WLM queue per user group -- one for the BI role with a healthy, protected memory allocation and concurrency scaling enabled so dashboard queries can burst to Redshift's elastic concurrency scaling clusters under load instead of queuing behind analysts, and a separate, smaller queue for the analyst role with its own capped memory allocation so a runaway query in that queue can only ever consume the analysts' own slice, never the BI queue's. On top of queue-level memory isolation, I'd add Query Monitoring Rules scoped to the analyst queue specifically: a hard abort rule when query_execution_time exceeds a threshold (here, 30 minutes) so a genuinely runaway query gets automatically terminated rather than running for hours, and a log-only rule on query_temp_blocks_to_disk to catch and record queries spilling heavily to disk (a sign of a bad join or missing stats) even if they don't hit the time threshold, so there's a record to go investigate without killing every slightly-expensive query. The default queue remains small and reserved as a safety net for anything not matching either query_group/user_group definition. This setup means the BI team's queue is structurally protected by memory isolation alone -- even before any rule fires, an analyst's runaway query physically cannot consume memory allocated to the BI queue.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to solve this with one shared queue and a rule -- the real fix is giving each group its own queue with its own memory allocation, so a runaway analyst query is mechanically boxed into the analyst slice and literally cannot touch the BI queue's memory, rule or no rule. Then on top of that isolation, I'd add a query monitoring rule on the analyst queue specifically that auto-aborts anything running past 30 minutes, because at that point it's very unlikely to be an intentional long report and much more likely to be a bad join someone forgot a filter on. I'd also log, not abort, on heavy disk spill, since that's a useful early signal of a query that's about to go sideways, without being aggressive enough to kill something that's just legitimately a bit expensive. The BI team never has to know any of this happened, because their queue was never at risk in the first place -- that's the point of isolating by queue before reaching for rules.
commonMistakes: Relies only on a query monitoring rule without first isolating memory by queue, so a runaway query can still starve other queues before the rule fires
Sets the abort threshold on the BI queue instead of scoping it to the analyst queue specifically
Doesn't differentiate 'log' vs. 'abort' actions, aborting queries that were just moderately expensive
Forgets a default/catch-all queue for sessions that don't match any defined query_group/user_group
keyPoints: Isolates memory by WLM queue per user group before relying on any rule
Writes correct WLM JSON configuration with distinct queues and memory_percent_to_use allocations
Scopes query monitoring rules specifically to the analyst queue, not globally
Distinguishes abort (hard stop) vs. log (observe) actions appropriately

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs queue-level memory isolation as the primary fix
Provides correct, working WLM JSON configuration
Scopes query monitoring rules appropriately with sensible thresholds
Distinguishes abort vs. log actions appropriately

questions.title: Grant a Cross-Account Analyst Column-Level Access via Lake Formation
questions.prompt: A data scientist in Account B needs read access to three non-sensitive columns of a customer table that lives in Account A's Lake Formation-governed catalog, and must not see the email or SSN columns. Write the AWS CLI commands you'd run in Account A to make this cross-account, column-level grant.
questions.modelAnswer: The correct call is lakeformation grant-permissions with a TableWithColumns resource specification, not a plain Table resource -- specifying ColumnNames explicitly is what makes this a column-level grant rather than table-wide access, and the principal is the cross-account IAM role ARN directly (Account A's Lake Formation grants permissions to an external account's principal natively, without needing the consumer account to separately 'accept' the table the way RAM resource shares sometimes require, though for cross-account Lake Formation sharing via AWS RAM that acceptance step does apply to the database/table-level share itself). Granting SELECT scoped to exactly ['customer_id','signup_date','region'] means the analyst's queries will succeed against those three columns and fail (or simply not see the columns) for email and ssn, enforced by Lake Formation at query time for any Lake-Formation-aware engine (Athena, Redshift Spectrum) the analyst's role is used through. The step that's easy to miss: this Lake Formation grant alone is not sufficient -- the analyst's role in Account B also needs its own IAM policy permitting the underlying service API calls (e.g., athena:StartQueryExecution, glue:GetTable) against the resource; Lake Formation and IAM are both required, layered gates, not substitutes for each other. I'd verify the grant with list-permissions before telling the data scientist it's ready, rather than assuming the grant call succeeding means the end-to-end access actually works.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key detail here is using TableWithColumns in the resource spec, not just Table -- that's what turns this into a column-level grant instead of giving the analyst the whole table including email and SSN. I'd explicitly list the three columns they're allowed to see, grant SELECT only, and target the principal as their role's ARN directly, since Lake Formation can grant across accounts natively. The thing I always double check afterward is that the analyst's role in their own account also has an IAM policy letting it actually call Athena or Glue APIs -- a Lake Formation grant alone doesn't help if their role can't even invoke the query API, and that gap produces a confusing error that looks like the Lake Formation grant didn't work when it actually did. I'd run list-permissions afterward to confirm the grant looks exactly like I intended before telling anyone it's ready, rather than trusting that the grant call returning success means the whole chain works end to end.
commonMistakes: Grants permissions against a plain Table resource instead of TableWithColumns, exposing all columns including sensitive ones
Assumes the Lake Formation grant alone is sufficient without the consumer's own IAM policy permitting the API call
Doesn't verify the grant with list-permissions before declaring it done
Grants broader permissions (ALL, or SELECT with grant option) than the scenario requires
keyPoints: Uses TableWithColumns with an explicit column list for true column-level restriction
Grants the minimum necessary permission (SELECT only, no grant option)
Targets the cross-account principal's role ARN correctly
Notes the consumer-side IAM policy requirement as a separate, necessary layer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working CLI command using TableWithColumns for column-level restriction
Grants least-privilege permissions appropriately scoped
Explains the separate consumer-side IAM requirement
Proposes verifying the grant before declaring it complete

questions.title: Write a Cross-Account S3 Bucket Policy and Matching Assume-Role Trust Policy
questions.prompt: Account A owns an S3 bucket holding curated Parquet files that Account B's Glue jobs need to read. Write both halves of the access: Account A's bucket policy granting the cross-account role read access, and Account B's IAM role trust policy allowing that role to be assumed appropriately for this use case.
questions.modelAnswer: The key design decision here is that this scenario doesn't actually require a cross-account assume-role chain at all -- it requires a resource-based policy (the S3 bucket policy) granting the Account B role direct permission, plus an identity-based policy on that same Account B role granting it permission to call those S3 actions. Both halves are required because S3 access is evaluated as the intersection of what the resource policy allows and what the calling principal's own identity policy allows; missing either one results in access denied. The bucket policy's Principal is the full ARN of Account B's Glue job role (not the account root, which would be too broad, and not a wildcard), scoped to exactly the actions (GetObject, ListBucket) and the specific prefix the Glue jobs actually need, not the whole bucket if other prefixes hold data this role shouldn't see. The role's own trust policy in Account B simply allows the Glue service itself (glue.amazonaws.com) to assume it when a Glue job runs under that role -- that's a same-account service trust relationship, separate from and not to be confused with the cross-account S3 access, which doesn't require Account B's role to assume anything in Account A at all. A common error is trying to set up STS AssumeRole cross-account chaining when a direct resource-based S3 grant is simpler, sufficient, and the more standard pattern for this exact use case.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd clarify first is that this doesn't need a cross-account assume-role dance -- S3 supports direct resource-based grants, so Account A's bucket policy can name Account B's role ARN directly and grant it read access to a specific prefix. That bucket policy alone isn't enough though; Account B's role also needs its own identity policy allowing it to call GetObject and ListBucket, because S3 checks both sides and denies if either is missing. Separately, and unrelated to the cross-account piece, Account B's role needs a trust policy letting the Glue service itself assume it when a job runs -- that's just normal same-account Glue setup, not part of the cross-account mechanism at all. I'd scope the bucket policy resource ARN to the specific prefix the Glue jobs actually read, not the whole bucket, so this role's blast radius if compromised stays limited to exactly what it needs.
commonMistakes: Tries to set up an unnecessary cross-account STS AssumeRole chain instead of a direct S3 resource-based grant
Writes only the bucket policy without the matching identity policy on the consuming role
Grants the Principal as the entire account root instead of the specific role ARN
Scopes the bucket policy resource to the whole bucket instead of the specific prefix needed
keyPoints: Correctly identifies this as a direct resource-based S3 grant, not a cross-account assume-role scenario
Writes both the bucket policy and the matching consumer-side identity policy
Scopes the Principal to the specific role ARN, not the account root
Scopes resource ARNs to the needed prefix rather than the whole bucket

questions.title: Configure a Glue Crawler to Exclude Partial-Landing Files and Enable Bookmarks on the ETL Job
questions.prompt: A Glue crawler keeps cataloging temporary '.tmp' and in-progress upload files from an S3 landing prefix as if they were real data files, corrupting the schema it infers. Write the crawler configuration excluding those files, and the Glue job parameter enabling job bookmarks so the downstream ETL job only processes new data on each run.
questions.modelAnswer: The crawler's Exclusions patterns are glob-style and evaluated relative to each S3 target's path, so excluding **.tmp, **/_tmp*, and **/*.inprogress specifically filters out exactly the file-naming conventions causing bad schema inference, without needing to restructure the landing prefix itself; I'd confirm the real naming pattern the upload process actually produces rather than guessing, since getting the glob wrong either excludes nothing or excludes real data files that happen to share a substring. On the job side, --job-bookmark-option set to job-bookmark-enable is what activates bookmark tracking at all -- the default is job-bookmark-disable, so a job that was never explicitly enabled for bookmarks has been reprocessing all data on every run regardless of anything else being correct. For bookmarks to actually behave correctly across runs, the job script itself also needs to call job.init() at the start and job.commit() at the end using the Job class from awsglue.job, since the bookmark state is only persisted on a successful commit -- enabling the option alone without those calls in the script doesn't actually track progress. I'd test this by running the job twice in a row against the same data and confirming the second run processes zero new records, which is the concrete verification that bookmarking is actually working end to end, not just configured.
questions.professionalAnswer: For the crawler, I'd use Exclusions with glob patterns matching however the upload process actually names its temp files -- I wouldn't guess at this, I'd check the real file names landing in that prefix first, then write the pattern to match exactly that convention. For the job, the critical flag is --job-bookmark-option set to job-bookmark-enable, because the default is actually disabled, so if nobody explicitly turned this on, the job's been silently reprocessing everything every single run. I'd also make sure the script itself calls job.init() and job.commit(), since the bookmark only actually advances on a successful commit -- just setting the argument without those calls in the code doesn't track anything. And I wouldn't trust this is working just because I set the flag -- I'd run the job twice back to back and confirm the second run picks up zero new rows, because that's the only real proof the bookmark is functioning.

Sets --job-bookmark-option without confirming the script calls job.init() and job.commit()
Assumes job bookmarks are enabled by default
Doesn't verify bookmark behavior with a two-run test before trusting it in production

Correctly sets --job-bookmark-option to job-bookmark-enable
Notes job.init()/job.commit() as required in the script for bookmarks to persist
Proposes a concrete verification test (second run processes zero new rows)

questions.title: Write a Step Functions State Machine Orchestrating Glue and EMR With Retry and Catch
questions.prompt: Write the Amazon States Language (ASL) for a Step Functions state machine that runs a Glue job, then an EMR step, with a retry policy on transient Glue failures and a catch that routes any unrecoverable failure to a cleanup/notification state instead of leaving the execution simply failed.
questions.modelAnswer: Using the .sync service integration suffix on both the Glue and EMR tasks is the key detail that makes this a true orchestration rather than a fire-and-forget: without .sync, startJobRun and addStep return immediately after triggering the job/step, and Step Functions would move to the next state before the Glue job or EMR step has actually finished, which breaks the intended sequencing entirely. The Retry block on the Glue state is scoped specifically to transient, retryable error types (a concurrent-runs conflict, a timeout) with exponential backoff, rather than a blanket retry on every error type, because retrying a genuine job-logic failure (bad data, a script bug) three times just delays the inevitable and wastes compute -- only errors that are plausibly transient should be retried automatically. The Catch block on both the Glue and EMR states routes to a shared NotifyFailure state rather than letting the execution simply end in a Failed status with no human visibility; capturing the error into $.error via ResultPath preserves the actual failure details so the SNS notification is specific and actionable rather than generic. I'd also note that in a real deployment, NotifyFailure might additionally need a cleanup step (terminating a transient EMR cluster, for example) before or alongside the notification, since a failed pipeline leaving orphaned paid infrastructure running is its own problem this design should account for depending on whether the EMR cluster is transient-per-run or shared.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail I'd point out first is the .sync suffix on both the Glue and EMR integrations -- without it, Step Functions fires the job and immediately moves on, which would completely break the sequencing we actually want here. For retries, I scoped the Retry block to specific, plausibly-transient error types with backoff, not a blanket retry-on-everything, because retrying an actual script bug three times just burns time and compute before failing anyway. Both states catch into the same NotifyFailure state, and I'm putting the real error into $.error with ResultPath so whatever goes to SNS actually tells someone what broke instead of a generic 'something failed.' One thing I'd flag in a real review: if that EMR cluster is a long-lived shared cluster, NotifyFailure is probably fine as-is, but if it's a transient cluster spun up just for this pipeline, I'd want a termination step in the failure path too, so a failed run doesn't leave a cluster running and billing with nobody watching it.
commonMistakes: Omits the .sync suffix, causing Step Functions to move on before the Glue job/EMR step actually completes
Applies a blanket Retry on all error types instead of scoping it to transient failures
Lets executions end in Failed status with no Catch/notification path
Doesn't consider whether a failed transient EMR cluster needs explicit cleanup
keyPoints: Uses .sync service integrations so the state machine correctly waits for job/step completion
Scopes Retry to specific transient error types with backoff, not a blanket retry
Routes failures to a shared Catch/notification state with the real error preserved
Considers whether failure handling needs a cleanup step for transient infrastructure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, valid ASL with .sync integrations for proper sequencing
Sound, appropriately scoped Retry policy
Sound Catch policy routing to a real failure-handling state
Considers cleanup implications for transient infrastructure on failure

questions.title: Configure an EMR Instance Fleet With a Spot Allocation Strategy for a Transient Spark Job
questions.prompt: Write the EMR cluster launch configuration (AWS CLI create-cluster) for a nightly, fault-tolerant Spark aggregation job, using an instance fleet with a diversified Spot allocation strategy for task nodes and on-demand for the master/core nodes, to minimize cost while keeping the cluster resilient to Spot interruptions.
questions.modelAnswer: The design puts Spot risk only where the cluster can absorb it without correctness or availability consequences: master and core nodes run on-demand, because losing the master ends the cluster and losing a core node risks HDFS data the job may depend on mid-run, while task nodes -- which run Spark executors but hold no HDFS data -- are the correct place for Spot, since losing a task node just means YARN reschedules that work elsewhere, which Spark's fault tolerance already handles for a job like this. The price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy selects Spot capacity pools balancing low interruption likelihood against price, which is the right default for a fault-tolerant batch job over the cheapest-price-only strategy, since minimizing interruption frequency reduces wasted recompute time, which is itself a cost. Diversifying across four similar-but-distinct instance types (m5, m5a, m5d, m4, all with equal WeightedCapacity) spreads the fleet across different Spot capacity pools, so an interruption event hitting one instance type's pool doesn't take out the whole task fleet simultaneously -- this is the actual mechanism that makes Spot viable at any real reliability bar, not just a nice-to-have. The SpotSpecification's TimeoutDurationMinutes with TimeoutAction set to SWITCH_TO_ON_DEMAND is a safety net: if Spot capacity genuinely can't be fulfilled within 15 minutes, the fleet falls back to on-demand rather than leaving the job stalled indefinitely waiting for Spot capacity that may not materialize, trading some cost savings for a guarantee the job actually completes. --auto-terminate ensures this transient cluster bills only for the job's actual runtime rather than becoming an unnoticed persistent cluster.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core decision is where to take Spot risk. Master and core go on-demand, no question -- losing the master kills the cluster, and core nodes can hold HDFS data this run might need. Task nodes are the right place for Spot, because they're pure compute for Spark executors with no data to lose, and losing one just means YARN reschedules that slice of work. For the allocation strategy, I'd use price-capacity-optimized rather than chasing the absolute lowest price, because for a batch job, getting interrupted and having to recompute is its own hidden cost -- a slightly pricier but more stable pool often wins overall. I'd diversify across several similar instance types with equal weighted capacity so one Spot pool's interruption wave doesn't take out the whole task fleet at once -- that diversification is really what makes Spot reliable enough to trust here, not any single setting. And I added a 15-minute timeout that falls back to on-demand if Spot capacity just isn't available, because a job that never starts because it's waiting on Spot capacity is worse than paying on-demand price occasionally. Auto-terminate at the end keeps this a transient, job-scoped cluster instead of something somebody has to remember to shut down.
commonMistakes: Puts master or core nodes on Spot, risking the whole cluster or HDFS data to an interruption
Uses only a single instance type for the Spot task fleet, concentrating interruption risk in one capacity pool
Chases lowest price only, ignoring interruption frequency as a real cost (wasted recompute)
Omits a Spot timeout/fallback, risking the job never starting if Spot capacity isn't available
Forgets --auto-terminate, leaving a transient job cluster running indefinitely
keyPoints: Correctly places Spot risk only on stateless task nodes, not master/core
Diversifies across multiple instance types to spread Spot capacity pool risk
Uses an interruption-aware allocation strategy appropriate for a fault-tolerant batch job
Includes a Spot timeout fallback and auto-termination for a transient cluster

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly scopes Spot usage to task nodes only
Correct, working instance fleet configuration with diversification
Chooses and justifies an appropriate allocation strategy
Includes sensible fallback/termination behavior

questions.title: Reshard a Kinesis Stream and Verify Consumers Follow the New Shard Lineage
questions.prompt: A Kinesis stream currently has 4 shards and is throttling under increased load. Write the AWS CLI command to reshard it up to 8 shards via a uniform scaling split, and describe exactly how you'd verify afterward that your KCL-based consumer application picked up the new shards correctly with no data loss or duplication.
questions.code:
# Reshard from 4 to 8 shards via uniform scaling (splits each existing shard's hash-key range in two)
aws kinesis update-shard-count \
  --stream-name orders-stream \
  --target-shard-count 8 \
  --scaling-type UNIFORM_SCALING

# Confirm the new shard topology and parent-child lineage
aws kinesis describe-stream-summary --stream-name orders-stream
aws kinesis list-shards --stream-name orders-stream \
  --query 'Shards[].{ShardId:ShardId,ParentShardId:ParentShardId}'
questions.modelAnswer: update-shard-count with UNIFORM_SCALING splits every existing shard's hash-key range roughly in half, doubling the shard count predictably in one operation, which is the right choice here over manually issuing individual split-shard calls since uniform scaling is explicitly designed for this double-the-capacity case and handles the hash-key math correctly without manual range calculation. After the reshard, the stream briefly has a mix of the old parent shards (still CLOSED but retaining already-written records for the retention period) and new, OPEN child shards actively receiving new records -- list-shards with ParentShardId exposes this lineage directly, which is exactly what a correct consumer needs to walk. For a KCL-based consumer application, verification is largely automatic and low-risk by design: KCL's lease/checkpoint model tracks each shard's processing state in its DynamoDB lease table, detects that parent shards have closed, finishes draining any remaining records from them, and then automatically picks up the new child shards once the parent lease work is marked complete -- so the correctness check is confirming the lease table shows new leases created for the child shard IDs, confirming no consumer errors/exceptions appeared in the application logs during the transition window, and confirming via CloudWatch's IncomingRecords/GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds metrics that processing lag didn't spike and stay elevated after the reshard (a temporary small blip during the transition is normal; a sustained climb would indicate the consumer isn't correctly picking up the new shards). If this were a hand-rolled, non-KCL consumer instead, I would not assume this works automatically -- a custom consumer needs to explicitly re-list shards and follow ParentShardId lineage itself, and I'd test that logic specifically rather than assuming reshard-safety by default.
questions.professionalAnswer: UNIFORM_SCALING is the right scaling type here because it's purpose-built for exactly this -- roughly doubling shard count by splitting every existing shard's range in half, without me having to calculate hash-key boundaries by hand. Once that's done, I'd pull list-shards and look at the ParentShardId field to see the new lineage clearly: old shards closed, new shards open, parent-child relationships visible. Because this is a KCL-based consumer, most of the real work is already handled -- KCL tracks shard state in its DynamoDB lease table and will finish draining the old shards before picking up the new children automatically. My actual verification is checking that lease table for new leases on the child shard IDs, watching the application logs for anything unusual during the window, and watching IteratorAgeMilliseconds in CloudWatch to make sure lag didn't climb and stay elevated -- a small blip during the transition is fine, a sustained climb isn't. If this were a custom consumer instead of KCL, I'd treat all of that as unverified until I confirmed the code itself re-lists shards and follows the parent-child chain, because that behavior isn't free outside of KCL.
commonMistakes: Uses individual split-shard calls instead of update-shard-count with UNIFORM_SCALING for a simple doubling case
Assumes any consumer automatically handles the reshard transition without distinguishing KCL from custom consumers
Doesn't check the lease table or shard lineage, relying only on 'no errors seen' as verification
Doesn't use a lag metric (IteratorAgeMilliseconds) to confirm processing caught up after the transition
keyPoints: Uses the correct CLI command and scaling type for this specific reshard case
Describes the parent-child shard lineage correctly via ParentShardId
Explains how KCL's lease/checkpoint model handles the transition automatically
Proposes concrete verification steps (lease table, logs, lag metric) rather than assuming success

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working reshard command with appropriate scaling type
Correctly explains shard lineage and the parent/child relationship
Correctly explains KCL's automatic handling of the transition
Proposes concrete, specific verification steps

questions.title: Write a Redshift Spectrum External Schema and Table to Query Partitioned S3 Parquet Data
questions.prompt: Write the Redshift SQL to create an external schema pointing at the Glue Data Catalog, and an external table definition over partitioned Parquet order files in S3 (partitioned by year and month), including how you'd add new partitions as they land.
questions.code:
-- External schema backed by the Glue Data Catalog
CREATE EXTERNAL SCHEMA spectrum_orders
FROM DATA CATALOG
DATABASE 'orders_lake_db'
IAM_ROLE 'arn:aws:iam::111111111111:role/RedshiftSpectrumRole'
CREATE EXTERNAL DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS;

-- External table over partitioned Parquet files
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE spectrum_orders.orders (
    order_id       BIGINT,
    customer_id    BIGINT,
    order_total    DECIMAL(12,2),
    order_ts       TIMESTAMP
)
PARTITIONED BY (year SMALLINT, month SMALLINT)
STORED AS PARQUET
LOCATION 's3://curated-data-bucket/orders/';

-- Register a newly landed partition explicitly
ALTER TABLE spectrum_orders.orders
ADD PARTITION (year = 2026, month = 10)
LOCATION 's3://curated-data-bucket/orders/year=2026/month=10/';

-- Or let a Glue crawler keep partitions in sync automatically instead of manual ALTER TABLE calls
questions.modelAnswer: The external schema statement doesn't create or own the data -- it attaches Redshift's query engine to an existing Glue Data Catalog database, and the IAM_ROLE specified must have both Glue Data Catalog read permissions and S3 read permissions on the underlying location, since Spectrum queries execute against S3 directly via the Spectrum compute layer, not by loading data into the cluster. The external table's PARTITIONED BY clause declares the partition columns (year, month) separately from the data columns, matching the Hive-style partition folder structure (year=2026/month=10/) in S3, and critically, declaring a partitioned external table does not automatically discover existing partitions -- Redshift needs each partition explicitly registered, either via individual ALTER TABLE ... ADD PARTITION statements (fine for occasional, known partitions) or, far more commonly in a production pipeline with daily/monthly data landing continuously, via a Glue crawler scheduled to run after each load and automatically add newly discovered partitions to the Glue Catalog, which Spectrum then sees without any manual Redshift-side DDL. Choosing between the two is purely about automation: a one-time backfill or rarely-changing dataset can use manual ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION; a continuously arriving dataset should use a scheduled crawler (or MSCK REPAIR TABLE as a one-shot full partition discovery, though that rescans the entire S3 prefix and gets expensive as the dataset grows, making it a poor recurring solution compared to a crawler).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the external schema line first, because it trips people up -- it's not creating a database, it's pointing Redshift at a Glue Catalog database that already exists (or creating it there if it doesn't), and the IAM role attached needs both Glue and S3 read permissions, since Spectrum reads straight from S3 rather than loading anything into the cluster. For the table, PARTITIONED BY has to match the actual Hive-style folder layout in S3 -- year=2026/month=10 -- and the detail that surprises people is that creating the table doesn't automatically discover any partitions; Redshift won't see year=2026/month=10 until something explicitly tells it that partition exists. For a one-off backfill, I'd just run ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION by hand. But for anything landing continuously, I wouldn't want to run manual DDL every day -- I'd point a Glue crawler at the same location on a schedule, and let it keep the catalog's partition list current automatically, which Spectrum then just picks up for free. I'd specifically avoid relying on MSCK REPAIR TABLE as a recurring job, since it rescans the whole prefix every time and gets slower and more expensive as the dataset grows.
commonMistakes: Assumes creating a partitioned external table automatically discovers existing S3 partitions
Doesn't specify or explain the IAM role's dual requirement (Glue Catalog + S3 read)
Uses MSCK REPAIR TABLE as a recurring, scheduled solution instead of a crawler for continuously arriving data
Mismatches the PARTITIONED BY column definitions against the actual S3 folder naming convention
keyPoints: Correctly creates an external schema backed by the Glue Data Catalog with the right IAM role requirements
Correctly defines a partitioned external table matching the S3 folder structure
Explains that partitions must be explicitly registered, not auto-discovered
Recommends a crawler over manual DDL or MSCK REPAIR for continuously landing data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working external schema and table DDL
Correctly explains the IAM role's dual Glue+S3 permission requirement
Correctly explains partition registration is not automatic
Recommends an appropriate ongoing partition-management approach

questions.title: Write a DMS Table Mapping JSON for a Selective CDC Migration
questions.prompt: You're migrating only the orders and customers tables (not the entire schema) from an on-prem SQL Server database to Aurora PostgreSQL using DMS, with CDC enabled, and need to exclude a legacy audit_log table that happens to live in the same schema. Write the DMS table mapping rules JSON.
questions.modelAnswer: The most precise approach here is NOT a wildcard include-everything-then-exclude pattern across the whole schema, because that silently migrates every future table ever added to dbo unless someone remembers to add an exclusion -- for a genuinely selective migration (only orders and customers, explicitly), I'd use two targeted selection rules with rule-action include, each with an exact table-name matching 'orders' and 'customers' respectively, rather than a wildcard include plus an exclude rule for audit_log, since the wildcard approach is actually the wrong tool for 'only these two tables' even though it happens to produce the same initial result -- it's not forward-safe if the schema changes. Rule evaluation order matters: DMS evaluates selection rules in rule-id order, and the first matching rule for an object wins, so if a wildcard-include is used it must be rule-id 1 with the specific exclude at a higher rule-id (evaluated after) to actually override it for that one table, or table-level includes should simply be used directly to express true selectivity. The transformation rule renaming the dbo schema to public isn't a DMS requirement, but is a sensible practical step here given the target is PostgreSQL, where public is the idiomatic default schema rather than dbo, which is SQL Server's convention. For CDC specifically, these same table-mapping rules apply to both the full load and the ongoing CDC replication phase, so getting the selection right once correctly scopes both phases rather than needing separate configuration.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd actually push back on the wildcard-include-then-exclude pattern for this specific ask, because the requirement is 'only these two tables,' not 'everything except this one table' -- those sound similar but behave very differently the moment someone adds a third table to that schema later. So I'd write two explicit, exact-match selection rules for orders and customers, nothing wildcarded, which is both clearer about intent and safer against future schema drift. I'd also throw in a schema-rename transformation rule from dbo to public, since that's not a DMS requirement but it is the idiomatic default on the PostgreSQL side, and I'd rather make that call explicitly now than have everyone wonder why the target schema is called dbo on a Postgres database. One thing worth saying out loud to whoever's reviewing this: these same rules govern both the initial full load and the ongoing CDC stream, so getting the table selection right here scopes the whole migration, not just the first pass.
commonMistakes: Uses a wildcard include across the whole schema with an exclude for one table, which isn't safe against future schema changes for a genuinely selective migration
Doesn't account for selection rule evaluation order when mixing wildcard and specific rules
Forgets that table mapping rules govern CDC as well as the full load, not just the initial migration
Doesn't consider schema-name conventions differing between source (dbo) and target (public) engines
keyPoints: Chooses explicit, exact-match selection rules for a genuinely selective migration rather than wildcard-plus-exclude
Understands DMS selection rule evaluation order
Notes table mapping rules apply to both full load and ongoing CDC
Considers schema-naming convention differences between source and target engines

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working table mapping JSON expressing true selectivity
Correctly explains selection rule evaluation order
Notes the rules apply to both full load and CDC phases
Considers schema-naming convention differences sensibly

questions.title: Write a Cost Allocation Tagging Policy and a Cost Explorer CLI Query by Team
questions.prompt: Design and write an AWS Organizations tag policy enforcing a mandatory 'team' and 'cost-center' tag on all taggable data platform resources, plus the Cost Explorer CLI call you'd run monthly to break down spend by team for a chargeback report.
questions.modelAnswer: The Organizations tag policy operates as a compliance/visibility layer, not a hard preventive control by itself -- enforced_for flags resources as non-compliant in the Tag Policies compliance report if the tag is missing or has a value outside the allowed list, but a tag policy alone does not block resource creation; to actually prevent untagged resources from being created, this needs to be paired with an SCP (denying resource creation actions unless the required tag is present in the request, using aws:RequestTag conditions) or a Service Catalog / Config-rule-based preventive control. I'd deploy the tag policy first for visibility and a compliance dashboard, and add the SCP enforcement as the actual blocking mechanism once teams have had a grace period to retrofit existing resources, since a sudden hard block on an environment with lots of pre-existing untagged resources tends to cause more operational pain than it prevents. For the Cost Explorer query, --group-by Type=TAG,Key=team requires that 'team' first be activated as a cost allocation tag in the Billing console (tag policies and cost allocation tag activation are two separate, both-required steps) -- a tag can be enforced by policy and still invisible to Cost Explorer if it was never activated for cost allocation, which is a common gap that makes a chargeback report quietly incomplete for weeks before anyone notices.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be upfront that a tag policy alone doesn't stop anyone from creating an untagged resource -- it just makes that resource show up as non-compliant in a report. If the real goal is actually preventing untagged resources, that needs an SCP with a RequestTag condition denying the create action outright, and I'd roll that out as a second phase after giving teams time to tag what already exists, rather than flipping on a hard block immediately and breaking everyone's existing automation. For the Cost Explorer side, there's a step people forget constantly: the tag has to be separately activated as a cost allocation tag in Billing before Cost Explorer's group-by will even see it -- having a tag policy enforcing 'team' doesn't automatically make 'team' usable in a cost report. I'd check that activation explicitly before telling finance the chargeback report is ready, because otherwise you get a clean-looking tag policy and a cost report that's quietly missing data for weeks.
commonMistakes: Assumes an Organizations tag policy alone prevents untagged resources from being created
Doesn't mention the separate requirement to activate a tag as a cost allocation tag in Billing before Cost Explorer can group by it
Rolls out a hard SCP-based tagging block with no grace period for existing untagged resources
Scopes the tag policy to too few or the wrong resource types for the platform's actual services
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes a tag policy (compliance/visibility) from an SCP (preventive enforcement)
Writes a correct, scoped Organizations tag policy for the platform's resource types
Notes the separate cost-allocation-tag activation requirement for Cost Explorer
Writes a correct Cost Explorer CLI query grouped by the tag

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains tag policy vs. SCP enforcement distinction
Provides a correct, reasonably scoped tag policy
Notes the cost-allocation-tag activation requirement
Provides a correct Cost Explorer CLI query

questions.title: Write an SCP Denying Non-Approved Regions for a Data Platform Organization
questions.prompt: Compliance requires that no data platform resources are ever created outside us-east-1 and eu-west-1, across every member account in the organization, with an explicit exception for global/non-regional services like IAM and CloudFront. Write the Service Control Policy.
questions.modelAnswer: The structural key to this SCP is using NotAction together with a region Condition rather than trying to Deny every regional service action individually -- NotAction here means the Deny statement applies to every action EXCEPT the ones listed (IAM, Organizations, CloudFront, Route 53, Support, STS, Budgets, Cost Explorer -- all genuinely global or non-regional services), which is both far more maintainable than enumerating every regional AWS service explicitly and correctly future-proofs against new services, since any new regional service AWS launches is automatically covered by this deny without the policy needing an update. The Condition using aws:RequestedRegion with StringNotEquals against the two approved regions means the deny only fires when a request targets a region outside the approved list, so creating an S3 bucket or Redshift cluster in us-east-1 or eu-west-1 is unaffected, while the same call targeting ap-southeast-1 is blocked at the IAM evaluation level before it ever reaches the service. I'd explicitly include sts:*, budgets:*, and ce:* in the exception list because those are genuinely non-regional or need to function platform-wide regardless of region restrictions (STS for assume-role chains across the org, Budgets/Cost Explorer for the finance visibility this very platform needs); omitting them is a common mistake that breaks unrelated functionality while trying to lock down regions. I'd test this against a non-production OU first with a deliberate attempt to create a resource in a disallowed region, confirming it's denied, before attaching it broadly, since an SCP mistake applies org-wide immediately and is a very blunt instrument to get wrong.
questions.professionalAnswer: The pattern I'd use is NotAction plus a region condition, not a long Deny list of every regional action I can think of -- NotAction flips it around to 'deny everything except this short list of truly global services,' which means any new regional AWS service automatically gets caught by this policy without me having to remember to update it later. The condition is aws:RequestedRegion not equal to our two approved regions, so anything targeting us-east-1 or eu-west-1 sails through untouched, and anything else gets denied before it even reaches the service. I'd be careful about the exception list -- IAM and CloudFront are the obvious ones, but I'd also exclude STS, Budgets, and Cost Explorer explicitly, because those need to work regardless of region and I've seen SCPs like this accidentally break assume-role chains or cost visibility because someone forgot them. Before attaching this broadly, I'd test it against one non-production OU first and actually try to create something in a disallowed region to confirm it gets denied, because an SCP mistake here is organization-wide and immediate.
commonMistakes: Enumerates every regional service action individually in a Deny list instead of using NotAction with the global-service exceptions
Forgets to exclude genuinely global/non-regional services (IAM, CloudFront, Route 53, STS) from the deny, breaking unrelated functionality
Uses StringEquals instead of StringNotEquals, inverting the policy's logic
Attaches the SCP org-wide without testing it against a non-production OU first
keyPoints: Uses NotAction with a region condition for a maintainable, future-proof policy
Correctly scopes the aws:RequestedRegion condition with StringNotEquals
Includes a correct, complete list of genuinely global/non-regional service exceptions
Proposes testing in a non-production OU before org-wide attachment

Correctly identifies and includes necessary global-service exceptions
Explains the policy's evaluation logic accurately
Proposes a sound testing/rollout approach

questions.title: Write a Glue Data Quality Ruleset (DQDL) for an Orders Table
questions.prompt: Write a Glue Data Quality ruleset in DQDL enforcing: order_id is never null and always unique, order_total is always positive, order_status is one of a fixed set of values, and the table's row count hasn't dropped by more than 10% compared to typical volume. Explain what happens to rows failing each rule under a 'drop' enforcement policy versus a 'fail' policy.
questions.code:
Rules = [
    ColumnValues "order_id" is not null,
    IsUnique "order_id",
    ColumnValues "order_total" > 0,
    ColumnValues "order_status" in ["PENDING", "SHIPPED", "DELIVERED", "CANCELLED"],
    RowCount > 9000
]
questions.modelAnswer: Each rule in DQDL maps to a specific evaluation: ColumnValues 'order_id' is not null checks for nulls row by row, IsUnique checks for duplicate values across the whole column (not just within a single batch, if run against the full table), the order_total check is a simple numeric range assertion, the order_status check validates against an explicit allow-list so any unexpected status value (a typo, a new status someone forgot to add here) fails the rule, and RowCount is an aggregate check against the whole dataset's row count rather than a per-row check, which is the right tool for catching a silent upstream data loss (a broken extract that only pulled a fraction of the expected rows) that none of the per-row rules would ever catch, since every individual row could still pass its own checks while the dataset as a whole is catastrophically incomplete. Under a 'drop' enforcement policy, any row failing a per-row rule (null order_id, duplicate order_id, non-positive total, invalid status) is silently removed from the output while the pipeline continues and reports success, with the drop count captured in the pipeline's data quality metrics -- this is appropriate when violating rows are expected, known-bad noise that shouldn't halt the whole pipeline, but it requires active monitoring of the drop count, since a creeping drop rate with no alert is exactly the kind of silent data loss that erodes trust in a pipeline everyone assumes is fine because it's green. The RowCount rule, being an aggregate check rather than per-row, behaves differently even under 'drop' semantics in practice -- there's no individual row to drop for a dataset-level cardinality violation, so this kind of rule is typically configured to fail the pipeline outright regardless of the per-row policy, which is exactly the right call: a 10%+ unexplained drop in total row count is a sign something upstream broke, not noise to quietly tolerate.
questions.professionalAnswer: Each line does something specific: not-null and uniqueness on order_id catch the two classic primary-key problems, the positive-total check catches bad data at the row level, and the status allow-list check catches anything that isn't one of the values we actually expect, including a typo or a genuinely new status nobody told the pipeline about. The RowCount rule is doing a different job entirely -- it's not checking any individual row, it's checking whether the whole dataset looks complete, which is the only way to catch an upstream extract that silently only grabbed a fraction of what it should have, since every row that did make it through could pass every other rule individually. On enforcement: if I set the per-row rules to 'drop,' bad rows just quietly disappear and the pipeline stays green, which is fine for noise I expect and plan to monitor, but it needs an actual alert on the drop count, not just silent tolerance. For RowCount specifically, I wouldn't use 'drop' at all, because there's no single row to drop for a dataset-wide volume problem -- that one should fail the pipeline outright, because a double-digit unexplained drop in row count means something upstream is broken, and I'd much rather have a loud failure than a quiet, slowly eroding one.
commonMistakes: Doesn't distinguish per-row rules from the dataset-level RowCount aggregate rule
Applies 'drop' semantics to the RowCount rule without recognizing it should typically fail the pipeline instead
Doesn't flag that 'drop' mode needs active alerting on the drop count, not silent tolerance
Writes an incomplete or overly loose status allow-list that doesn't actually catch bad values

Correctly distinguishes per-row rules from the dataset-level RowCount check
Explains 'drop' vs. 'fail' semantics accurately for per-row rules
Recognizes RowCount-style aggregate rules should typically fail rather than drop

Correctly explains drop vs. fail enforcement semantics
Correctly distinguishes per-row vs. aggregate rule behavior
