questions.title: Nightly Load and Morning Reports Are Deadlocking Each Other
questions.prompt: The nightly ETL load now runs long enough to overlap with early-morning reporting queries, and you're seeing a spike in deadlock errors (1205) exactly in that overlap window. Write the query you'd use to capture the actual deadlock graphs (not just the error count), and describe the architectural fix once you've confirmed the access pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: SQL Server Profiler is deprecated, so I'd capture real deadlock graphs through Extended Events -- either reading the always-on system_health session's xml_deadlock_report, or standing up a dedicated session -- and extract the XML to see exactly which two statements and which objects/lock modes were involved. That turns 'we have deadlocks' into a concrete finding, like 'the ETL's bulk insert into FactOrderSales and a reporting SELECT doing a range scan are colliding on the same rows.' Once that's confirmed, I'd rank the fix options by durability: first, enable READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT so reporting SELECTs stop taking the shared locks that participate in the deadlock at all, which addresses it structurally rather than by luck of timing; second, shrink and restructure the ETL's transactions so they hold locks for the shortest possible time and touch narrower row ranges, through smaller batches or partition-aligned loads; third, if this keeps recurring, separate the workloads architecturally -- widen or shift the load window, or move reporting onto a readable secondary -- so the two workloads stop contending for the same locks on the same instance entirely. I'd recommend RCSI as the fast structural win and workload separation as the long-term answer if the overlap keeps growing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't propose a fix off an error count alone -- I want the actual deadlock graph first, so I'm pulling it from the system_health Extended Events session rather than reaching for Profiler, which is deprecated at this point. Once I can see exactly which two statements and which rows are colliding, I can say something specific, like 'the nightly bulk insert and a reporting range scan are fighting over the same rows,' instead of just 'we have deadlocks.' From there, my go-to structural fix is read-committed snapshot isolation, because it takes the reporting side out of the locking picture entirely instead of just making it less likely to collide. If the client's really pushing both workloads hard, I'd also talk about shrinking the ETL's transactions and, longer term, moving reporting to a readable secondary -- but I'd never reach for NOLOCK as the answer here, because trading a deadlock for a dirty read isn't actually a fix.
questions.example:
-- Query system_health's ring buffer for recent deadlock graphs
SELECT
    xed.value('(event/@timestamp)[1]', 'datetime2') AS EventTime,
    xed.query('.') AS DeadlockGraph
FROM sys.fn_xe_file_target_read_file('system_health*.xel', NULL, NULL, NULL) AS f
CROSS APPLY (SELECT CAST(f.event_data AS XML) AS xed) AS d
WHERE xed.value('(event/@name)[1]', 'varchar(100)') = 'xml_deadlock_report'
ORDER BY EventTime DESC;
commonMistakes: Tries to diagnose deadlocks from just the error count/frequency instead of capturing the actual graph
Jumps straight to NOLOCK on the reporting queries as a 'fix', reintroducing dirty-read risk
Only addresses the symptom (overlap timing) without checking whether RCSI would remove the lock conflict structurally
Recommends a replica without first confirming the deadlock is lock-contention, not resource-contention
keyPoints: Uses Extended Events (not deprecated Profiler) to capture real deadlock graphs
Translates the captured graph into a concrete statement-level root cause before proposing a fix
Evaluates RCSI as a structural fix for reader/writer lock conflicts
Considers transaction shrinkage and workload separation (replica) as complementary long-term fixes
Avoids NOLOCK as a quick-fix answer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct approach to capturing real deadlock graph evidence
Correctly reasons from captured evidence to root cause
Proposes RCSI or equivalent structural fix with justification
Considers workload separation/transaction design as durable long-term fix

questions.title: A Report Query That Used to Run in 2 Seconds Now Takes Over a Minute
questions.prompt: A nightly report query filtering orders by date has gone from roughly 2 seconds to over a minute as the Orders table grew past 40 million rows. The WHERE clause uses a function on the indexed OrderDate column to normalize it before comparing. Nobody changed the query text or the index. Walk through your diagnostic sequence and provide the corrected query.
questions.modelAnswer: First I'd pull the actual execution plan (not estimated) for the query and check whether it's doing an Index Seek or a Scan on OrderDate -- on a 40M-row table, a scan where a seek should be possible is the key signal. The WHERE clause wraps the indexed column in CONVERT(date, OrderDate), and applying a function to the column itself makes the predicate non-SARGable: SQL Server can't use the index's sorted order to seek, because it would have to evaluate CONVERT() against every row's OrderDate before it even knows which rows match, forcing a full scan. This likely always technically had this issue, but it only became painfully visible once the table grew enough that scanning became expensive -- small tables hide non-SARGable predicates because a full scan is cheap when there's little data. Fix: rewrite the predicate to leave the column bare and move the transformation to the literal side, using a range comparison instead of transforming OrderDate: WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-10-08' AND OrderDate < '2026-10-09'. This lets the optimizer seek directly against the OrderDate index. I'd confirm the fix by re-checking the execution plan for an Index Seek and comparing logical reads/duration before and after.
questions.professionalAnswer: I don't start by looking at the index or assuming it got dropped or fragmented -- I go get the actual execution plan first, because 'nothing changed' usually means the query had a latent problem the whole time that only became expensive once the table crossed some size. And sure enough, the plan shows a full scan on a 40-million-row table even though there's an index sitting right there on OrderDate. The WHERE clause is the giveaway: CONVERT(date, OrderDate) = '...' wraps the indexed column in a function, and the moment you do that, the optimizer can't use the index's sort order to seek -- it has to convert every single row before it can compare anything, so a scan is the only option it has left. This bug was there on day one, it just didn't matter when the table was small enough that a full scan was basically free; growth is what exposed it, not a change to the query or index. The fix is just to stop touching the column and instead express the same filter as a range against the raw OrderDate value -- greater than or equal to midnight on the target day, less than midnight the next day -- so the predicate stays SARGable and the optimizer can seek straight to the right rows. I make the change, pull the plan again, confirm it's an Index Seek now, and compare logical reads before and after so I have real numbers to point to, not just 'it feels faster.'
commonMistakes: Assuming something must have changed (index dropped, stats stale) instead of checking whether the predicate was always non-SARGable
Not pulling the actual execution plan and instead guessing based on query text alone
Rebuilding or adding indexes without first fixing the function-wrapped predicate that prevents any index from being seek-able
Fixing it by wrapping the literal in the same function (CONVERT on both sides) instead of removing the function from the column side entirely
Not validating the fix by comparing before/after execution plans or logical reads
Blaming table growth alone as 'just needs more hardware' instead of identifying the specific non-SARGable predicate
keyPoints: Pulls the actual execution plan to confirm a scan where a seek should be possible
Correctly identifies the function-wrapped column as the SARGability problem
Explains why this was a latent issue exposed by growth rather than a new regression
Rewrites the predicate as a range comparison against the bare column instead of transforming the column
Confirms the fix via execution plan (Index Seek) and reads/duration comparison
Understands that the index itself was never the problem

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses actual execution plan to diagnose scan vs seek
Correctly identifies non-SARGable predicate as root cause
Corrected SQL properly rewrites as a bare-column range predicate
Validates fix with plan/read comparison

questions.title: Databricks Job Cluster Costs Spike 10x Overnight
questions.prompt: Your Databricks cost dashboard shows DBU consumption jumped roughly 10x overnight with no new workload launched by anyone on the team, and finance is asking for an explanation before the month closes. Walk through how you'd investigate this and what you'd expect to find.
questions.modelAnswer: A sudden 10x overnight spike with no new workload points to one of a small number of mechanisms, and the investigation should rule them in or out in order of likelihood rather than guessing. First, pull the account's cluster event logs and billable usage system tables (system.billing.usage) filtered to the spike window, grouped by cluster and job, to see which specific compute resource actually drove the jump -- this turns 'costs spiked' into 'cluster X ran for 14 hours instead of its normal 20 minutes.' The most common root causes at this signature are: a runaway autoscaling job where a bad join or skewed partition caused the cluster to scale to its max node count and stay pinned there without actually making progress; a job whose cluster was configured without an automatic termination timeout, so it kept running (and billing) long after the job's actual work finished or failed; or a zombie all-purpose cluster that someone left running interactively and forgot, accumulating idle DBU-hours at full size overnight. Each has a distinct signature in the event log: autoscaling-to-max with flat progress looks very different from a cluster sitting idle at a fixed size for hours. Once the specific cluster and cause are identified, the immediate fix is to terminate it and look at whether a cluster policy would have prevented this -- enforcing a max node count, requiring auto-termination after N minutes of idle time, and restricting interactive all-purpose clusters from running unattended overnight are all policy-level guardrails, not one-off fixes. For the finance conversation, the answer needs to be the specific mechanism and dollar amount, plus the policy change that makes this structurally harder to repeat -- not just 'we turned off a cluster.'
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I say anything to finance, I want the actual billing data, not a guess -- so I'm pulling system.billing.usage filtered to the spike window and grouping by cluster to find exactly which compute resource drove the number up tenfold. In my experience this is almost always one of three things: a job that autoscaled to its ceiling and got stuck there churning on a bad join, a cluster with no auto-termination timeout that just kept running after the actual work was done, or an all-purpose cluster someone left running interactively overnight. Whichever it is, I want to be able to tell finance the specific story -- 'cluster X ran for 14 hours instead of 20 minutes because of a skewed join' -- rather than a vague apology. And the fix I bring back isn't just killing that one cluster; it's a cluster policy that caps max nodes and forces auto-termination, because the actual failure here is that nothing was stopping a misbehaving job from running up an unbounded bill, and that's a policy gap, not a one-off mistake by whoever launched the job.
commonMistakes: Speculates about the cause without pulling actual billing/usage system table data first
Doesn't distinguish between autoscaling-to-max-with-no-progress vs. simple idle/forgotten cluster -- different root causes, different fixes
Fixes the one cluster but doesn't propose a cluster policy to prevent recurrence
Doesn't consider that a missing auto-termination timeout is often the simplest and most common cause
Reports the dollar impact to finance without identifying the specific mechanism
keyPoints: Uses system.billing.usage / cluster event logs to find the specific resource responsible
Distinguishes runaway autoscaling, missing auto-termination, and zombie interactive clusters as distinct causes
Connects root cause to a specific, verifiable story (which cluster, how long, why)
Proposes cluster policies (max nodes, auto-termination) as the durable fix
Separates the immediate incident fix from the structural prevention

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes concrete investigation using billing/usage data
Correctly enumerates plausible root-cause mechanisms
Proposes cluster policy guardrails as the durable fix
Frames findings in terms finance/stakeholders can act on

questions.title: Redshift Queries Are Queuing for Minutes During Peak Reporting Hour
questions.prompt: Every morning at 9am, when the whole company opens its BI dashboards at once, Redshift query wait times spike into minutes even though the queries themselves run fast once they start. No single query looks slow in isolation. Walk through how you'd diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer: Queries that run fast individually but wait minutes to start is a classic WLM queuing symptom, not a query performance problem, so I'd go straight to STV_WLM_QUERY_STATE and the WLM queue metrics (via the console's Query Monitoring view or SVL_QUERY_QUEUE_INFO) to see queue wait time versus execution time per query during the 9am window specifically -- confirming that wait time, not execution time, is what's spiking. The most likely root cause at this signature is a WLM queue with too few concurrency slots for the actual peak concurrent query count: if the BI queue is configured for, say, 5 concurrent slots and 9am brings 30 simultaneous dashboard refreshes, 25 of those queries sit queued no matter how fast each one runs once it gets a slot. I'd check the queue's configured concurrency against the actual concurrent query count during the spike to confirm this specifically, rather than assuming. The durable fixes, not mutually exclusive: enable Concurrency Scaling on the BI queue, which automatically routes queued queries to transient, elastically-provisioned clusters during bursts like this exact 9am spike, at an additional cost but with no manual intervention needed; increase the queue's static concurrency slot count if the workload is predictable and a fixed higher number comfortably covers peak load; or, if individual query memory footprint is small, consider whether increasing concurrency is safe without starving per-query memory (more concurrent slots means less memory per slot at a fixed total allocation, which can turn a queuing problem into a disk-spill problem if not checked). I would not assume this needs a bigger cluster -- a concurrency/queue-depth problem often doesn't need more raw compute at all, it needs more queue slots or elastic burst capacity.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd rule out is that any individual query is actually slow -- if execution time looks fine and it's wait time spiking specifically at 9am, that's a queuing problem, not a performance problem, and I'd confirm that split directly from the WLM query state views rather than assuming. Once confirmed, my working theory is almost always that the BI queue just doesn't have enough concurrency slots for how many people actually open their dashboards at the same moment -- if the queue's capped at 5 and 30 people hit refresh together, 25 of them wait no matter how fast each query runs once it starts. From there I've got two real levers: turn on Concurrency Scaling so Redshift spins up transient burst clusters automatically during exactly this kind of spike, or raise the queue's concurrency if the load pattern is predictable enough that a higher fixed number comfortably covers it. I'd specifically avoid jumping to 'we need a bigger cluster,' because that's throwing compute at a queue-depth problem, and I'd check that raising concurrency doesn't starve per-query memory and just trade queuing for disk spill instead.
commonMistakes: Investigates individual query performance instead of checking queue wait time vs. execution time first
Jumps to resizing the cluster bigger instead of addressing WLM queue concurrency/depth
Raises queue concurrency without checking the per-query memory allocation impact
Doesn't consider Concurrency Scaling as a burst-specific solution
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes queue wait time from query execution time as the actual symptom
Confirms the diagnosis using WLM query state/queue metrics views
Identifies insufficient concurrency slots as the likely root cause
Proposes Concurrency Scaling and/or concurrency tuning, checking the memory-per-slot tradeoff

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes queuing from execution-time performance
Uses appropriate diagnostic views to confirm the root cause
Proposes concurrency scaling and/or queue tuning as the fix
Avoids the 'just resize the cluster' non-fix

questions.title: Analysts Get PERMISSION_DENIED on a Table That Just Moved Under Lake Formation Governance
questions.prompt: A team just migrated an existing Glue Catalog database to Lake Formation governance so they could add column-level permissions. The next morning, every analyst who used to query the table through Athena gets a permission-denied error, even analysts who should still have full access. Diagnose the likely cause and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The most common cause of this exact symptom is that bringing a database under Lake Formation governance changes the authorization model entirely -- before migration, access was governed purely by IAM policies on the underlying S3 location and Glue Catalog API permissions, which is how the analysts' existing roles were set up to work; after migration, Lake Formation becomes the authority for data-level permissions, and critically, Lake Formation permissions are NOT automatically backfilled from whatever IAM access those roles previously had. Unless someone explicitly re-grants Lake Formation permissions (database and table-level SELECT at minimum) to each role/principal that needs access, every one of them loses access the moment the underlying IAM-based path stops being how the authorization decision gets made, even though their IAM policy may still technically say they have Glue/S3 permissions -- Lake Formation's grant is now also required and the IAM policy alone is no longer sufficient. The fix is to explicitly grant the needed Lake Formation permissions to every analyst role that should retain access, ideally by first auditing exactly who had legitimate access before migration (from IAM policy analysis or prior query logs) and issuing matching Lake Formation grants rather than guessing, since the goal of the migration was finer-grained control, not an accidental full lockout. I'd also check whether the migrating team used the Lake Formation 'Grant on target' default behavior during migration (there's a setting that can preserve existing IAM-based access during the transition if configured) to see whether this was a configuration step that was simply missed, versus an inherent, unavoidable part of the migration that always requires re-granting.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is almost always the same story: moving a database under Lake Formation governance swaps which system actually makes the access decision, and Lake Formation does not automatically carry over whatever IAM access people already had. So analysts whose roles technically still have the old IAM/Glue/S3 permissions get denied anyway, because Lake Formation's own grant is now also required and nobody issued it yet. My first move is to confirm that's actually what happened -- check whether Lake Formation permissions exist at all for the affected roles on this database/table -- and if they don't, that confirms the migration step of re-granting access just didn't happen. The fix is straightforward but needs to be done carefully: audit who actually had legitimate access before the migration, and issue matching Lake Formation grants rather than guessing or over-granting out of urgency to unblock people. I'd also go back and check whether the migration had an option to preserve existing access during the transition that just wasn't used, so this doesn't repeat on the next table that gets migrated.
commonMistakes: Assumes the analysts' IAM roles themselves broke, rather than recognizing Lake Formation grants are a separate, additional requirement
Grants overly broad Lake Formation permissions to unblock people quickly instead of matching their prior legitimate access
Doesn't check whether a migration setting to preserve existing access was available but unused
Treats this as an IAM policy bug and starts editing IAM policies instead of issuing Lake Formation grants
keyPoints: Correctly identifies that Lake Formation governance requires its own explicit grants, not inherited from prior IAM access
Explains why existing IAM permissions alone become insufficient post-migration
Proposes auditing prior legitimate access before issuing matching grants, rather than guessing
Considers whether the migration process had a setting to preserve access that was missed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the Lake Formation grant gap as root cause
Explains why IAM access alone is no longer sufficient post-migration
Proposes a sound, audited remediation rather than overly broad re-granting
Considers process improvement for future migrations

questions.title: Cross-Account S3 Access Breaks Immediately After a New SCP Rolls Out
questions.prompt: A Glue job in Account B reading curated data from Account A's S3 bucket via a cross-account role was working fine for months. This morning it started failing with access-denied errors, right after the security team deployed a new SCP across the organization restricting allowed regions. Nothing about the IAM roles or bucket policy changed. Diagnose the likely cause.
questions.modelAnswer: SCPs apply to every principal in every account under the affected OU, including roles used for legitimate, long-standing cross-account access -- they're evaluated independently of and prior to any IAM or resource-based policy decision, so a new SCP can silently break access that no IAM or bucket policy change caused at all, which matches 'nothing about the roles or bucket policy changed' exactly. The specific mechanism here is almost certainly that the new region-restriction SCP is evaluated against aws:RequestedRegion for the API call being made, and if the Glue job's S3 client, STS assume-role call, or the Glue job's own region doesn't match the SCP's allowed region list -- which can happen subtly, for instance if the cross-account role assumption or the S3 request is being made from or targeting a region not on the approved list, even if the bucket's actual data region is approved -- the SCP denies the call before IAM or the bucket policy is ever consulted. I'd confirm by checking CloudTrail for the specific denied API call's errorCode (an SCP-caused denial shows as an explicit deny from an organization policy, distinguishable from an IAM-policy-caused denial in the event detail) and checking exactly which region the denied call was actually evaluated against. The fix is either to add an explicit exception/condition to the SCP for this legitimate cross-account access pattern if it's a known, approved exception, or more likely, to correct whichever part of the Glue job's configuration (its own region, or an STS endpoint it's calling) is making a call against a now-restricted region that it didn't need to be using in the first place. I would not simply exempt the whole role from the SCP without understanding exactly which call is being blocked and why, since that risks quietly widening an intentional security control rather than fixing the specific, narrow issue.
questions.professionalAnswer: The timing is the whole story here -- nothing in IAM or the bucket policy changed, but a brand-new, org-wide SCP just did, and SCPs apply to every principal in scope regardless of how long their access has legitimately worked. My first move is CloudTrail, specifically looking at the denied call's error detail, because an SCP-caused deny looks different from an IAM-policy deny in the event, and that tells me definitively whether this is the SCP or something else entirely coincidental. My working theory is that the region restriction is catching some part of this cross-account flow -- maybe the STS assume-role call or the Glue job's own configured region -- that's targeting a region outside the new allow-list, even if the actual data lives in an approved region. Once I confirm exactly which call and which region, the fix is narrow: either this is a legitimate pattern that needs an explicit SCP exception, or the Glue job's configuration needs to stop making a call against a region it never actually needed. I wouldn't just carve this one role out of the SCP broadly, because that undoes the point of the security team's change instead of fixing the actual, specific issue.
commonMistakes: Investigates IAM roles or the bucket policy first, missing that the timing points directly at the new SCP
Doesn't use CloudTrail to distinguish an SCP-caused denial from an IAM-policy-caused denial
Proposes broadly exempting the role from the SCP instead of identifying and fixing the specific region mismatch
Assumes the bucket's data region alone determines compliance, ignoring that other calls (STS, API endpoint) in the flow have their own region
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the new SCP's timing as the key diagnostic clue
Uses CloudTrail to distinguish SCP-caused denial from IAM/resource-policy denial
Identifies that multiple calls in a cross-account flow each have their own region to check
Proposes a narrow, specific fix rather than a broad SCP exemption

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the SCP as the likely root cause based on timing
Proposes using CloudTrail to confirm the specific denial source
Correctly reasons about region evaluation across the multi-step cross-account flow
Proposes a narrow, appropriate fix rather than broadly weakening the SCP

questions.title: An EMR Spark Job Keeps Failing Mid-Run With Lost Executors
questions.prompt: A large nightly EMR Spark job on a Spot-heavy task fleet has started failing intermittently with 'ExecutorLostFailure' errors about two-thirds through the run, roughly twice a week, with no code changes. Walk through your diagnostic approach and what you'd actually change.
questions.modelAnswer: ExecutorLostFailure with no code change and an intermittent, not-every-run pattern on a Spot-heavy task fleet points first at Spot interruptions as the most likely mechanism, so I'd check CloudWatch and EMR's own instance state change logs for Spot interruption notices correlated with the failure timestamps before assuming anything about the Spark job's logic -- if the task nodes losing executors line up with Spot reclaim events, this is an infrastructure-availability problem, not an application bug, and 'no code changes' is exactly what you'd expect in that case. If that correlation holds, the real question is why the job fails instead of recovering: Spark is designed to tolerate executor loss by rescheduling lost tasks on remaining executors, so a job failing outright on executor loss (rather than just running a bit slower) suggests either insufficient spark.task.maxFailures tolerance (too low a retry count before Spark gives up on a task entirely), or that the lost executor was holding shuffle data or cached partitions that downstream stages depended on and that aren't easily recomputed, which can cascade into a stage failure rather than a simple retry. I'd also check whether the cluster's Spot diversification is thin enough that an interruption wave can take out a large fraction of the task fleet simultaneously rather than just one or two executors, which would turn a normally-recoverable loss into a job-ending one. The concrete changes: increase spark.task.maxFailures and spark.stage.maxConsecutiveAttempts to give Spark more room to retry before giving up; broaden Spot instance type diversification across the task fleet to reduce the chance of correlated interruption; and consider External Shuffle Service or enabling dynamic allocation with shuffle tracking so that losing an executor doesn't lose shuffle data that's expensive to recompute. If Spot interruption rates for this workload's chosen instance types/pools are simply too high for a two-thirds-through-the-run job that's expensive to restart, I'd also consider shifting a portion of the fleet to on-demand for the specific later stages that are more failure-sensitive.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I touch any Spark config, I want to know if this correlates with Spot interruptions, because an intermittent failure with zero code changes on a Spot-heavy fleet is exactly the signature of infrastructure reclaiming capacity out from under the job, not a logic bug. I'd check CloudWatch and EMR's instance state logs against the failure timestamps first. If that lines up, my next question isn't 'why did Spot take an instance' -- that's expected and fine -- it's 'why is Spark not recovering from it gracefully,' because losing an executor is supposed to be survivable via task rescheduling. That usually comes down to too few retries configured, or the lost executor holding shuffle data that's expensive enough to recompute that the stage just gives up. So the real fix is giving Spark more retry headroom, diversifying the Spot instance types further so one interruption wave doesn't take out a correlated chunk of the fleet at once, and looking at shuffle resilience options so losing one executor doesn't cascade into losing a whole stage. If none of that gets the failure rate low enough for a job this expensive to restart, I'd move the later, more failure-sensitive stages to on-demand rather than fighting Spot interruptions the whole way through.
commonMistakes: Investigates the Spark job's business logic first instead of checking for Spot interruption correlation
Treats Spot interruption itself as the bug, rather than the job's insufficient recovery/retry configuration
Doesn't consider shuffle data loss as a reason executor loss cascades into stage failure
Proposes abandoning Spot entirely instead of tuning retry tolerance and diversification first
keyPoints: Correlates failure timestamps with Spot interruption events before investigating application logic
Identifies insufficient task/stage retry tolerance as the likely reason loss isn't recoverable
Considers shuffle data loss as a cascading-failure mechanism
Proposes concrete config changes (retry tolerance, diversification, shuffle resilience) over abandoning Spot

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly correlates the failure with Spot interruption as the likely root cause
Explains why executor loss should be recoverable and what prevents that here
Proposes concrete, sound configuration fixes
Considers a sensible fallback (partial on-demand) if Spot risk remains too high

questions.title: Kinesis Consumer Lag Keeps Growing Even Though the Stream Has Plenty of Shards
questions.prompt: A Kinesis stream has 20 shards, well above the throughput the traffic should need, but one specific consumer application's IteratorAgeMilliseconds metric keeps climbing hour over hour while most shards show healthy, low lag. Diagnose the likely cause and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: Growing lag on specific shards while most shards are healthy, despite an overall shard count that looks more than sufficient, points at a hot-shard/skewed-partition-key problem rather than an overall capacity problem -- if records are being distributed across shards by a partition key that isn't actually uniform (a customer ID where a handful of customers generate the overwhelming majority of traffic, or a fixed/low-cardinality key like a region code), some shards receive far more than their 1MB/sec or 1000 records/sec share while others sit nearly idle, and the consumer processing those specific overloaded shards falls progressively behind even though the stream's aggregate, total capacity (20 shards' worth) is more than enough on paper. I'd confirm this by checking per-shard incoming bytes/records metrics (not just the stream-level aggregate) to see whether traffic is actually skewed toward a small number of shards, and I'd check the consumer's own per-shard processing time to see whether it's genuinely CPU/processing-bound on those specific shards rather than something generic. If partition key skew is confirmed, resharding alone will not fix it -- splitting a hot shard without changing the partition key strategy just creates two still-hot child shards sharing the same skewed key distribution between them, so the actual fix is upstream: choosing a higher-cardinality, more uniformly distributed partition key (or adding a salt/hash suffix to a low-cardinality key to spread a dominant key's traffic across more shards deliberately), which is a producer-side change, not a shard-count change. A secondary possibility worth ruling out is that the consumer application itself has uneven per-shard processing cost (one shard's records are more expensive to process than others for business-logic reasons unrelated to volume), which would need application-level profiling rather than a Kinesis-side fix at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: Twenty shards healthy in aggregate but lag climbing on specific ones is the signature of hot-shard skew, not insufficient total capacity, so adding more shards blindly almost never fixes this -- I'd go check per-shard incoming bytes and records first, not the stream-level aggregate, to see if traffic is actually lopsided toward a small number of shards. If a handful of partition keys are generating the bulk of traffic -- a few big customers, or a low-cardinality key like region -- those specific shards are simply getting hammered regardless of how many total shards exist. The trap here is that resharding those specific hot shards doesn't actually fix the underlying problem, because splitting a skewed shard just gives you two children sharing the same skewed key distribution. The real fix is on the producer side: pick a higher-cardinality partition key, or deliberately salt a low-cardinality key so a dominant value's traffic spreads across more shards instead of concentrating on one. I'd also sanity-check that the consumer itself isn't just slower to process certain shards for unrelated business-logic reasons, since that's a separate problem that looks similar from the lag metric alone.

Resharding hot shards without changing the partition key strategy, producing two children with the same skew
Doesn't check per-shard metrics specifically, relying only on stream-level aggregates
Doesn't consider the consumer's own per-shard processing cost as an alternative explanation

Uses per-shard metrics, not stream-level aggregates, to confirm the skew
Explains why resharding alone doesn't fix a partition-key-skew problem
Proposes a producer-side partition key fix (higher cardinality or salting)

questions.title: A Glue Job Silently Reprocesses Everything After a Minor Script Change
questions.prompt: A Glue ETL job with bookmarks enabled has been running correctly for months. After a developer made what looked like a cosmetic refactor to the script (renaming a variable and reorganizing some transform steps), the next run reprocessed the entire multi-year dataset instead of just new data, duplicating records downstream. Diagnose what happened.
questions.modelAnswer: Job bookmark state is tied not just to the job's name but to its transformation context -- an internal signature Glue derives from the structure of the DynamicFrame operations in the script, used to match bookmark state to the specific transform it belongs to. A refactor that looks purely cosmetic from a human-readability standpoint (renaming a variable, reordering independent steps) can still change that underlying transformation context if it alters the actual sequence or structure of DynamicFrame transform calls Glue tracks bookmark state against, even if the net business logic is identical -- when that happens, Glue can no longer match the existing bookmark state to the 'new' transformation context and effectively treats this as a job that's never run before, reprocessing everything from the beginning. This is exactly the failure mode because it requires zero intent and gives no warning -- the job doesn't error, it just quietly does the wrong (very expensive and duplicating) thing and reports success. The immediate fix is to identify and roll back or correct the duplicated downstream records (since this already shipped a multi-year reprocess into production tables), likely via a deduplication pass keyed on whatever natural key exists, or restoring from a pre-run snapshot if available. The durable fix is process, not code: any script change beyond truly trivial edits (comments, logging) needs to be treated as a potential bookmark-breaking change and explicitly tested in a non-production environment first by confirming a bookmark-enabled run against already-bookmarked data correctly processes zero new rows after the refactor, before it ever reaches production -- 'looks cosmetic' is not sufficient evidence of safety for a bookmark-sensitive script.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mechanism here is that Glue's bookmark isn't just keyed to the job's name, it's keyed to something like a fingerprint of the actual transform structure in the script, and a change that looks purely cosmetic to a person -- renaming a variable, reordering a couple of independent steps -- can still shift that underlying fingerprint enough that Glue can't match the old bookmark to it anymore. When that happens, Glue doesn't error, it just quietly treats this as a brand-new job with no history and reprocesses everything, which is about the worst possible failure mode because nothing looks wrong until the duplicate records show up downstream. Immediate priority is fixing the damage -- dedup the reprocessed records against a natural key, or restore from a snapshot if one exists. The real fix going forward is process: I'd tell the team that for a bookmark-enabled job, there's no such thing as a 'purely cosmetic' script change that's exempt from testing -- any refactor needs to be run once against already-processed data in a non-prod environment first, specifically checking that it picks up zero new rows, before it's trusted in production. 'It looked harmless' isn't a test.
commonMistakes: Assumes the refactor couldn't have affected bookmark behavior because the business logic was unchanged
Doesn't explain the transformation-context/fingerprint mechanism tying bookmark state to script structure
Jumps to disabling bookmarks platform-wide instead of fixing the process gap that allowed an untested refactor to ship
Doesn't address the immediate data cleanup (duplicated downstream records) alongside the root-cause fix
keyPoints: Correctly explains that bookmark state is tied to transformation context, not just job identity
Explains why a 'cosmetic' refactor can still break that context and trigger a full reprocess
Addresses the immediate need to clean up duplicated downstream data
Proposes a durable process fix (pre-production bookmark-safety testing for any script change)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the transformation-context mechanism causing the reprocess
Addresses the immediate data cleanup need
Proposes a durable process fix for future script changes
Avoids an overly broad fix (disabling bookmarks entirely)

questions.title: A Step Functions Execution Fails With a States.DataLimitExceeded Error
questions.prompt: A Step Functions state machine that passes a Glue job's full output list between states starts failing with 'States.DataLimitExceeded' after a source dataset grew larger than usual. Diagnose the cause and describe how you'd redesign the workflow.
questions.modelAnswer: Step Functions caps the size of the JSON data passed between states (and in/out of the execution) at 256KB, which is a hard limit that exists regardless of execution type or account, and it's unrelated to how long or how compute-intensive the actual Glue job is -- the state machine's own data payload, not the underlying job's output data, is what's being measured. This fails here because the design is passing the Glue job's full output list (presumably a list of file paths, record identifiers, or similar) directly through the state machine's data flow as execution state, and as the source dataset grows, that list eventually crosses 256KB and the execution fails at the state transition carrying it, regardless of whether the Glue job itself completed successfully. The fix is architectural, not a retry or limit increase (there is no limit increase available for this): the state machine should never carry bulk data as its own payload. Instead, the Glue job should write its output list to S3 (as it most likely already does implicitly as a side effect, or explicitly as a manifest file), and the state machine should pass only a small reference -- the S3 URI of that manifest/output location -- between states, with any downstream state that needs the actual list reading it from S3 directly rather than receiving it inline via the state machine's data. This is a general pattern, not a one-off fix: any Step Functions design should treat the state machine's JSON payload purely as control-flow metadata (status, S3 locations, record counts, job ARNs) and never as a vehicle for the actual bulk data itself, precisely because growth in the real dataset will eventually exceed the 256KB ceiling no matter how comfortably it fits today.
questions.professionalAnswer: The 256KB limit on data passed between states is one of those things that doesn't bite you until a dataset finally grows past whatever you were implicitly relying on, and that's exactly what happened here -- the design was passing the Glue job's actual output list through the state machine itself, which works right up until the list's JSON representation crosses that ceiling, and then it just fails, with no limit increase to ask for. The fix isn't a workaround, it's correcting the pattern: the state machine should only ever carry small references -- an S3 URI, a job ID, a status -- never the actual bulk payload. So I'd have the Glue job write its output list to S3 as a manifest, pass just that S3 path through the state machine, and have any downstream state that actually needs the list read it from S3 directly. I'd also flag this as a design principle for the team going forward, not just a one-off patch, because this exact failure mode will resurface in any other workflow that's accidentally treating Step Functions' data flow as a place to carry real data instead of control-flow metadata.
commonMistakes: Tries to request a limit increase for the 256KB payload cap, which doesn't exist for this limit
Treats this as a one-off bug in this specific workflow rather than a general anti-pattern
Proposes compressing or truncating the payload instead of moving bulk data out of the state machine's data flow entirely
Doesn't recognize that the Glue job itself succeeded; only the state machine's own data handling failed
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the 256KB state machine payload limit as the cause
Distinguishes the state machine's data limit from the Glue job's own execution success
Proposes passing an S3 reference instead of bulk data through the state machine
Frames this as a general design principle, not a one-off patch

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the payload size limit as the root cause
Correctly distinguishes state machine data limits from job execution success
Proposes the correct architectural fix (S3 reference pattern)
Frames the fix as a reusable design principle

questions.title: A DMS CDC Task Falls Further and Further Behind During a Large Migration
questions.prompt: A DMS task migrating a high-write on-prem database is in its CDC phase, catching up after the full load. Replication lag, instead of shrinking toward zero, keeps growing over several days. Walk through your diagnostic sequence.
questions.modelAnswer: Growing (not shrinking) CDC lag means the task is processing changes slower than the source is generating them, so the investigation needs to identify which side of that imbalance is the bottleneck rather than assuming either side by default. First, I'd check the DMS replication instance's own CloudWatch metrics -- CPUUtilization, FreeableMemory, and specifically CDCLatencySource vs. CDCLatencyTarget, which separate 'DMS is behind reading the source's change stream' from 'DMS is behind applying changes to the target' and point the investigation in a completely different direction depending on which one is actually growing. If CDCLatencySource is growing, the replication instance itself is likely undersized for the source's write volume -- insufficient CPU/memory to keep up with reading and parsing the transaction/redo log stream -- and the fix is to scale up the replication instance class. If CDCLatencyTarget is growing while source latency is stable, the target database is the bottleneck -- common causes are insufficient target write capacity (an undersized Aurora/RDS instance class, or a target still building large indexes/constraints that slow every write), too few DMS parallel load/apply threads configured for the target, or large unbatched LOB columns forcing slow, one-at-a-time LOB processing mode instead of batch-optimized processing. I'd also check whether the target has indexes and constraints that were enabled too early -- a common mistake is leaving secondary indexes active during the CDC catch-up phase, which slows every single write; best practice is often to defer non-critical secondary index creation until after the bulk of CDC catch-up, if the migration tooling/plan allows it. The fix, once the bottleneck side is identified, is specific to that side -- scale the replication instance, scale the target, tune LOB handling mode, or adjust parallel apply settings -- rather than a generic 'add more resources everywhere' response.
questions.professionalAnswer: Growing lag, not shrinking, tells me the imbalance is getting worse, not just present, so I need to find out which side of the pipe is actually the bottleneck before I touch anything. DMS actually splits this out for you -- CDCLatencySource versus CDCLatencyTarget -- and that split changes my entire next step. If source latency is climbing, the replication instance itself probably can't keep up reading the source's change stream fast enough, and that's a sizing problem on the DMS instance. If target latency is climbing while source is fine, the target database is the bottleneck, and that's usually either an undersized target, too few parallel apply threads, or -- this one catches people constantly -- secondary indexes still active on the target during CDC catch-up, which slows down every single write landing there. I'd check LOB handling too, since large LOB columns in non-optimized mode can tank apply throughput all by themselves. Whatever I find, the fix is specific to that one bottleneck, not a blanket 'throw more resources at the whole thing' response.
commonMistakes: Doesn't distinguish source-side vs. target-side latency before proposing a fix
Assumes the DMS replication instance is always the bottleneck without checking target-side metrics
Doesn't consider that active secondary indexes on the target slow every write during CDC catch-up
Doesn't check LOB column handling mode as a potential apply-throughput bottleneck
keyPoints: Uses CDCLatencySource vs. CDCLatencyTarget to localize the bottleneck before acting
Considers replication instance sizing as the source-side fix
Considers target sizing, parallel apply threads, and active indexes as target-side causes
Considers LOB handling mode as a specific, often-overlooked apply bottleneck

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses source vs. target latency metrics to localize the bottleneck
Identifies plausible source-side root causes and fixes
Identifies plausible target-side root causes and fixes, including indexes and LOB handling
Proposes a bottleneck-specific fix rather than a generic resource increase

questions.title: Redshift Spectrum Queries Suddenly Slow Down After a Partition Count Explosion
questions.prompt: A Redshift Spectrum external table over S3 data, partitioned by year/month/day/hour, has been performing well for a year. After switching an upstream pipeline to write smaller, more frequent files, Spectrum query latency has tripled even though the total data volume barely changed. Diagnose the cause.
questions.modelAnswer: A Spectrum query's planning cost scales with the number of partitions and files it has to enumerate and prune against, not just total data volume -- if an upstream pipeline change shifted from writing fewer, larger files per partition to many smaller files at the same total data volume, the partition metadata and file listing Spectrum has to process during query planning grows substantially even though nothing about the actual bytes of data changed, and very small files also hurt the actual scan phase, since reading many small files carries more per-file open/read overhead than reading fewer larger ones, with no corresponding benefit in parallelism once file count far exceeds the available Spectrum compute slots. I'd confirm this by checking the actual average file size in the affected partitions before and after the pipeline change (via S3 inventory or a quick listing), and checking SVL_S3QUERY_SUMMARY or the query's own explain plan for file count scanned and time spent in S3 scan versus aggregation -- a jump in files-scanned-per-partition with roughly flat total bytes is the confirming signal. The fix is on the write side, not the query side: configure the upstream pipeline (whether it's a Glue job, Kinesis Firehose buffering, or application-level batching) to target a healthier file size, typically in the 128MB-1GB range for Parquet depending on the engine's recommendations, by adjusting buffer/batch size or adding a compaction step that periodically merges many small files into fewer larger ones within each partition -- a compaction job run on a schedule (hourly or daily) is a common, durable pattern when the source can't be tuned to write larger files directly. I would not try to fix this purely from the Spectrum/Redshift side, since the root cause is upstream file layout, not anything about how the external table or query is defined.
questions.professionalAnswer: Total data volume staying flat while latency triples, right after a pipeline change to smaller, more frequent files, is exactly the small-files problem -- Spectrum's planning cost scales with how many files and partitions it has to enumerate, not just total bytes, and lots of tiny files also just carry more per-file overhead during the actual scan with no real parallelism benefit once file count outpaces available compute slots. I'd confirm it quickly by checking average file size before and after the pipeline change and looking at files-scanned in the query's explain output -- if that jumped while bytes stayed flat, that's the confirmation. The fix has to happen upstream, not in Redshift -- I'd get the pipeline writing fewer, larger files by adjusting its buffer or batch size, or if the source genuinely can't write larger files directly, add a scheduled compaction job that merges small files within each partition into a healthier size. I wouldn't spend time trying to tune this from the Spectrum or query side, because the actual problem is sitting in S3's file layout, not in how the external table is defined.

Doesn't connect 'flat data volume, higher latency' to a small-files problem specifically

Doesn't propose a concrete remediation (buffer tuning or scheduled compaction)

Proposes a concrete way to confirm it (file size/count comparison, scan plan metrics)
Correctly locates the fix upstream in the pipeline's write pattern, not in Redshift/Spectrum
Proposes a specific remediation (batch/buffer tuning or scheduled compaction)

questions.title: A Monthly AWS Bill Shows a Huge, Unexplained Line Item With No Obvious Owner
questions.prompt: This month's AWS bill shows a large, unfamiliar charge under a service nobody remembers provisioning, and Cost Explorer's tag breakdown shows it as 'untagged.' Walk through exactly how you'd track down what it is, who owns it, and whether it should be decommissioned.
questions.modelAnswer: Since the cost allocation tag breakdown is unhelpful here (untagged), I'd go around it rather than through it: Cost Explorer's own 'Usage Type' and 'Linked Account' grouping (not just tags) will at minimum identify which account and which specific AWS service/usage type the charge belongs to, which narrows the search dramatically even with zero tags. From there, CloudTrail's event history (or, for older activity beyond its default retention, a configured CloudTrail trail with S3-archived logs) lets me search for the resource creation events for that service type in that account around when the charge started appearing, which typically reveals the IAM principal (user or role) that actually created it and the timestamp -- that's usually enough to identify an owner even when tags were never applied. If CloudTrail history doesn't reach back far enough, AWS Config (if enabled) maintains a configuration history and resource inventory that can also identify when a resource was created and its attributes. Once I have the resource identified and dated, I'd check whether it's still being used (CloudWatch utilization/access metrics for compute, access logs for storage, connection counts for databases) before concluding it's safe to decommission -- an untagged resource is often also an unmonitored one, and 'nobody remembers it' is not the same as 'nobody is using it'; I've seen untagged legacy resources turn out to be quietly load-bearing. Only after confirming genuine non-use (or getting explicit sign-off from whoever CloudTrail identifies as the creator, if they're still reachable) would I decommission it. The durable fix, regardless of what this specific resource turns out to be, is the SCP/tag-policy enforcement gap that let an untagged resource get created and run unnoticed long enough to generate a surprise bill line -- I'd flag that as the real finding to bring back to the team, not just 'we found and deleted one thing.'
questions.professionalAnswer: Tags being empty just means I go around them instead of through them. Cost Explorer's linked-account and usage-type breakdown still works without any tags, so that's my first stop to narrow down which account and which specific service this actually is. From there, CloudTrail is where I find out who actually created it -- searching resource-creation events for that service around when the charge first showed up usually surfaces the IAM principal and the exact timestamp, which gets me an owner even with zero tagging discipline on the resource itself. Before I touch anything, though, I want to know if it's actually being used right now -- untagged doesn't mean unused, and I've been burned before by assuming a forgotten-looking resource was dead when it was quietly serving something real. So I check utilization or access metrics first, and I'd try to actually reach whoever CloudTrail says created it before decommissioning anything. And honestly, the resource itself is almost the smaller story here -- the bigger finding I'd bring back to the team is that our tagging enforcement has a gap that let this run unnoticed long enough to show up as a surprise line item, and that's the thing actually worth fixing.

questions.title: A Cross-Account Glue Job Can't Decrypt Its Source Data After a KMS Key Rotation
questions.prompt: A Glue job in Account B has been reading KMS-encrypted objects from Account A's S3 bucket for months via a cross-account grant. After Account A's security team rotates the customer-managed KMS key (creating a new key and re-encrypting new objects with it, per policy), the Glue job starts failing to decrypt newly written objects while older objects still decrypt fine. Diagnose the cause.
questions.modelAnswer: This points at a specific, common KMS rotation mistake: 'rotating a key' in the sense of creating a brand-new CMK and re-encrypting new objects with it is a different operation from KMS's own automatic key rotation (which rotates the underlying cryptographic material behind the same key ARN and ID, transparently, with zero impact to existing grants or policies) -- if Account A's team created an actual new CMK (new key ID/ARN) rather than relying on automatic rotation of the existing key, then every cross-account permission previously granted (the key policy's cross-account principal statement, and Account B's own IAM policy permitting kms:Decrypt against the old key's specific ARN) was scoped to the OLD key's ARN and does not automatically carry over to the new key -- older objects, still encrypted under the old key, decrypt fine because the old grants are still valid and that key still exists; newly written objects encrypted under the new key fail because neither side's permission structure has been updated to reference the new key's ARN at all. The fix is to replicate the same cross-account grant structure for the new key: update the new CMK's key policy to include the same cross-account principal statement that existed on the old key, and update Account B's IAM policy to permit kms:Decrypt against the new key's ARN specifically (ARNs in IAM/KMS policies don't support wildcarding across unrelated key IDs safely, so this needs an explicit, deliberate update, not a guess). I'd also flag this as a process gap for Account A's security team: any 'key rotation' that actually means creating a new CMK (rather than relying on KMS's built-in automatic annual rotation of an existing key's material) needs to include updating every downstream cross-account grant as part of the same change, not as an afterthought discovered via a consumer's job failure.
questions.professionalAnswer: The giveaway is that old objects still decrypt and new ones don't -- that tells me the rotation wasn't KMS's built-in automatic key rotation, which rotates material behind the same key ARN with zero impact on existing grants. This sounds like the security team created an actual new CMK and started encrypting new objects with it, which means every cross-account permission that existed -- the key policy's grant to Account B's role, and Account B's own IAM policy permitting decrypt -- was scoped to the old key's specific ARN and just doesn't apply to the new one at all. Old objects still work because the old key and its grants are still there; new objects fail because nothing's been set up yet for the new key. The fix is mechanical but has to happen on both sides: update the new key's policy to grant the same cross-account access the old key had, and update Account B's IAM policy to allow decrypt against the new key's specific ARN. The bigger thing I'd flag to the security team is that this should have been part of the same change -- a key 'rotation' that actually swaps in a new CMK needs updating every downstream cross-account grant as a required step, not something a consuming team discovers by their job breaking.
commonMistakes: Confuses creating a new CMK with KMS's automatic key rotation of an existing key's material
Doesn't explain why old objects still decrypt while new ones fail (the key ARN distinction)
Updates only one side (key policy or consumer IAM policy) instead of both
Doesn't flag the process gap that let a new-key rollout ship without updating cross-account grants
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes a new CMK creation from KMS's automatic key material rotation
Explains why old objects still decrypt while new ones fail, based on key ARN scoping
Proposes updating both the key policy and the consumer IAM policy for the new key
Flags the process gap for future key rollouts

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes new-CMK creation from automatic key rotation
Correctly explains the old-vs-new object decrypt behavior
Proposes the correct two-sided fix for the new key
Flags the process gap for future rotations

questions.title: Athena Queries Over a Kinesis Firehose-Delivered Dataset Are Suddenly Timing Out
questions.prompt: A Kinesis Firehose delivery stream writes records to S3 every 60 seconds (its default buffering interval), and Athena queries over that data, which used to run in seconds, now regularly time out. The team recently increased ingest volume by onboarding a new, high-throughput data source onto the same Firehose stream. Diagnose the cause.
questions.modelAnswer: Firehose's buffering model writes one file per buffering interval (or buffer size, whichever triggers first) per delivery stream, so a fixed 60-second interval at a MUCH higher ingest volume doesn't produce fewer, bigger files automatically -- if the buffer size threshold wasn't also increased, higher throughput at the same time-based interval can actually still produce a reasonable file size, but the far more common and classic version of this exact problem is the opposite: a Firehose stream configured with a short buffering interval produces many small files per hour regardless of volume, and adding a new high-throughput source onto the SAME delivery stream multiplies the total number of small files being produced per interval, without necessarily making each individual file meaningfully bigger -- more sources funneling into the same short-interval stream means more total objects landing in S3 per unit time, and Athena's query planning and execution cost scales with the number of files and partitions it has to open and scan, so a growing small-files problem is the most likely explanation for a timeout appearing right after onboarding a new source onto the same stream. I'd confirm by checking the actual file count and average file size in the affected S3 prefix before and after the new source was onboarded -- a sharp increase in file count with flat or only modestly increased total bytes per file confirms this. The fix: either increase Firehose's buffering size/interval settings (fewer, larger files per delivery, at the cost of slightly higher end-to-end latency, which is usually an acceptable tradeoff if 60-second freshness isn't a strict requirement) or route the new high-throughput source onto its own separate Firehose delivery stream (writing to a different S3 prefix, or the same prefix with a scheduled downstream compaction job merging files), rather than funneling ever-more volume through one stream's fixed small-file cadence. I would not try to fix this from the Athena/query side -- the file layout upstream is the actual problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: The timing -- right after a new high-throughput source got added to the same Firehose stream -- is the big clue. Firehose writes one file per buffering interval per stream, so if that interval is still short, adding a lot more volume onto the same stream doesn't make each file meaningfully bigger, it just means a lot more total small files landing in S3 per hour, and Athena's planning and scan cost scales with file count, not just total bytes. I'd confirm quickly by checking file count and average file size in that prefix before and after the new source was onboarded -- if file count jumped while average size stayed flat or barely moved, that's the answer. The fix is upstream, not in the query: either widen Firehose's buffering interval or size so it's producing fewer, larger files -- which is fine if slightly higher latency is acceptable -- or give the new high-throughput source its own separate delivery stream entirely rather than sharing the original stream's small-file cadence. I wouldn't spend time trying to tune the Athena side here, since the actual problem is sitting in how many objects Firehose is producing upstream.

Assumes higher throughput automatically means bigger files without checking the buffering configuration
Doesn't connect multiple sources sharing one delivery stream to a multiplied small-files problem
Proposes an Athena-side fix instead of addressing the upstream file layout

Connects multiple sources sharing one delivery stream to a multiplied file-count problem
Proposes a sound way to confirm (file count/size comparison)
Proposes the correct upstream fix (buffering tuning or separate delivery streams)

Connects the new source onboarding to a multiplied file-count effect
Proposes a sound confirmation method
