questions.title: Design an Org-Wide Cost Governance Model for Databricks Clusters
questions.prompt: A company with 15 teams running Databricks workloads has no consistent cluster governance -- some teams run all-purpose clusters for scheduled jobs, auto-termination is inconsistently configured, and nobody has visibility into which team is driving which cost. Design a cost governance model covering cluster policy, job vs. all-purpose usage, and budget accountability.
questions.modelAnswer: The core architectural tool here is Databricks cluster policies, which let a platform team define and enforce constraints (max node count, allowed instance types, mandatory auto-termination timeout, mandatory tags) at the policy level so individual engineers can't configure a cluster outside acceptable bounds -- rather than relying on 15 teams to independently remember and apply cost best practices, the policy becomes the enforced default. I'd design a small set of tiered policies: a 'job cluster' policy for scheduled/automated workloads (ephemeral, spun up per job, auto-terminating on completion, which is inherently cheaper than persistent all-purpose clusters for anything non-interactive), and an 'interactive/all-purpose' policy with a mandatory short auto-termination timeout (e.g., 30-60 minutes of idle time) and a capped max node count, since all-purpose clusters are for active development, not for running unattended scheduled jobs -- the current state of 'teams run all-purpose clusters for scheduled jobs' is itself the single biggest avoidable cost driver, since job clusters are billed only for the job's actual runtime while all-purpose clusters bill for however long they stay up, idle or not. Every policy should mandate cost-attribution tags (team, cost-center, environment) at cluster-creation time, enforced by the policy itself rather than relying on voluntary tagging discipline, which is what makes real chargeback possible afterward. For visibility, the Databricks system tables (system.billing.usage joined to cluster tags) feed a cost dashboard broken down by team/cost-center, reviewed on a regular cadence -- and budget accountability means each team gets a visible, owned number, with alerting when a team's trailing consumption trend suggests they'll exceed a set threshold, so a cost conversation happens proactively rather than at month-end reconciliation. Migrating existing ad hoc all-purpose-for-scheduled-jobs patterns to proper job clusters, enforced going forward via policy rather than a one-time cleanup, is the single highest-leverage structural change in this list.
questions.professionalAnswer: If I only get to fix one thing here, it's that teams are running all-purpose clusters for scheduled jobs -- that's the single most expensive habit in this list, because all-purpose clusters bill for however long they're up, idle included, while a job cluster only bills for the actual job runtime and auto-terminates the moment it's done. So step one is cluster policies: a job-cluster policy for anything scheduled/automated, and a separate interactive policy for actual development work, with a short mandatory auto-termination timeout and a capped node count baked into the policy itself, not left to each engineer's discretion. I want cost-attribution tags -- team, cost center, environment -- enforced at the policy level too, because voluntary tagging never survives contact with 15 different teams' habits, and without consistent tags there's no real chargeback story. Once that's in place, the system billing tables joined to those tags give me an actual per-team cost dashboard, reviewed regularly, with alerts when a team's trend is heading toward a problem -- because the goal isn't to surprise anyone with a bill at month-end, it's for each team to own a visible number and see it coming.
commonMistakes: Proposes cost dashboards/reporting without addressing cluster policy enforcement as the actual root cause
Doesn't identify all-purpose-clusters-for-scheduled-jobs as the single biggest avoidable cost driver
Relies on voluntary tagging discipline instead of enforcing tags at the cluster-policy level
Doesn't distinguish appropriate use cases for job clusters vs. all-purpose clusters
No proactive alerting on cost trend, only after-the-fact monthly reporting
keyPoints: Identifies all-purpose clusters running scheduled jobs as the primary avoidable cost driver
Proposes tiered cluster policies (job vs. interactive) with enforced auto-termination and node caps
Enforces cost-attribution tags at the policy level, not via voluntary discipline
Builds per-team cost visibility from system billing tables joined to enforced tags
Adds proactive trend-based alerting, not just after-the-fact reporting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies all-purpose-for-scheduled-jobs as the primary cost driver
Proposes sound tiered cluster policy design
Proposes enforced tagging for real cost attribution
Proposes proactive cost visibility/alerting, not just reporting

questions.title: Design a Multi-Account AWS Data Platform Landing Zone With Lake Formation
questions.prompt: A company is standing up a new multi-account AWS data platform: a central data lake account, several producer accounts (each team's raw/curated data), and several consumer accounts (BI, data science, finance). Design the account structure, where Lake Formation's metadata and permissions live, and how a producer's data becomes discoverable and governable by consumers without granting broad cross-account S3 access.
questions.modelAnswer: The standard, durable pattern is a hub-and-spoke model with a dedicated central 'data lake' or 'shared services' account hosting the Lake Formation-governed Glue Data Catalog as the single source of truth for metadata and permissions, while the underlying data itself can physically remain in each producer account's own S3 buckets (Lake Formation supports registering S3 locations that live in different accounts under one central catalog, via resource links and cross-account data location registration) -- this avoids forcing every producer team to migrate their actual data into a shared bucket, which is operationally painful and raises its own blast-radius concerns, while still centralizing where permissions are declared and audited. Producer accounts register their S3 locations with the central Lake Formation catalog (granting the catalog's data lake administrator role access to their bucket) and create/update table metadata in the shared catalog describing their data, making it discoverable without yet granting anyone read access to the actual bytes -- registration and permission-granting are deliberately separate steps. Consumer accounts receive access entirely through Lake Formation grants issued from the central catalog -- database, table, or column/row-level SELECT permissions granted to specific IAM principals in the consumer account -- rather than through direct S3 bucket policies or IAM cross-account roles pointing at producer buckets, which is the critical architectural discipline: no consumer account should ever need a direct IAM/S3 relationship with a producer account's bucket, because that would bypass the fine-grained governance the whole design exists to centralize. AWS RAM (Resource Access Manager) is the underlying mechanism Lake Formation uses to share catalog resources across accounts, and because the catalog is centralized, a single audit of Lake Formation's grants gives a complete picture of who can see what across the entire platform, which a model of scattered bucket policies and ad hoc cross-account roles across dozens of account pairs could never give cleanly. SCPs at the OU level (producer OU, consumer OU, platform OU) provide the account-wide guardrail layer underneath all of this, but the actual data-level governance decision always routes through the one central catalog.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set this up hub-and-spoke: one central account owns the Lake Formation-governed Glue Catalog as the single source of truth, but I would not force every producer team to move their actual data into that central account's buckets -- that's a painful migration and it concentrates blast radius in one place unnecessarily. Instead, producer accounts register their own S3 locations with the central catalog and publish table metadata there, which makes their data discoverable without yet granting anyone read access to it -- registration and granting access are two separate steps on purpose. The rule I'd enforce hardest: no consumer account ever gets a direct IAM role or bucket policy pointing at a producer's S3 bucket. Every single grant to a consumer flows through Lake Formation permissions issued from the central catalog, so if someone asks 'who can see this table,' there's exactly one place to check the answer, not forty scattered bucket policies to audit. SCPs at the OU level give me the account-wide guardrails underneath all of this, but the actual governance decision -- who sees what data -- always goes through that one catalog, never around it.
commonMistakes: Forces all producer data to physically migrate into a central account's buckets instead of using cross-account location registration
Allows consumer accounts to get direct IAM/S3 cross-account access to producer buckets, bypassing centralized governance
Conflates data location registration with granting access, treating them as one step
Doesn't mention AWS RAM as the underlying cross-account sharing mechanism for the catalog
keyPoints: Designs a hub-and-spoke model with a central Lake Formation-governed catalog as the single source of truth
Keeps data physically in producer accounts via cross-account location registration rather than forced migration
Enforces that all consumer access flows through central Lake Formation grants, never direct cross-account S3/IAM
Mentions AWS RAM as the sharing mechanism and SCPs as the underlying account-wide guardrail

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a sound hub-and-spoke multi-account topology
Correctly handles data location without forced migration
Enforces centralized Lake Formation grants as the only access path for consumers
Mentions the correct supporting mechanisms (RAM, SCPs)

questions.title: Design an Enterprise Redshift Topology: RA3, Spectrum, and Data Sharing Across BI and ML Clusters
questions.prompt: An enterprise has one production Redshift cluster serving BI dashboards and a growing data science team that wants heavy, unpredictable ad hoc compute against the same data without risking the BI cluster's stability. Design a multi-cluster Redshift architecture using RA3 nodes, Spectrum, and data sharing that solves this without duplicating the underlying data.
questions.modelAnswer: The architectural move is to stop treating 'one cluster for everyone' as the default and instead provision a second, independently-sized RA3 cluster (or Redshift Serverless endpoint) dedicated to the data science team's workload, sized and scaled for its own bursty, unpredictable compute pattern without any ability to starve the BI cluster -- RA3's managed storage architecture is what makes this clean, because the actual data lives in managed storage decoupled from any one cluster's compute, and Redshift data sharing lets the new ML cluster read the BI cluster's (producer) live data directly, with no ETL, no copy, and no staleness beyond normal consistency, by granting specific databases/schemas as shared objects to the consumer cluster. This solves the stability problem completely: a runaway ad hoc query on the ML cluster can only ever consume the ML cluster's own compute, never touch the BI cluster's WLM queues, memory, or concurrency at all, because the two are fully separate compute layers, even though they're reading the same underlying managed-storage data. For data that genuinely lives in the lake rather than in Redshift (raw/intermediate datasets the data science team also needs, that were never curated into the warehouse), Spectrum lets either cluster query that S3-resident data directly without an additional data-sharing relationship, extending the same 'don't duplicate data to get access to it' principle to the lake side of the house. Cost-wise, this isn't free -- you're now paying for two clusters' compute instead of one -- but the alternative (one shared cluster, unpredictable ad hoc compute contending with BI dashboards) is a recurring reliability and trust problem, not a cost savings; I'd position this as isolating a known instability risk with a bounded, predictable new cost, rather than a pure cost optimization. I'd also set the ML cluster's workload to Redshift Serverless specifically if its usage pattern is genuinely spiky/intermittent rather than steady, since Serverless's pay-per-use model fits unpredictable ad hoc analytics better than a continuously-provisioned second cluster would.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fix here isn't tuning WLM harder on one shared cluster -- it's giving the data science team their own cluster, because no queue configuration fully protects BI from truly unpredictable, heavy ad hoc compute sharing the same box. I'd stand up a second RA3 cluster, or a Serverless endpoint if their usage is genuinely spiky rather than steady, and use Redshift data sharing so that new cluster reads the BI cluster's live data directly -- no copy, no ETL, no staleness beyond the normal consistency window. That's what actually solves the stability problem: a bad query on the data science side can only ever burn their own cluster's compute, full stop, because the two clusters don't share anything except the view into the same underlying managed storage. For anything that's genuinely lake-resident rather than warehouse data, Spectrum covers that the same way, without us duplicating it anywhere. I'd be upfront that this costs more, not less -- two clusters instead of one -- but I'd frame that as the price of actually isolating a real reliability risk, not something that's going to show up as a savings line.
commonMistakes: Tries to solve this purely with WLM tuning on a single shared cluster instead of separating compute
Proposes duplicating/ETL-ing data into a second cluster instead of using data sharing
Doesn't mention RA3's managed storage as the architectural enabler of data sharing without duplication
Presents the two-cluster design as a cost optimization rather than honestly framing it as added cost for isolation
keyPoints: Proposes a separate, independently-scaled cluster/endpoint for the unpredictable workload
Uses Redshift data sharing to avoid duplicating data between the clusters
Explains RA3's managed storage as what makes data sharing possible without copying
Uses Spectrum for genuinely lake-resident data on either cluster
Honestly frames the cost tradeoff as isolation, not savings

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes correct workload isolation via a separate cluster/endpoint
Correctly uses data sharing to avoid duplication
Correctly explains RA3/managed storage's enabling role
Honestly frames the cost tradeoff

questions.title: EMR at Scale: Spot Fleet Strategy vs. EMR Serverless Across a Platform's Many Batch Workloads
questions.prompt: A platform runs 40 different nightly Spark batch jobs with wildly different data volumes and resource needs. Design a decision framework for which workloads go on EMR Serverless versus a shared, policy-governed Spot-heavy EMR cluster fleet, and how you'd prevent the inevitable sprawl of 40 teams each wanting their own cluster configuration.
questions.modelAnswer: At 40 jobs, the first architectural decision is refusing to let this become 40 bespoke cluster configurations -- that sprawl is itself the governance failure to design against, not an acceptable outcome of diverse workloads. I'd segment jobs by a small number of actual, measurable characteristics rather than by team identity: data volume variability (does this job's size swing night to night, or is it predictable), need for non-Spark engines or deep custom tuning, and runtime duration/latency sensitivity. Jobs with variable or unpredictable volume and standard Spark/Hive needs go on EMR Serverless, since its per-job auto-provisioning removes the sizing guesswork entirely for exactly this profile and removes 'should this cluster be bigger or smaller tonight' as a question anyone has to answer. Jobs with steady, predictable, large, or long-running profiles, or that need specific instance types/non-Spark engines/deep YARN tuning, go onto a small number of shared, policy-governed EMR cluster templates -- not 40 individual configurations, but perhaps 3-4 standard templates (e.g., 'standard Spark batch,' 'large shuffle-heavy Spark,' 'Hive-compatible') that cover the actual range of legitimate needs, each with its own Spot Fleet diversification strategy, auto-termination, and max-size guardrails defined once and reused. The governance mechanism preventing sprawl is treating cluster configuration as a managed, versioned artifact (via EMR cluster templates/blueprints or an internal Infrastructure-as-Code module) that teams select from and request parameters for, rather than a free-form configuration any team can author from scratch -- a platform team owns and reviews the small set of templates, and onboarding job #41 means picking the closest-fit existing template or making the case for a new one, not writing a one-off config. I'd track this discipline over time via a simple metric: number of distinct cluster configurations in use relative to number of jobs -- if that ratio keeps climbing toward 1:1, the governance is failing regardless of how good any individual job's setup looks.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd fight hardest against here is 40 jobs turning into 40 snowflake cluster configs, because that's not flexibility, that's an unmaintainable platform six months from now. My framework is simple: if a job's volume is unpredictable or swings a lot night to night and it's just standard Spark, it goes on EMR Serverless -- that removes the sizing guesswork entirely, which is exactly the problem with variable workloads. If a job is steady, large, long-running, or needs something Serverless doesn't support well -- a specific instance type, a non-Spark engine, deep tuning -- it goes on a shared EMR cluster, but not a bespoke one per job; I'd define maybe three or four standard cluster templates that cover the real range of legitimate needs, each with its own Spot diversification and guardrails baked in once. Onboarding job 41 means picking the closest template, not writing a new config from scratch, and if nothing fits, that's a conversation with the platform team about whether we need a new template, not a one-off exception. I'd actually track the ratio of distinct configurations to total jobs as a health metric -- if that number keeps climbing, the governance model is failing no matter how good any single job's setup looks in isolation.
commonMistakes: Allows each team to author its own bespoke cluster configuration, accepting sprawl as unavoidable
Doesn't propose a clear, measurable basis (volume variability, duration, engine needs) for the Serverless vs. cluster decision
Proposes EMR Serverless for every job regardless of fit, or clusters for every job regardless of fit
No concrete governance mechanism (templates, platform team review) to actually prevent future sprawl
keyPoints: Proposes a clear, measurable decision framework (volume variability, engine needs, duration) rather than team-based choice
Correctly scopes EMR Serverless and shared cluster templates to the right workload profiles
Proposes a small number of governed, reusable cluster templates instead of per-job configuration
Proposes a concrete metric/mechanism to prevent configuration sprawl over time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sound, measurable decision framework for Serverless vs. cluster
Correctly scopes each option to the right workload profile
Proposes a concrete governance mechanism preventing config sprawl
Proposes a way to measure/track the governance over time

questions.title: Design a Kinesis Ingestion Architecture With Multi-Shard Rebalancing and Managed Flink Aggregation at Scale
questions.prompt: A platform needs to ingest clickstream events from a mobile app at a scale that will grow from thousands to potentially millions of events per second over the next two years, compute rolling real-time engagement metrics, and land both raw and aggregated data for later batch analysis. Design the end-to-end streaming architecture.
questions.modelAnswer: Given the scale trajectory described (thousands growing toward millions of events/sec over two years), I'd start the ingestion layer on Kinesis Data Streams in On-Demand mode rather than manually provisioning and resharding a fixed shard count for a workload whose growth curve is this uncertain -- On-Demand autoscales shard count transparently as throughput grows, removing the operational burden of forecasting and manually resharding repeatedly over a two-year growth period, with a switch to Provisioned mode considered later only if the workload's throughput becomes predictable enough that Provisioned's lower unit cost at steady, known volume becomes worth the operational tradeoff. Partition key design is the other critical early decision, independent of shard count or mode: events should be keyed by something with genuinely high cardinality and even distribution (a hashed user or device ID, not a low-cardinality field like event type or app version) so that as shard count grows with volume, traffic actually spreads across the growing shard count rather than concentrating on a few hot shards regardless of how many shards exist -- this decision is nearly impossible to retrofit painlessly later, so it needs to be right from day one. For the real-time rolling engagement metrics (session duration, rolling active-user counts, windowed aggregates), Managed Service for Apache Flink is the correct consumer, since this is genuinely stateful, event-time-aware, windowed computation that Lambda's invocation model isn't built for -- Flink reads directly from the Kinesis stream, maintains checkpointed window state, and writes aggregated results to wherever they're consumed next (a fast-access store like DynamoDB for live dashboards, and/or back into a second stream for further downstream consumption). For landing both raw and aggregated data for batch analysis, Kinesis Data Firehose (a second, separate consumer of the same source stream, which Kinesis supports via multiple independent consumers, ideally using enhanced fan-out for Flink's dedicated throughput so Firehose's batch-oriented reads don't compete with Flink's low-latency reads) delivers the raw event stream to S3 in a partitioned, compacted layout for later Athena/Redshift Spectrum analysis, while Flink's aggregated output is separately persisted (either via Firehose again from Flink's output stream, or a direct sink) to its own curated location. Enhanced fan-out is the detail that prevents this multi-consumer design from degrading either consumer's throughput as volume grows, since without it, multiple consumers reading the same shards share that shard's fixed read throughput rather than each getting their own dedicated 2MB/sec per shard.
questions.professionalAnswer: Given this is going from thousands to potentially millions of events per second over two years, I wouldn't start by hand-provisioning and manually resharding a fixed-shard stream -- I'd put Kinesis in On-Demand mode so shard count scales with actual throughput automatically, and revisit Provisioned mode later only once the volume is predictable enough that the cost tradeoff actually favors it. The decision I'd be most careful about upfront, though, isn't shard count at all -- it's the partition key. It needs to be something genuinely high-cardinality and evenly distributed, like a hashed device ID, because a bad partition key choice means traffic concentrates on a few shards no matter how many total shards exist, and that's painful to fix after the fact. For the real-time rolling metrics, this is genuinely stateful windowed computation, so I'd put Managed Flink directly on the stream rather than trying to hand-roll that with Lambda, and have it write results to something fast like DynamoDB for live dashboards. For landing both raw and aggregated data for batch analysis, I'd add Firehose as a second, independent consumer of the same stream -- and I'd specifically turn on enhanced fan-out so Flink's low-latency reads and Firehose's batch-oriented reads aren't competing for the same shard's fixed throughput as volume climbs, because without that, scaling up actually starts working against both consumers at once.
commonMistakes: Provisions a fixed shard count and commits to manual resharding for a workload with this much growth uncertainty
Doesn't address partition key design as a critical, hard-to-retrofit early decision
Proposes Lambda for the stateful windowed aggregation instead of Managed Flink
Doesn't mention enhanced fan-out, risking throughput contention between multiple consumers as volume grows
keyPoints: Chooses On-Demand mode given the uncertain, large growth trajectory
Treats partition key design as a critical, early, hard-to-retrofit decision
Uses Managed Flink for genuinely stateful, windowed real-time aggregation
Uses Firehose as an independent second consumer for raw+aggregated batch landing
Uses enhanced fan-out to prevent multi-consumer throughput contention at scale

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly chooses scaling mode given the growth trajectory
Correctly addresses partition key design as critical and early
Correctly applies Managed Flink for the stateful aggregation need
Designs a sound multi-consumer landing architecture with enhanced fan-out

questions.title: Design a Step Functions Hub Pipeline Orchestrating Dozens of Teams' Pipelines Platform-Wide
questions.prompt: A platform wants a single orchestration layer that triggers and sequences dozens of teams' individually-owned Glue, EMR, and Lambda pipelines, with per-team visibility into their own pipeline's status without exposing the whole platform's internals to every team. Design the Step Functions architecture.
questions.modelAnswer: A single, monolithic state machine trying to encode dozens of teams' individual pipeline logic is the wrong architecture at this scale -- it becomes an unreviewable, high-blast-radius single point of failure where one team's change risks breaking every other team's pipeline, and it makes per-team visibility into 'their' status awkward since everyone's logic lives in one shared execution. The correct pattern is a hub-and-spoke state machine design: each team owns and maintains its own 'spoke' state machine, encoding that team's specific pipeline logic (its Glue jobs, EMR steps, Lambda functions, in whatever sequence and with whatever error handling that team's pipeline actually needs), which that team can change independently without coordinating with anyone else or risking other teams' pipelines. A central 'hub' state machine (or an EventBridge-based trigger layer feeding into each spoke directly) handles platform-wide concerns -- overall scheduling/triggering, cross-team dependency ordering where one team's pipeline genuinely depends on another's completion (via Step Functions' ability to start an execution of another state machine and optionally wait for it), and platform-wide status aggregation -- without needing to know the internal step-by-step details of any individual team's spoke. For per-team visibility without full platform exposure, each team's own observability (CloudWatch dashboards, or a status API) should read that team's own spoke's execution history directly (standard, fully-detailed Standard workflow execution history, scoped by IAM to that team's resources), rather than trying to carve a filtered view out of one shared, platform-wide state machine's history, which would require much more complex access control to achieve the same isolation this design gets for free. This architecture also directly limits blast radius: a bug in one team's spoke state machine can at most break that team's own pipeline, never cascade into breaking the orchestration of the other 39 teams' pipelines, which a single shared state machine fundamentally cannot guarantee.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back hard on the idea of one giant state machine encoding every team's pipeline logic, because that becomes a single point of failure where any one team's change can break everyone else's pipeline, and it makes 'show this team only their own status' an access-control headache instead of something that falls out naturally. My architecture is hub-and-spoke: every team owns their own state machine with their own Glue/EMR/Lambda sequencing and error handling, and they can change it freely without touching anyone else's. A thin hub layer handles the platform-wide concerns -- triggering, and any genuine cross-team dependencies, using Step Functions' ability to kick off and optionally wait on another state machine's execution -- without needing to understand the internals of any one team's pipeline. For visibility, each team just looks at their own spoke's execution history directly, scoped by IAM to their own resources, which gives them full detail on their own pipeline with zero chance of seeing anyone else's internals, and without me having to build some custom filtered view into a shared execution log. The real win of this design is blast radius: a bug in one team's spoke can only ever break that one team's pipeline, never cascade into the other 39.
commonMistakes: Proposes one monolithic state machine encoding every team's pipeline logic
Doesn't address blast-radius isolation between teams' pipelines
Proposes building a custom filtered view into a shared execution history instead of giving teams direct, scoped access to their own spoke
Doesn't address how genuine cross-team dependencies are handled in a decentralized design
keyPoints: Rejects a monolithic state machine in favor of a hub-and-spoke design
Gives each team ownership of their own independently-changeable spoke state machine
Uses a thin hub layer for platform-wide triggering and genuine cross-team dependencies
Achieves per-team visibility via scoped, direct access to each team's own execution history

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rejects a monolithic design in favor of hub-and-spoke
Designs sound team ownership and blast-radius isolation
Designs a sound mechanism for platform-wide triggering/cross-team dependencies
Designs sound, scoped per-team visibility

questions.title: Scaling Glue Job Bookmarks and Data Quality Gates Across Thousands of Jobs
questions.prompt: A platform is growing from dozens to thousands of Glue ETL jobs across many teams. Design the structural approach to keeping job bookmarks reliable and enforcing a consistent data quality gate across all of them, without requiring a central team to review every individual job's script.
questions.modelAnswer: At thousands-of-jobs scale, the only sustainable model is templated, enforced standards rather than central review of individual scripts -- a platform team cannot and should not review a thousand scripts by hand, so the architecture needs to make the correct behavior the path of least resistance for every team authoring a new job. For bookmarks, I'd provide a standard job template/library (a shared internal Glue job skeleton or a thin Python wrapper module) that correctly calls job.init() and job.commit() and that explicitly discourages the kind of 'cosmetic refactor that breaks the transformation context' failure mode by keeping bookmark-sensitive logic isolated and documented in the template rather than left to each team's own interpretation; alongside this, I'd build a lightweight automated check (run in CI before a job's script is deployed) that executes the job against a small fixture dataset twice in a row and asserts the second run processes zero new records when bookmarks are enabled, catching a bookmark-breaking change automatically before it ships, rather than relying on every team remembering to test this manually. For data quality, I'd provide a small number of standard, reusable Glue Data Quality rulesets (DQDL) as shared library components -- common patterns like 'primary key not null and unique,' 'numeric column within expected range,' 'row count within N% of trailing average' -- that teams attach to their own tables with their own thresholds, rather than writing custom validation from scratch each time, plus a platform-wide requirement (enforced via a required CI step, not a policy document) that every production Glue job must include at least a baseline ruleset before it can deploy. Crucially, this is enforcement-by-tooling, not governance-by-request: both the bookmark test and the data quality ruleset requirement should be CI gates that block a deploy on failure, because a platform of a thousand jobs cannot rely on a central team manually verifying compliance across all of them, and 'ask teams nicely to follow the standard' does not scale past the dozens-of-jobs stage this platform is already leaving behind.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest answer at this scale is that a central team reviewing a thousand scripts by hand just isn't a plan -- it has to be enforcement through tooling, not through a review queue. For bookmarks, I'd give every team a shared job template that already correctly calls job.init() and job.commit(), so the easy path is also the correct path, and I'd back that up with an automated CI check that actually runs the job twice against a small fixture and asserts the second run picks up zero new rows -- that catches a bookmark-breaking refactor automatically, before it ships, instead of relying on a thousand different engineers remembering to test it themselves. For data quality, I'd build a small library of reusable Glue Data Quality rulesets covering the common patterns -- key integrity, range checks, row-count sanity -- that teams attach with their own specific thresholds rather than writing validation from scratch every time, and I'd make at least a baseline ruleset a required, CI-enforced step before any production job can deploy, not a guideline in a wiki somewhere. The core principle I'd defend in any review of this design: at a thousand jobs, 'ask nicely and document the standard' has already failed, and the only thing that actually scales is making compliance something the pipeline enforces automatically.
commonMistakes: Proposes a central team reviewing every job's script manually, which doesn't scale to thousands of jobs
Relies on documentation/policy alone ('teams should follow this standard') instead of automated CI enforcement
Doesn't propose a concrete, automated test for bookmark-breaking changes
Doesn't propose reusable, shared data quality rule components, leaving each team to build validation from scratch
keyPoints: Rejects manual central review as unscalable at thousands-of-jobs scale
Proposes a standard job template/library reducing the chance of bookmark-breaking mistakes
Proposes an automated CI test that specifically catches bookmark-breaking changes before deploy
Proposes reusable Glue Data Quality rule components enforced via CI, not policy alone

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rejects manual review as the scaling mechanism
Proposes a sound templating/library approach to bookmark reliability
Proposes a concrete automated test catching bookmark-breaking changes
Proposes reusable, CI-enforced data quality components

questions.title: Design a Large-Scale On-Prem-to-AWS Database Migration Using DMS
questions.prompt: A company needs to migrate 200+ on-prem SQL Server databases (varying sizes, some over 1TB) to Aurora PostgreSQL within six months, with each application team responsible for their own database's cutover timing. Design the migration architecture, including how DMS resources are provisioned and managed at this scale, and how you'd sequence 200 independent cutovers safely.
questions.modelAnswer: At 200+ databases, the architecture has to be templated and largely automated, not 200 individually hand-built DMS tasks -- I'd build a standard migration pipeline (parameterized by source connection details, target database name, and table mapping) deployable via Infrastructure as Code, so onboarding database #150 means supplying parameters to an existing, tested pattern rather than someone hand-configuring a new DMS task from scratch, which both scales the team's actual capacity and reduces the chance of a one-off misconfiguration on any given migration. For replication instance provisioning, I would NOT share one large replication instance across all 200 migrations -- that creates both a performance bottleneck (database #180's CDC catch-up competing for the same instance's CPU/memory as database #50's) and a single point of failure where one replication instance issue could stall many migrations simultaneously; instead, I'd provision replication instances per-migration (or in small, isolated pools grouped by rough size/criticality tier) that get torn down after each cutover completes, keeping the per-migration blast radius small and cost proportional to actual migration activity rather than a large standing instance running for six months regardless of how many migrations are actively in CDC phase at any moment. For sequencing 200 independent cutovers, each with its own team-controlled timing, I'd design this as a self-service pattern with platform-provided guardrails rather than a central scheduler dictating every team's cutover date: each team's migration pipeline runs full-load-plus-CDC and sits in a 'ready to cut over' state once validation passes, and the team triggers their own cutover when ready, within an overall six-month program deadline enforced by a visible, shared tracking dashboard (not a hard technical gate) showing which of the 200 are migrated, in-progress, or not yet started, so the program can identify and intervene on stragglers well before the deadline rather than discovering a pile-up in month 5. For heterogeneous SQL-Server-to-PostgreSQL migrations specifically at this volume, I'd pair the AWS Schema Conversion Tool's automated conversion reporting with a required sign-off step per database (not skippable) confirming someone has reviewed SCT's compatibility report for untranslatable stored procedures/triggers before that database's cutover is allowed, since this is exactly the kind of correctness risk that a templated, high-velocity migration program could otherwise silently paper over at scale.
questions.professionalAnswer: Two hundred databases in six months only works if this is a templated, largely self-service pipeline, not 200 individually hand-built migrations -- I'd build one parameterized, IaC-deployed migration pattern and have each team supply their own connection details and table mapping into it, so onboarding database 150 is a config exercise, not a bespoke build. On replication instances, I'd specifically avoid one shared big instance for all 200 -- that's both a performance bottleneck when several migrations are in CDC at once and a single point of failure for the whole program. I'd provision per-migration (or small isolated pools by size tier), torn down after cutover, so cost tracks actual activity and one instance problem can't stall unrelated migrations. For sequencing, since each team owns their own cutover timing, I wouldn't try to centrally schedule 200 cutover dates -- I'd make each migration self-service once it's validated and sitting ready, with a shared, visible tracking dashboard against the six-month deadline so the program can spot and intervene on stragglers in month 2 or 3, not discover a pile-up in month 5. And because this is heterogeneous -- SQL Server to Postgres -- I'd make a per-database sign-off on the Schema Conversion Tool's compatibility report a required, non-skippable step before cutover, because a program moving this fast is exactly where an untranslated stored procedure quietly slips through if nobody has to explicitly check.
commonMistakes: Proposes 200 individually hand-built DMS tasks instead of a templated, parameterized pipeline
Shares one large replication instance across all migrations, creating a bottleneck and single point of failure
Proposes a centrally-dictated cutover schedule instead of a self-service model with program-level tracking
Doesn't address heterogeneous schema/code conversion risk (SCT review) as a required gate at this scale
keyPoints: Designs a templated, parameterized, IaC-deployed migration pattern rather than 200 bespoke builds
Avoids a single shared replication instance; uses per-migration or pooled, torn-down instances
Designs a self-service cutover model with program-level visible tracking rather than central scheduling
Adds a required SCT compatibility sign-off gate for the heterogeneous migration risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a sound templated/self-service migration pipeline at this scale
Correctly designs replication instance provisioning to avoid bottleneck/SPOF
Designs a sound decentralized cutover sequencing approach with tracking
Addresses heterogeneous migration correctness risk with a concrete gate

questions.title: Design a Cost Governance Architecture Across an Entire AWS Data Platform
questions.prompt: Design a complete cost governance architecture for an AWS data platform spanning Redshift, EMR, Glue, Kinesis, and S3 across 20 teams: covering tagging enforcement, commitment strategy (Savings Plans/RIs/Spot), budget alerting, and how cost accountability is actually assigned to each team.
questions.modelAnswer: The foundation everything else depends on is enforced, not voluntary, tagging -- an AWS Organizations tag policy defining the required tags (team, cost-center, environment) paired with SCPs using aws:RequestTag conditions to deny resource creation for taggable services unless those tags are present, rolled out with a grace period for existing untagged resources rather than an immediate hard block; without this foundation, every other piece of cost governance (chargeback, budgets, commitment planning) is working from incomplete data and will quietly mislead whoever relies on it. On top of that foundation: cost allocation tags activated in Billing (a separate, easily-forgotten step from the tag policy itself) feed a Cost Explorer/QuickSight dashboard broken down by team and service, refreshed on a regular cadence and reviewed with each team, not just centrally. For commitment strategy, I'd size Compute Savings Plans against the platform's aggregate, historically-observed steady-state baseline (not per-team, since Savings Plans apply account/org-wide and don't need per-team allocation to work correctly), covering a deliberately conservative percentage of that baseline rather than 100%, with Spot specifically scoped to fault-tolerant workloads (EMR task nodes, batch Glue jobs where interruption-and-retry is safe) and never to Redshift clusters, EMR master/core nodes, or anything stateful/SLA-critical. Budget alerting needs to be per-team and proactive, not platform-wide and reactive: AWS Budgets configured per cost-center/team tag, with alerts firing on trending-toward-overage (using the forecast feature, not just actual-spend-exceeded) so a team sees a problem forming in week 2 of the month, not a bill shock in week 4. Accountability is the governance piece that actually makes all of this stick: each team should see their own cost dashboard as a visible, owned number (not a report that lands in their inbox and gets ignored), ideally with a lightweight monthly review cadence where a team explains any significant month-over-month change, which creates the social/organizational pressure that technical tooling alone never fully achieves -- a dashboard nobody is accountable for explaining tends to get ignored regardless of how good the underlying data is.
questions.professionalAnswer: Nothing else in this works without enforced tagging first -- I'd put an Organizations tag policy and a paired SCP in place requiring team and cost-center tags on creation, rolled out with a grace period so I'm not breaking 20 teams' existing automation on day one. That's the foundation; everything downstream of it -- chargeback, budgets, commitment planning -- is only as good as that tagging discipline. One step people forget: activating those tags as cost allocation tags in Billing is separate from the tag policy itself, and I'd check that explicitly rather than assume it happened. For commitments, I'd size Savings Plans against the platform's aggregate steady-state usage, not per-team, since Savings Plans work at the account/org level anyway, and I'd deliberately not cover 100% of that baseline so we have headroom if it shrinks. Spot gets scoped tightly to fault-tolerant workloads only -- EMR task nodes, retryable batch Glue jobs -- never Redshift, never anything stateful. For budgets, I want per-team alerts using the forecast feature, so a team sees they're trending toward a problem in week two, not finding out after the bill posts. But the piece that actually makes any of this stick long-term is accountability -- each team needs to see their own number as theirs to own, ideally with a short monthly check-in where they explain a real change, because a dashboard nobody has to explain anything about just gets ignored no matter how accurate the underlying data is.
commonMistakes: Proposes chargeback/budgeting without first addressing enforced (not voluntary) tagging as the foundation
Forgets the separate cost-allocation-tag activation step in Billing
Sizes commitment coverage per-team instead of against aggregate platform usage
Scopes Spot too broadly, including stateful or SLA-critical workloads
Proposes only reactive, platform-wide budget alerting instead of per-team, forecast-based alerts
Doesn't address organizational accountability, treating this as a purely technical/tooling problem
keyPoints: Establishes enforced tagging (tag policy + SCP) as the governance foundation
Correctly sizes commitment strategy against aggregate usage with deliberate headroom
Correctly scopes Spot to fault-tolerant workloads only
Designs per-team, forecast-based proactive budget alerting
Addresses organizational accountability as a necessary complement to the technical design

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Establishes enforced tagging as the foundation with correct mechanism
Designs a sound commitment strategy (Savings Plans/Spot scoping)
Designs sound, proactive per-team budget alerting
Addresses organizational accountability, not just tooling

questions.title: Design the KMS Key and Lake Formation Permission Architecture for a Regulated Multi-Tenant Platform
questions.prompt: A platform stores data for multiple external customers (multi-tenant) in a shared AWS account, subject to a contractual requirement that no customer's data can ever be decrypted or queried by code/roles belonging to another customer's workload, even accidentally. Design the KMS key strategy and Lake Formation permission model that enforces this.
questions.modelAnswer: Given the contractual bar is 'never, even accidentally,' the design needs to make cross-tenant access structurally impossible, not just policy-disallowed -- a single shared KMS key for all tenants' data would mean any role with decrypt permission on that key could, through a misconfigured grant or an IAM policy mistake, read any tenant's data, so the architecture should use one customer-managed KMS key per tenant, each with a key policy granting decrypt access only to that specific tenant's workload role(s), never a broader principal. This means a misconfiguration (an overly broad IAM policy, an accidental Lake Formation grant) involving Tenant A's workload role still cannot decrypt Tenant B's data, because Tenant B's data was never encrypted with a key Tenant A's role has any path to -- the isolation is enforced by the encryption boundary itself, not solely by an access policy that could be misconfigured. On the Lake Formation side, I'd mirror this with per-tenant databases/schemas in the Glue Catalog (not one shared database with row-level tenant filtering, which still relies entirely on every single grant being configured correctly to maintain isolation) -- a per-tenant database boundary, combined with Lake Formation grants scoped per-tenant database to only that tenant's own role, means a Lake Formation grant mistake for Tenant A's role is scoped to Tenant A's own database structurally, not just by convention. Combining both layers -- per-tenant KMS keys AND per-tenant catalog databases with matching grants -- creates defense in depth: even if one layer is somehow misconfigured, the other layer still blocks cross-tenant access, which is the actual bar 'never, even accidentally' requires, since relying on a single layer (even a well-configured one) being perfectly correct forever is not a credible guarantee at any real scale or team-change velocity. I'd also recommend an automated, scheduled audit (not just point-in-time manual review) checking that no KMS key policy or Lake Formation grant ever references a principal outside its own tenant's expected role set, catching drift before it becomes an actual incident.
questions.professionalAnswer: 'Never, even accidentally' tells me policy alone isn't a strong enough guarantee -- I want the isolation to be structural, not just correctly configured. So every tenant gets their own customer-managed KMS key, with a key policy scoped to only that tenant's workload role, never anything broader. That means even if someone misconfigures an IAM policy for Tenant A's role, there's no path for it to decrypt Tenant B's data, because Tenant B's data was never encrypted under a key Tenant A's role has any relationship to at all -- the encryption boundary itself is doing the enforcement, not just an access policy that could theoretically be wrong. I'd mirror that on the Lake Formation side with per-tenant Glue databases rather than one shared database with row-level filtering, because row-level filtering still depends on every grant being perfectly correct forever, while a separate database per tenant means a bad grant for Tenant A is still scoped to Tenant A's own database by construction. Running both layers together is the real point -- if one layer ever gets misconfigured, the other one still holds the line, which is the only way I'd actually trust a 'never, even accidentally' commitment at scale. And I'd add a scheduled automated audit checking for any KMS or Lake Formation grant that references a principal outside its expected tenant, so drift gets caught before it turns into an actual breach.
commonMistakes: Proposes a single shared KMS key for all tenants with access controlled purely by IAM/grant policy
Proposes row-level tenant filtering in one shared database as sufficient isolation, relying entirely on grant correctness
Treats a single layer of control (KMS or Lake Formation alone) as sufficient for a 'never, even accidentally' requirement
No automated drift detection/audit mechanism, relying only on initial correct configuration
keyPoints: Proposes per-tenant KMS keys so cross-tenant decryption is structurally impossible, not just policy-disallowed
Proposes per-tenant Glue databases rather than shared-database row filtering for the same structural reason
Explains the defense-in-depth value of combining both layers
Proposes an automated, scheduled audit to catch configuration drift

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes per-tenant KMS keys for structural isolation
Correctly proposes per-tenant catalog databases over shared-database filtering
Explains the defense-in-depth rationale for combining both layers
Proposes an automated audit/drift-detection mechanism

questions.title: AWS Certified Data Engineer-Caliber System Design: A Lake-Plus-Warehouse Platform From Scratch
questions.prompt: Design, end to end, a new AWS data platform for a retail company: ingesting daily batch sales data from 500 stores' POS systems plus a real-time clickstream from their e-commerce site, landing both in a governed data lake, serving a Redshift-based BI layer, and supporting ad hoc data science access -- at the level of system design expected for the AWS Certified Data Engineer - Associate exam.
questions.modelAnswer: Ingestion splits by source pattern: the 500 stores' daily batch POS extracts land in a raw S3 zone (partitioned by date and store), likely delivered via a scheduled upload or DMS if sourced from each store's local database, while the e-commerce clickstream flows through Kinesis Data Streams (On-Demand, given retail traffic's seasonal and promotional spikes are hard to forecast precisely) into both a raw S3 landing zone (via Firehose) and a real-time aggregation path (Managed Flink) for live metrics. A Glue Data Catalog, governed by Lake Formation, sits over the S3 raw and curated zones as the single metadata and permissions layer -- Glue Crawlers (or Glue job-managed schema registration, preferred for anything with a known, controlled schema to avoid crawler-inferred schema drift surprises) catalog both the batch and streaming-landed data, and Glue ETL jobs (with bookmarks enabled, and Glue Data Quality rules gating the output) transform raw data into a curated zone -- deduplicated, conformed, partitioned appropriately for downstream query patterns (likely by date for both sources, given typical retail reporting needs). The curated zone feeds two consumption paths: Redshift (RA3 nodes, loaded via COPY from the curated S3 data or incrementally via Glue, with Spectrum available for anything that doesn't need to be physically loaded) serves the BI layer with predictable, governed schemas and strong query performance for recurring dashboards, while data scientists get ad hoc access either directly via Athena against the curated (and raw, where relevant) S3 zones -- avoiding the need to load everything into Redshift just to let data science poke at it -- or via Redshift data sharing from a read replica/second cluster if their workload needs are heavy enough to risk BI stability on a shared cluster. Orchestration across the batch pipeline (ingest -> catalog -> transform -> quality gate -> load) runs through Step Functions (Standard, given the multi-hour, auditable nature of a nightly retail batch load), with CloudWatch providing end-to-end pipeline monitoring and alerting at each stage. Security threads through all of it: IAM least-privilege roles per service/job, Lake Formation column/row-level grants for anything genuinely sensitive (customer PII in the clickstream data, for instance), and KMS encryption at rest on every S3 zone and the Redshift cluster. This is exactly the kind of multi-service, lake-plus-warehouse design the Data Engineer - Associate exam tests: knowing which AWS service fits which part of the pipeline, not just that each service individually exists.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split ingestion by pattern first: the 500 stores' daily batch extracts land in a raw S3 zone, partitioned by date and store, while the e-commerce clickstream goes through Kinesis -- On-Demand mode, since retail traffic around promotions and holidays is genuinely hard to forecast precisely -- feeding both a raw S3 landing path via Firehose and a real-time aggregation path via Managed Flink for live metrics. Everything sits under one Lake Formation-governed Glue Catalog, with Glue ETL jobs -- bookmarks on, Data Quality rules gating the output -- turning raw data into a curated zone that's deduplicated and sensibly partitioned for how it'll actually get queried. From there, two consumption paths: Redshift on RA3 nodes for the BI layer, where dashboards need predictable performance and governed schemas, and Athena directly against the curated S3 zone for data science ad hoc work, so I'm not forcing every exploratory query through a load into Redshift first. Orchestration for the nightly batch runs on Step Functions Standard, since this is a multi-hour pipeline where I actually want full execution history for debugging. And security runs through the whole thing, not bolted on at the end -- least-privilege IAM per service, Lake Formation column-level grants on anything like customer PII in the clickstream, and KMS encryption everywhere data rests. This is really the core skill the Data Engineer exam is testing: knowing which service earns its place in which part of the pipeline, not just that AWS has a service for everything.
commonMistakes: Doesn't differentiate ingestion architecture for the batch vs. streaming source, forcing both through the same pattern
Loads everything into Redshift rather than using Athena/Spectrum for ad hoc data science access to curated lake data
Doesn't mention Lake Formation governance or column-level protection for sensitive clickstream data (PII)
Omits orchestration, monitoring, or security as distinct, necessary architectural layers rather than afterthoughts
keyPoints: Correctly differentiates batch and streaming ingestion architecture by source pattern
Designs a governed lake (Glue Catalog + Lake Formation) as the central metadata/permissions layer
Correctly splits BI (Redshift) and data science (Athena/Spectrum) consumption paths
Addresses orchestration, monitoring, and security as integral architectural layers, not afterthoughts

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs differentiated batch and streaming ingestion
Designs a sound governed lake and catalog layer
Correctly designs BI and data science consumption paths appropriately
Integrates orchestration, monitoring, and security throughout the design
