questions.title: Design an AWS Landing Zone for Onboarding an Acquired Company's Data Estate
questions.prompt: Your company just acquired a smaller company that runs its own separate AWS environment with its own data platform. Leadership wants that acquired company's data estate integrated into the parent's multi-account AWS Organization within a year, without disrupting the acquired team's ability to keep operating day to day. Design the onboarding approach.
questions.modelAnswer: The right first move is NOT a rushed lift-and-shift of the acquired company's AWS account into the parent Organization -- it's inviting their existing account(s) into the parent Organization as member accounts via AWS Organizations' account invitation flow, which preserves their existing resources, workloads, and day-to-day operations completely untouched while bringing them under the parent's organizational umbrella for billing consolidation and future governance, all without a single resource needing to move. Once inside the Organization, I'd apply a deliberately staged set of SCPs -- starting permissive (closer to whatever the acquired account already had) and tightening gradually toward the parent's standard guardrails over weeks or months, rather than immediately applying the parent's full production SCP set on day one, since an abrupt, strict SCP change on an account that was previously unrestricted is a well-known way to break working production systems the acquired team depends on, which directly conflicts with the 'don't disrupt day-to-day operations' requirement. For actual data integration (the harder, longer-term part), I'd treat this as a parallel, deliberately paced workstream separate from the Organizations onboarding: setting up cross-account Lake Formation data sharing (or resource-based S3 access) so the parent's platform can start reading the acquired company's curated data early, well before any full migration, which delivers real integration value immediately without forcing a risky wholesale data migration on a deadline. The actual migration of workloads/data into the parent's standard account structure (if that's ultimately the goal, versus permanent cross-account sharing) should be sequenced by risk and value -- lower-risk, well-understood datasets first, to build pattern and confidence, with anything core to the acquired team's daily operations migrated last and only once the new environment has been proven on the lower-risk items. I'd set the one-year target as a milestone for 'meaningfully integrated and governed,' not necessarily 'fully migrated,' since over-promising a full technical migration within a year while also promising zero disruption to a live, operating team is often not an honest combination of commitments.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move would specifically not be rushing their account into a lift-and-shift -- I'd invite their existing AWS account into our Organization as-is via the standard account invitation flow, which brings them under our organizational umbrella for billing and future governance without moving or touching a single one of their existing resources. From there, I'd apply our SCPs gradually, starting close to whatever constraints they already had and tightening toward our standard guardrails over weeks, not on day one -- slamming a strict, unfamiliar SCP set onto a previously-unrestricted account is a reliable way to break something they depend on, and that directly works against the 'don't disrupt their operations' ask. For the actual data integration, I'd run that as its own separate, slower-paced track -- setting up Lake Formation cross-account sharing so our platform can start reading their curated data early, which gets real integration value flowing well before any full migration happens. Any eventual migration of their workloads into our standard structure I'd sequence by risk: lower-stakes, well-understood datasets first to build confidence and a proven pattern, and anything core to their daily operations last, only once we've shown the new environment works on the easy stuff. And I'd be honest with leadership that a one-year target realistically means 'meaningfully integrated and governed,' not 'fully migrated' -- promising both a full migration and zero disruption on a one-year clock isn't a credible combination.
commonMistakes: Proposes an immediate lift-and-shift or full migration instead of an Organizations invitation preserving existing operations
Applies the parent's full, strict SCP set immediately, risking breaking the acquired team's working systems
Conflates data integration (cross-account sharing) with full data migration as if they're the same step
Doesn't sequence migration by risk, or overpromises full migration within the deadline while also promising zero disruption
keyPoints: Proposes Organizations account invitation to preserve existing operations, not a rushed lift-and-shift
Proposes gradual, staged SCP tightening rather than immediate full enforcement
Separates data integration (cross-account sharing) from full data migration as distinct workstreams
Sequences any migration by risk and sets an honest, realistic milestone for the deadline

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes preserving operations via Organizations invitation, not a rushed migration
Proposes sound, gradual SCP rollout
Correctly separates data integration from full migration as workstreams
Sets a realistic, honest milestone framing for the deadline

questions.title: Design a Disaster Recovery Architecture for a Cross-Region AWS Data Platform
questions.prompt: Design a disaster recovery strategy for a data platform built on S3, Glue, Redshift, and Step Functions, covering a full regional outage of the platform's primary region, with a target of a few hours of recovery time and minimal data loss for the curated Redshift layer specifically.
questions.modelAnswer: The DR design needs to be layered by service, since each one has a different native cross-region capability and a different appropriate strategy -- there's no single 'turn on DR' switch for a platform this heterogeneous. S3 is the easiest piece: enabling S3 Cross-Region Replication on the raw and curated buckets gives a continuously-replicating copy in the DR region with minimal operational effort, and S3's durability characteristics mean this layer is close to a solved problem once CRR is configured correctly with the right IAM roles and replication rules. Glue's actual job definitions, scripts, and catalog metadata are not natively cross-region replicated, so these need an explicit, automated process -- Infrastructure as Code (the Glue jobs, crawlers, catalog database/table definitions) deployed to both regions as part of normal CI/CD, treating the DR region's Glue environment as a standing, code-deployed twin rather than something built manually during an actual disaster, when speed and calm execution are both compromised. Redshift, given the explicit 'minimal data loss for curated data' requirement, needs the most deliberate design: Redshift doesn't natively replicate a live cluster cross-region continuously, so the practical options are (a) automated, cross-region-copied snapshots on a tight schedule (hourly or more frequent, depending on how much data loss -- the gap since the last snapshot -- is actually tolerable) that can be restored into a new cluster in the DR region during an actual failover, accepting data loss bounded by the snapshot interval, or (b) for a tighter RPO, maintaining a warm standby cluster in the DR region kept reasonably current via Redshift data sharing or a parallel load pipeline that writes to both regions' curated layers, which costs meaningfully more (a second running cluster) but gets much closer to minimal data loss than snapshot-based recovery. Given 'minimal data loss' is explicitly called out for Redshift specifically, I'd lean toward the warm-standby-with-dual-write approach for the curated layer rather than snapshot-only, accepting the added cost as the direct, necessary tradeoff for that stated requirement. Step Functions state machine definitions (being just JSON/code) deploy to both regions via the same CI/CD as Glue; actual in-flight executions at the moment of a regional outage are not something that can be 'failed over' mid-execution, so the DR runbook needs an explicit step to identify and safely restart any interrupted pipeline executions in the DR region rather than assuming failover resumes them automatically. I'd validate all of this with a scheduled, actual DR drill (not a tabletop exercise alone) at least annually, since an untested DR plan commonly fails in ways that only show up during a real cutover attempt.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design this service by service, because there's no single switch that covers a stack this varied. S3 is the straightforward piece -- Cross-Region Replication on the raw and curated buckets, configured correctly, and that layer's basically handled. Glue is different: its job code and catalog metadata don't replicate cross-region on their own, so I'd deploy Glue's jobs and catalog definitions to both regions through normal CI/CD as a standing, always-current twin, rather than trying to stand that up manually during an actual outage when nobody's thinking clearly under pressure. Redshift is where I'd spend the most design effort, because 'minimal data loss' was called out specifically for the curated layer. Redshift doesn't natively replicate a live cluster cross-region, so the real choice is snapshot-based recovery, which is cheaper but bounds your data loss to the snapshot interval, or a warm standby cluster kept current via data sharing or a dual-write pipeline, which costs more but actually delivers on 'minimal' data loss. Given that requirement was stated explicitly, I'd go with the warm standby and just own the added cost as the price of that specific ask. Step Functions definitions deploy the same way as Glue's code, but I'd be upfront that executions already in flight when the region goes down aren't something that automatically resumes in the other region -- the runbook needs an explicit step for identifying and safely restarting interrupted pipelines. And none of this is real until it's been tested with an actual drill, not just a tabletop discussion, at least once a year, because DR plans reliably fail in ways nobody predicts until someone actually tries the cutover.
commonMistakes: Treats DR as a single uniform strategy across all services instead of designing per-service based on native capability
Proposes only snapshot-based Redshift recovery despite the explicit 'minimal data loss' requirement for that specific layer
Doesn't address that Glue job code/catalog metadata needs explicit cross-region deployment, assuming it replicates automatically
Doesn't address in-flight Step Functions executions at the moment of failover
Proposes a DR plan with no scheduled drill/validation
keyPoints: Designs per-service DR strategy rather than one uniform approach
Correctly uses S3 CRR for the storage layer
Correctly addresses Glue code/catalog needing explicit cross-region IaC deployment
Chooses a Redshift DR approach that honestly matches the stated minimal-data-loss requirement
Addresses in-flight execution handling and recommends a scheduled, real DR drill

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs sound, correctly differentiated per-service DR strategies
Correctly matches the Redshift DR approach to the stated data-loss requirement
Addresses Glue/Step Functions code and in-flight execution handling
Recommends real, scheduled DR validation

questions.title: Design a Data Mesh Using Lake Formation Cross-Account Sharing Between Domain Teams
questions.prompt: Leadership wants to move from one centralized data engineering team owning all pipelines to a data mesh model, where each business domain (orders, inventory, customer) owns and publishes its own data products, discoverable and consumable by other domains without a central team in the critical path. Design how Lake Formation and account structure support this.
questions.modelAnswer: A data mesh model maps cleanly onto one AWS account per domain (an 'orders' account, an 'inventory' account, a 'customer' account), each owning its own data pipeline, its own S3 storage, and critically, its own decision about what to publish as a 'data product' and to whom -- this is the architectural expression of domain ownership the mesh model requires, as opposed to the prior centralized model where one team's account/pipeline touched everything. A central 'catalog' or 'governance' account hosts the Lake Formation-governed Glue Data Catalog as the mesh's shared discovery layer, but critically, that central account does NOT own the actual pipelines or make domain-level data decisions -- its role is narrow: hosting the metadata catalog and the mechanics of cross-account registration/sharing, while each domain account registers its own tables into the shared catalog and independently decides, via its own Lake Formation grants, which consuming accounts/roles get access to which of its tables, at what grain (column/row level where needed) -- this is what keeps domain teams out of a central team's critical path for publishing or granting access, since the domain team itself issues the grant, not a central gatekeeper. For discoverability without requiring a central team's involvement, the catalog's table and column descriptions/metadata (ideally enriched with ownership, freshness SLAs, and a contact for the owning domain team, which Lake Formation's catalog metadata or an attached data catalog tool like DataZone can carry) let a consuming domain find and request access to another domain's data product by browsing the catalog, with the actual grant still issued by the producing domain, not by the central platform team acting as an approval bottleneck. The central governance account's remaining real job is defining and enforcing the baseline standards every domain's data product must meet to be published at all (a minimum data quality gate, required metadata fields, naming conventions) via a lightweight, automated certification check rather than manual gatekeeping -- this preserves genuine domain autonomy for publishing and granting access day to day, while still preventing the mesh from degrading into complete chaos with no baseline standard at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: The account structure should mirror the domain ownership the mesh model is actually asking for -- one account per domain, each owning its own pipeline and its own publishing decisions, which is a real architectural shift from one team's account touching everything. I'd still centralize the catalog itself, because discovery needs one place to look, but I'd be deliberate that the central account's job is narrow -- host the Lake Formation-governed catalog and the cross-account sharing mechanics, not make domain-level publishing or access decisions. Each domain registers its own tables into that shared catalog and issues its own Lake Formation grants to whoever wants to consume its data, which is the detail that actually keeps a central team out of the critical path -- the domain team grants access, not a central gatekeeper reviewing every request. For discoverability, I'd push domain teams to enrich their catalog entries with real metadata -- who owns it, how fresh it is, who to contact -- so another domain can find and request access just by browsing, rather than asking a central team 'what data exists.' The one thing I would keep centralized is a baseline certification bar -- a minimum data quality check, required metadata fields -- enforced automatically before anything can be published as a mesh data product, because without some baseline standard, a mesh model degrades into every domain doing whatever it wants with zero consistency, which isn't actually the goal either.
commonMistakes: Keeps one centralized account/team owning all pipelines, contradicting the actual goal of domain ownership
Has the central governance team issue or approve every cross-domain access grant, recreating the critical-path bottleneck the mesh model is meant to remove
Doesn't address discoverability (metadata, ownership, freshness) as part of the catalog design
Proposes zero central standards at all, risking the mesh degrading into inconsistent, ungoverned chaos
keyPoints: Maps domain ownership onto a per-domain account structure
Centralizes only the catalog/discovery mechanism, not domain-level publishing or granting decisions
Lets domain teams issue their own Lake Formation grants, keeping a central team out of the critical path
Proposes rich catalog metadata for discoverability and a lightweight, automated baseline certification standard

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly maps domain ownership onto account structure
Correctly scopes the central account's role to catalog/discovery, not gatekeeping
Designs domain-issued grants keeping the central team out of the critical path
Proposes sound discoverability metadata and a baseline certification standard

questions.title: Prioritizing a Backlog of Competing Dashboard Requests
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had a large backlog of dashboard and report requests from multiple departments, all claiming urgency. How did you build a prioritization framework and communicate it back to stakeholders?
questions.modelAnswer: The answer should quantify the backlog problem -- number of open requests, number of competing departments, and why 'everything is urgent' had become the default. It should describe a concrete prioritization framework rather than ad hoc judgment calls: scoring requests against criteria like business impact, number of downstream decisions affected, cost of delay, and build effort, and making that framework visible to requesters rather than opaque. It should show how the framework was communicated back to stakeholders whose requests ranked lower -- specifically how the candidate avoided just disappointing people silently, by explaining the reasoning and giving a realistic timeline. Strong answers mention a lightweight intake and triage process (a backlog board, a regular grooming cadence) so prioritization becomes repeatable rather than a one-time exercise, and close with a measurable outcome: reduced average time-to-delivery, fewer 'why hasn't my request been touched' escalations, or higher stakeholder satisfaction with transparency even when their request wasn't first in line.
questions.professionalAnswer: I inherited a backlog of 47 open dashboard requests across six departments, each department insisting theirs was the most urgent, with no shared criteria for sequencing any of it. I built a simple scoring model with four weighted factors -- number of people who'd use it regularly, whether it supported a recurring decision versus a one-off curiosity, estimated build effort, and cost of continuing to delay it -- and scored every open request against it in a spreadsheet I made visible to all six department leads, not just my own team. I ran a 30-minute session with each lead to walk through how their specific requests scored and why, which let me say 'your request is real and matters, here's exactly where it lands and why' instead of a vague 'we'll get to it.' Two leads pushed back hard on their ranking, and in one case they were right -- I'd underweighted a compliance-driven request from Legal that had a hard regulatory deadline I hadn't accounted for, so I added a deadline-override factor to the model. We moved to a visible Kanban board with a biweekly grooming session so this became routine instead of a one-time fire drill. Average time from request to delivery dropped from eleven weeks to under four, and escalations to my manager about 'my request is stuck' dropped to nearly zero because people could see exactly where they stood and why.
commonMistakes: No concrete scoring criteria, just 'we prioritized based on urgency'
Keeping the prioritization logic opaque instead of sharing it with requesters
Not addressing how deprioritized stakeholders were communicated with
Treating the first prioritization pass as final instead of being open to correction
No repeatable process established, just a one-time cleanup
No measurable improvement in delivery time or stakeholder satisfaction
keyPoints: Quantifies the backlog and the competing-urgency problem
Introduces a concrete, weighted prioritization framework
Makes the framework and resulting rankings visible to stakeholders
Shows willingness to revise the framework when a legitimate gap is found
Establishes a repeatable intake/grooming process, not a one-time fix
Gives a measurable improvement in delivery time or escalation volume

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Concreteness of the prioritization framework
Transparency with stakeholders about rankings and reasoning
Willingness to revise the framework when challenged
Repeatability of the process going forward
Measurable outcome

questions.title: Making the Business Case for Infrastructure-as-Code to Skeptical Leadership
questions.prompt: Your engineering director believes Terraform and Bicep are 'process overhead for a team that already knows how to click through the Azure portal carefully.' Tell me about a time you had to convince leadership who saw infrastructure-as-code as unnecessary bureaucracy to invest in adopting it, including how you dealt with the fact that the benefits are mostly about avoided future pain rather than immediate speed.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer recognizes the core difficulty of this pitch: IaC's value is largely preventive and shows up as incidents that didn't happen, which is a hard sell against the visible, immediate cost of slowing down a team that feels productive doing manual changes. It should describe grounding the pitch in the organization's own history rather than abstract best-practice arguments -- a specific outage or painful incident caused by configuration drift, an inconsistent environment, or a change nobody could reproduce, that leadership already remembers and regrets. It should show translating technical benefits into business language leadership cares about: mean time to recovery, audit and compliance readiness, onboarding time for new engineers, or the cost of an environment that can't be safely rebuilt. It should describe proposing a low-risk, bounded pilot -- codifying one well-understood, non-critical environment first -- rather than demanding a wholesale rewrite of all infrastructure, so leadership can see a real before/after without betting the farm. It should address the honest tradeoff: IaC adds some initial friction and learning curve, and a credible answer doesn't pretend otherwise but frames it as a near-term investment against a recurring future cost. The close should include a concrete leadership reaction or decision, not just a vague 'and eventually they agreed.'
questions.professionalAnswer: My director's actual words were close to 'we already know how to configure Azure, why add a layer,' and arguing abstract best practices at him was getting nowhere, so I stopped trying that and instead pulled our last two incident postmortems where the stated root cause was literally 'production environment configuration didn't match what we thought it was' -- one of those had cost us four hours of a Saturday. I reframed the pitch around those two incidents specifically: not 'IaC is a best practice' but 'here's two incidents, both preventable by the same missing thing, and here's what each one cost us in engineer-hours and customer impact.' Rather than asking for a full migration, I proposed codifying just our Fabric capacity and workspace provisioning in Bicep first, since it was well-understood, lower risk than our core Databricks environment, and still painful enough from manual portal drift that a win there would be visible. That pilot took about three weeks, and the real persuasion moment wasn't the code, it was a live demo where I intentionally 'broke' the dev environment and rebuilt it from the Bicep templates in under ten minutes in front of him, compared to the two-plus hours it had historically taken us to manually reconstruct a misconfigured environment. He didn't become an IaC evangelist overnight, but he approved extending it to our Databricks workspace provisioning next quarter, and he's since referenced that ten-minute rebuild demo himself when talking to his own leadership about why we invest in it.
commonMistakes: Argues from abstract best practice instead of the organization's own incident history
Pretends IaC has no near-term cost or learning curve to make the pitch easier
Asks for a wholesale infrastructure rewrite instead of a bounded, low-risk pilot
Frames the benefit only in engineering terms, never translated to business impact
No concrete leadership reaction, decision, or follow-on investment described
keyPoints: Grounds the pitch in a real, remembered incident rather than abstract best practice
Translates technical benefits into business terms leadership cares about
Proposes a bounded, low-risk pilot rather than a full rewrite
Is honest about the near-term cost and learning curve of adoption
Uses a concrete demonstration to make the benefit visceral, not theoretical
Shows a specific leadership decision or follow-on investment as the outcome

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Use of real incident history to ground the pitch
Translation of technical value into business language
Quality of the bounded pilot strategy
Honesty about tradeoffs and adoption cost
Concreteness of the leadership outcome

questions.title: Leading an On-Prem-to-AWS Migration Under a Hard Deadline
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you led a significant on-premises-to-AWS data platform migration with a fixed external deadline (a data center lease expiring, a contract ending). How did you sequence the work, manage the risk of something going wrong mid-migration, and handle the inevitable moment something didn't go according to plan?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer names the specific hard constraint driving the deadline (not just 'we had a deadline') and shows the candidate treating the deadline as fixed while the scope and sequencing were the actual variables they controlled -- describing an explicit risk-based sequencing decision (migrating lower-risk, well-understood systems first to build pattern and team confidence, saving the highest-risk or most business-critical system for a point where the process was proven) rather than an arbitrary or alphabetical order. It should describe concrete technical risk mitigation appropriate to a real migration -- a rollback plan for each cutover, a validation step before declaring any migration complete, running old and new in parallel for a defined window on at least the highest-risk system. The answer should include a genuine complication that happened mid-migration (not a success story with no friction) and show how the candidate responded: diagnosed it, communicated it transparently to stakeholders rather than hiding it, and adjusted the plan rather than panicking or forcing the original timeline through regardless of the new information. It should close with a concrete outcome: whether the deadline was hit, what had to flex (scope, a short extension, a temporary parallel-running cost) to make it work, and what the candidate would do differently given a similar deadline again.
questions.professionalAnswer: We had eleven months before our data center lease expired, no option to extend, and roughly 40 production data pipelines plus three Redshift clusters' worth of history to move. I treated the deadline as the one truly fixed variable and used sequencing as my actual risk lever -- we migrated the dozen lowest-risk, best-understood pipelines first, deliberately, so the team built real muscle memory on our DMS and Glue migration pattern before we touched anything business-critical. Each cutover had an explicit rollback plan and ran old-and-new in parallel for at least 48 hours before we called it done, and for the two most critical pipelines we ran parallel for two full weeks. About seven months in, the migration of our largest Redshift cluster hit a real problem -- our column encoding choices on the new RA3 cluster were producing query plans significantly slower than the old DC2 cluster for our worst offenders, something our earlier, smaller migrations hadn't surfaced. I didn't try to quietly patch around it on the original timeline; I went to leadership within 48 hours of confirming the problem, laid out exactly what was slow and why, and asked for a two-week schedule adjustment to redo the sort/distribution key design properly rather than ship something that would create a performance incident on day one in production. We got the two weeks, fixed the design properly, and still made the final deadline by about three weeks of margin, in large part because the early low-risk migrations had gone fast enough to bank that buffer. What I'd do differently: I'd have run a representative worst-case query benchmark against the new cluster earlier in the process instead of only after the full data load, since that's exactly the kind of problem that's far cheaper to catch before the heaviest migration, not after.
commonMistakes: Describes the deadline without naming the real sequencing/risk decisions made to meet it
Presents a frictionless success story with no real complication encountered mid-migration
Hides or minimizes a problem rather than communicating it transparently to stakeholders when it occurred
Doesn't describe concrete risk mitigation (rollback plans, parallel running, validation) appropriate to a real migration
No honest reflection on what would be done differently next time
keyPoints: Names the specific hard constraint and treats scope/sequencing as the controllable variables
Describes risk-based sequencing (lower-risk systems first) with concrete reasoning
Describes concrete technical risk mitigation (rollback plans, parallel running, validation)
Includes a genuine mid-migration complication and a transparent, adaptive response to it
Gives an honest outcome and a specific lesson for next time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Clarity and soundness of the risk-based sequencing strategy
Concreteness of technical risk mitigation described
Honesty and quality of the mid-migration complication and response
Concreteness of the outcome and reflection

questions.title: Designing and Rolling Out an Org-Wide AWS Data Governance Model
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you designed and rolled out a data governance model (permissions, tagging, access review) across an organization with multiple teams who previously had largely unrestricted, ungoverned access to shared AWS data resources. How did you get buy-in for restricting access people were used to having freely, and how did you handle the pushback?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer acknowledges directly that this is fundamentally a change-management problem, not just a technical rollout -- taking away access people are used to having, even access they didn't strictly need, reliably generates resistance regardless of how technically sound the new model is, and a credible answer shows the candidate anticipated and planned for that resistance rather than being surprised by it. It should describe how the new governance model's actual rules were derived (ideally from a real risk or incident, like an overly broad access grant that was discovered, or a compliance/audit requirement, rather than an abstract 'best practice' mandate with no concrete trigger) and how the rollout itself was sequenced -- typically starting with visibility/audit (showing teams what access currently exists, which is often itself eye-opening) before moving to actual restriction, and using a grace period or phased enforcement rather than an overnight hard cutover. It should include a specific instance of real pushback from a team or individual and show the candidate engaging with the substance of that pushback genuinely -- either finding a legitimate access need they'd missed and adjusting the model, or holding the line with clear reasoning when the pushback wasn't actually about a legitimate need. The close should include a measurable outcome (reduced number of over-privileged roles, a clean audit finding, faster access request turnaround under the new structured process) and show the governance model as sustained, not a one-time project.
questions.professionalAnswer: We had gotten to a point where dozens of roles across the data platform had broad read access to S3 buckets and Glue tables that had just been granted over time because it was easier than figuring out exactly what someone needed, and a routine security review flagged it as a real risk, not a hypothetical one. I didn't start with new restrictions -- I started with visibility, pulling a full access audit and sharing it with each team lead so they could see what their own team actually had, which was genuinely eye-opening for a couple of leads who didn't realize how broad some of their roles' access had become. From there I proposed a Lake Formation-based model with explicit, table-level grants replacing the broad bucket-level access, rolled out with a 60-day grace period where both the old and new access coexisted, so nobody's work broke on day one. The real pushback came from our data science lead, who argued the new model would slow down exploratory work where she genuinely didn't know in advance which tables she'd need. I took that seriously rather than dismissing it, and we ended up adding a self-service, time-boxed 'exploration grant' process -- a data scientist could request broad read access to a specific database for 14 days with automatic expiration, logged and reviewed, rather than either permanent broad access or a slow ticket-based request for every single table. That compromise actually made the model stronger, not weaker, because it solved a real need I hadn't fully accounted for in my first design. Six months in, over-privileged roles dropped by about 70%, our next security audit came back clean on this specific finding, and the exploration-grant process has become a standard part of onboarding new data scientists.
commonMistakes: Treats this as a purely technical rollout with no acknowledgment of the change-management challenge
Rolls out governance as an abstract best-practice mandate with no concrete, real trigger
Implements a hard, overnight restriction with no grace period or phased enforcement
Dismisses pushback rather than engaging with whether it reflects a legitimate need
No measurable outcome or evidence the governance model is sustained rather than a one-time project
keyPoints: Grounds the governance rollout in a real, concrete trigger rather than an abstract mandate
Sequences the rollout with visibility/audit first, then phased restriction with a grace period
Describes genuine engagement with real pushback, adjusting the model where legitimate
Gives a measurable, sustained outcome

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Acknowledges and plans for the change-management dimension explicitly
Soundness of the governance model design and rollout sequencing
Quality of engagement with real pushback
Concreteness and sustainability of the outcome

questions.title: Mentoring the On-Call Team Through a Redshift Cluster Outage During Peak Reporting
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time a critical Redshift cluster went down or became unusable during a high-stakes reporting window (month-end close, a board meeting, a major release), and you had to both resolve the incident and mentor a less experienced on-call engineer through it in real time. How did you balance moving fast with actually teaching, and what did you do differently afterward?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer describes a genuinely high-stakes incident with real specifics (what actually broke, why it mattered that it was happening during this particular window) rather than a generic 'the database went down' story, and shows the candidate making a deliberate choice about how to involve the junior engineer rather than simply taking over and leaving them to passively watch -- for instance, having the junior engineer drive the actual diagnostic commands while the candidate narrated reasoning and asked guiding questions, or explicitly dividing labor (junior handles stakeholder communication/status updates while the senior engineer focuses on the technical fix) so the junior still owns something real and learns from a different angle of the incident. It should acknowledge the genuine tension between speed and teaching honestly -- there's a real cost to slowing down to explain during an active incident, and a mature answer doesn't pretend that tension didn't exist, but shows a conscious decision about where teaching was worth the marginal time cost and where the candidate just took the controls because the stakes didn't allow for it. The close should include both the technical resolution and a concrete follow-up investment in the junior engineer's growth after the incident was over -- a retro walking through the decision tree, assigning them to drive the next drill or a related low-stakes incident solo -- showing the mentoring didn't end when the fire was out.
questions.professionalAnswer: Our production Redshift cluster hit a WLM memory exhaustion issue during month-end close, right as finance was running the reports that feed the board deck, and I was paired on-call with an engineer about eight months into the role. My first instinct was to just grab the keyboard and fix it myself, but I made a deliberate call: I'd narrate my diagnostic reasoning out loud and have her actually type the commands, so she wasn't just watching me work, she was doing the work with my reasoning attached to it in real time. I did take over directly for about ten minutes when I found the actual root cause -- a runaway ad hoc query someone had left running with no WLM limit -- because at that point speed mattered more than the teaching opportunity and I wasn't going to risk fumbling a live production fix to make a pedagogical point. While I terminated that query and adjusted the WLM config, I had her own the stakeholder communication -- drafting the status updates to finance leadership -- which was a different, equally real skill for her to practice under real pressure. We got reporting back up within about 25 minutes of the first alert. Afterward, I didn't just move on -- we spent 45 minutes in a retro walking through my actual decision tree, including the parts where I took over and why, not just the final fix, and I made sure she led the response solo on our next WLM-related alert a few weeks later, with me just available in the background rather than driving.
commonMistakes: Describes a generic incident with no real specificity about what broke or why the timing mattered
Takes over the entire incident with no attempt to involve or teach the junior engineer at all
Pretends there's no real tension between speed and teaching during an active incident
No concrete follow-up investment in the junior engineer's growth after the incident resolved
keyPoints: Describes a specific, high-stakes incident with real technical detail
Makes a deliberate, described choice about how to involve the junior engineer during the incident
Honestly acknowledges the speed-vs-teaching tension and when the candidate took direct control
Describes a concrete follow-up investment in the junior engineer's growth after resolution

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Specificity and stakes of the incident described
Quality of the real-time mentoring/involvement approach
Honest treatment of the speed-vs-teaching tension
Concreteness of post-incident mentoring follow-through

questions.title: Making the Technical Case for a Specific AWS Service to Skeptical Leadership
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to convince skeptical leadership to invest in adopting a specific, unfamiliar AWS service (Lake Formation, Managed Flink, Step Functions, or similar) when the existing, more familiar approach technically worked, just not well. How did you make the case without overselling it, and how did you handle it if leadership pushed back with a legitimate concern?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer names the specific service and the specific, concrete pain of the existing approach it would replace -- not 'it's better practice' but a quantified cost of the status quo (hours spent on manual permission management, a specific incident caused by the old approach's limitations, a growth trajectory the current approach won't scale to). It should show the candidate being honest about the new service's own costs and limitations as part of the pitch, not hiding them to make the case land more easily, since leadership discovering an unmentioned downside after approving the investment damages the candidate's credibility far more than naming it upfront. It should describe a specific, legitimate pushback from leadership (a cost concern, a timeline concern, a 'why not just fix the current approach' question) and show the candidate engaging with the substance of that concern rather than simply repeating the original pitch louder -- either providing new information that actually answers the concern, or acknowledging a real tradeoff and adjusting the proposal's scope. The close should describe a concrete decision and, ideally, an early result validating (or partially not validating) the original case, since a convincing behavioral answer doesn't need the outcome to be a total, unblemished win to be credible.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wanted to move our growing cross-account data sharing off of hand-written S3 bucket policies and onto Lake Formation, and our VP of Engineering's first reaction was 'we already have forty bucket policies working fine, why add a new system.' I didn't argue abstractly -- I pulled up the actual number of bucket policies we were maintaining at that point, walked through how long it took us to audit 'who can see what' the last time compliance asked (just over three days, manually cross-referencing policies), and showed that our data-sharing need was growing roughly 40% a year, meaning that three-day audit would become a week, then two weeks, on the current approach. I was upfront that Lake Formation meant a real migration effort and a learning curve for the team, and that it wouldn't pay for itself in week one -- I specifically didn't want him discovering that cost later and feeling like I'd undersold it. His pushback was fair: he asked whether this was really a Lake Formation problem or whether we just needed better internal tooling around our existing bucket policies. That was a legitimate point, and instead of just repeating my pitch, I went and actually prototyped a week of 'better tooling around bucket policies' versus a week of Lake Formation migration on our ten riskiest shares, and brought back a real comparison -- the tooling approach still left column-level PII exposure unsolved, which Lake Formation handled natively, and that specific gap is what actually got him to approve the full migration. Eight months in, our compliance audit time is down to under a day, though I'll admit the migration took about three weeks longer than I'd estimated, which I flagged proactively rather than letting him find out from a missed deadline.
commonMistakes: Pitches the new service with only its benefits, hiding its real costs or limitations
Responds to legitimate pushback by repeating the original pitch instead of engaging with the actual concern
Describes an unrealistically smooth, unblemished outcome with no honest complication
Doesn't quantify the actual cost of the status quo, relying on abstract 'best practice' framing
keyPoints: Names the specific service and quantifies the concrete cost of the status quo it would replace
Is honest about the new service's own costs and limitations as part of the pitch
Engages substantively with a specific, legitimate leadership pushback rather than repeating the pitch
Gives an honest outcome, including any miscalculation or partial shortfall

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Concreteness and quantification of the pitch
Honesty about the new approach's own costs/limitations
Quality of engagement with legitimate leadership pushback
Honesty and concreteness of the outcome

questions.title: Resolving a Cost-Attribution Dispute Between Two Teams Sharing an AWS Account
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time two teams sharing the same AWS account (or the same Redshift cluster, or the same Glue jobs) disagreed about whose workload was actually responsible for a cost increase, with each team pointing at the other. How did you get to the actual, fair answer, and how did you handle the interpersonal tension once you had it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer shows the candidate going to actual usage data rather than relying on either team's self-report or opinion to settle the dispute -- pulling specific, granular evidence (per-job Glue run costs, per-query Redshift WLM usage, per-cluster system billing tables) that can attribute the cost increase to a specific, verifiable cause, rather than a vague 'it's probably you.' It should describe a genuinely ambiguous or shared-responsibility finding where possible (the real answer in cost disputes is often 'both, partially, for different reasons' rather than a clean single culprit), and show the candidate communicating that nuanced finding honestly rather than picking a winner to avoid further conflict. It should address the interpersonal dimension directly -- how the candidate kept the conversation focused on the data and the shared problem of a rising bill rather than letting it become about which team was 'wrong' or who looked bad, especially if the data initially looked like it favored one team's narrative before a fuller investigation. The close should include a structural fix preventing the same dispute from recurring (better tagging, separate WLM queues, separate accounts) rather than just a one-time resolution of this specific disagreement.
questions.professionalAnswer: Our shared Redshift cluster's cost had jumped noticeably, and the BI team and the data science team were each pointing at the other's queries as the cause, with neither side having real evidence beyond 'it's probably them.' I pulled the actual per-query cost and resource consumption data from Redshift's system tables for the month, broken down by query group, and the real answer turned out to be less satisfying than either team wanted: BI's query volume had grown about 20% from a new dashboard rollout, and separately, a handful of data science's ad hoc queries were doing full table scans that were individually expensive but infrequent -- both contributed meaningfully, just through completely different mechanisms. When I brought that back to both teams together, I made a point of presenting it as 'here's what the data actually shows, and it's not a clean story where one of you was the problem' rather than picking a side, because the data genuinely didn't support a single culprit and framing it that way would have been dishonest just to resolve the conflict faster. That honesty actually defused most of the tension, because neither team felt like they'd been unfairly blamed, and the conversation shifted naturally to 'how do we fix both of these going forward' instead of continuing to argue about blame. The structural fix was separating them into distinct WLM queues with their own memory allocation and query monitoring rules, so from that point forward, each team's cost and resource impact was visible and bounded independently, and this exact kind of dispute couldn't recur because the data would be unambiguous per-queue from day one.
commonMistakes: Resolves the dispute based on opinion or seniority rather than pulling actual granular usage data
Picks a clean 'winner' in the dispute even when the real data shows shared or ambiguous responsibility
Lets the conversation become about blame/who was wrong rather than the shared problem of cost
No structural fix proposed, just a one-time resolution of this specific disagreement
keyPoints: Uses actual granular usage/cost data to settle the dispute rather than opinion
Honestly communicates a nuanced or shared-responsibility finding rather than picking a convenient winner
Manages the interpersonal tension by keeping focus on data and the shared problem
Proposes a structural fix preventing recurrence, not just resolving the one instance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Use of concrete, granular data to settle the dispute
Honesty in communicating a nuanced finding
Quality of interpersonal/conflict management
Soundness of the structural fix preventing recurrence

questions.title: Pushing Back on an Unrealistic AWS Migration Deadline
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time leadership set a migration or platform deadline you genuinely believed was technically unrealistic given the actual scope, and you had to push back. How did you make the case without just sounding like you were being difficult, and what was the actual resolution?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer avoids a vague 'I told them it was too aggressive' and instead shows specific, credible evidence behind the pushback -- a bottom-up estimate broken into the actual phases of work (discovery, migration pattern validation, per-system cutover, validation), ideally referencing a comparable prior migration's actual timeline as a reality check against the proposed one, rather than a gut feeling presented as fact. It should show the candidate coming not just with 'no' but with alternatives -- a reduced scope that fits the original deadline, or a phased approach that hits a meaningful milestone by the deadline while completing the rest later, giving leadership a real choice rather than a binary. It should address how the candidate handled it if leadership held firm on the original deadline despite the pushback -- whether that meant negotiating which specific risks they were explicitly accepting in writing, re-litigating scope one more time with new information, or ultimately executing against the original timeline while flagging the accepted risk clearly, rather than the candidate simply capitulating and acting as if the timeline had always been fine. The close should include what actually happened -- did the deadline hold, move, or did scope change -- with an honest account rather than the clean universal 'and leadership listened and extended it' outcome.
questions.professionalAnswer: We were asked to migrate our entire on-prem SQL Server estate -- around 60 databases -- to Aurora in ten weeks, driven by a vendor contract renewal date. I did the math from our actual experience on the handful of pilot migrations we'd already completed: those averaged about four days of real effort each once you counted schema conversion review, DMS setup, validation, and cutover, which put the honest total closer to six months of calendar time for 60 databases run by our team size, not ten weeks. I didn't just say 'this is too aggressive' -- I brought a specific alternative: migrate the 15 lowest-risk, highest-confidence databases within the ten-week window, which was genuinely achievable and gave the business something real to show for the deadline, while the remaining 45 followed over the subsequent four months on a committed schedule. Leadership initially pushed back, wanting all 60 in the original window, so I asked for a specific tradeoff decision instead of relitigating the whole estimate again: either accept the phased plan, or accept the original timeline with an explicit, written acknowledgment that we'd be skipping the validation and parallel-run steps on the riskier databases to hit it, which is a real risk I wanted documented, not quietly absorbed. They chose the phased plan once the risk was framed that concretely. We hit the 15-database milestone on time, and the full 60 finished about three weeks later than my original four-month estimate for the remainder, mostly due to two databases having more complex stored procedure logic than anyone had scoped going in -- which I flagged as soon as we found it rather than letting the final deadline surprise anyone.
commonMistakes: Pushes back with only a gut feeling or vague concern, no concrete estimate or evidence
Offers only objection with no alternative scope or phased proposal
Capitulates silently to the original deadline without documenting the accepted risk
Describes an unrealistically clean outcome with no honest complication or variance from the revised plan
keyPoints: Backs the pushback with a specific, evidence-based estimate, not just a feeling
Offers a concrete alternative (reduced scope or phased approach), not just an objection
Describes how risk was explicitly documented/accepted if leadership held firm
Gives an honest, specific account of what actually happened

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Evidence quality behind the pushback
Quality of the alternative proposed
Handling of continued leadership resistance
Honesty and specificity of the actual outcome

questions.title: Responding to a Security Audit Finding an Over-Permissioned IAM Role You Created
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time a security review or audit found that an IAM role you had personally created or approved was significantly over-permissioned, posing a real risk. How did you handle being the person responsible for the finding, and what did you change afterward?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer shows genuine, specific ownership of the mistake -- naming exactly what was over-permissioned and why it happened (time pressure, a broad managed policy used as a shortcut, uncertainty about exactly what permissions were needed so a wider grant 'to be safe' was used instead) -- rather than deflecting, minimizing, or blaming the audit process itself for being pedantic. It should describe a concrete, prompt remediation -- scoping the role down to the actual permissions in use, verified against real CloudTrail usage data rather than guessed, and testing that the narrowed role doesn't break the workload it supports before considering the fix complete. It should describe a genuine process change coming out of this, not just a one-off fix to this one role -- for instance, instituting a practice of using IAM Access Analyzer's policy generation from actual CloudTrail activity when creating new roles, or a peer-review requirement for any role with broad permissions before it ships. The close should reflect real, non-defensive accountability -- the candidate treating this as a legitimate finding that improved the platform's security posture, not an embarrassing event to minimize or move past quickly.
questions.professionalAnswer: A quarterly access review flagged a Glue job role I'd created for a new pipeline about four months earlier with AmazonS3FullAccess attached, when the job only ever needed read access to two specific prefixes. I'd used the managed policy because I was moving fast on a deadline and didn't want to debug a permissions error mid-deployment, told myself I'd narrow it later, and then genuinely forgot, which is exactly the kind of drift a review exists to catch, and I said that plainly rather than trying to justify it after the fact. For the fix, I pulled the role's actual CloudTrail activity over the prior 90 days to see precisely which S3 actions and prefixes it had really used, built a scoped policy matching that exactly, and tested it in a non-production copy of the pipeline before swapping it into production, rather than guessing at what it needed. The bigger change was process, not just this one role: I started using IAM Access Analyzer's policy generation feature, which builds a least-privilege policy directly from a role's actual observed CloudTrail usage, for every new role I create now, specifically so 'I'll narrow it later' isn't something I'm relying on my own memory to follow through on. I also volunteered this as an example in our team's next security training session, because I'd rather be the example of a mistake that got caught and fixed than pretend it didn't happen.
commonMistakes: Minimizes the finding or implies the audit was being overly strict
Describes only fixing this one role without any broader process change
Scopes down the role based on guessing at needed permissions instead of verifying against real usage data
Shows defensiveness rather than genuine ownership of the mistake
keyPoints: Takes genuine, specific ownership of why the over-permissioning happened
Remediates based on verified actual usage (CloudTrail), not guesswork
Tests the narrowed role before considering the fix complete
Describes a durable process change, not just a one-off fix

Soundness of the verified, tested remediation
Quality of the durable process change
Non-defensive, accountable framing throughout
