questions.title: Convincing a Team to Give Up Ad Hoc Bucket Policies for Lake Formation
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to convince a team that was comfortable managing data access through individual S3 bucket policies to adopt Lake Formation instead, when they saw it as an unnecessary layer on top of something that already worked for them. How did you address their actual day-to-day workflow concerns, not just the governance argument?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer recognizes that 'it already works for us' is a legitimate workflow concern, not just resistance to change, and addresses it on those terms rather than only re-arguing the governance/security case louder -- showing the candidate actually sat with the team's current day-to-day process (how they grant a new analyst access today, how long it takes, who they have to ask) before proposing the new model, so the pitch responds to their real friction points rather than a generic 'Lake Formation is better' argument. It should describe identifying a genuine, specific pain point in their current bucket-policy workflow that the team themselves would recognize as real (a slow, multi-step process to grant column-level access that currently requires physically splitting data into separate prefixes, or a recent instance where an overly broad bucket policy grant created exactly the kind of risk the team would rather not repeat) and showing how Lake Formation's grant model solves that specific friction, not just a theoretical future risk. It should describe a hands-on, low-stakes way the team got to experience the new model before being asked to commit to it broadly -- a pilot on one table or one dataset they chose, rather than being told the new model works based on the candidate's assurance alone. The close should include the team's own voice in the outcome -- a specific thing a team member said or did that signaled genuine adoption, not just compliance, plus an honest acknowledgment of what the team still didn't love about the new model.
questions.professionalAnswer: The data engineering team's response when I raised Lake Formation was basically 'our bucket policies work fine, what's the actual problem,' and arguing governance theory at them wasn't landing, so I stopped doing that and instead sat with them through their actual process for granting a new analyst column-level access to a customer table. It took them physically splitting the data into a separate S3 prefix with the sensitive columns stripped out, duplicating storage and adding a maintenance burden every time the schema changed -- a real, specific pain they already felt, even if they hadn't framed it as a Lake Formation problem. I proposed a pilot on exactly one table they picked themselves, showing them granting column-level access without any data duplication or prefix-splitting at all, and let them run their own next real access request through it rather than a staged demo. The lead engineer on that team, who'd been the most skeptical, ended up being the one who brought it to our next team meeting unprompted and said it had saved him an afternoon of prefix-splitting work that same week, which did more to get the rest of the team on board than anything I could have said myself. What they still didn't love, and I didn't pretend otherwise, was the learning curve on troubleshooting Lake Formation permission errors, which are genuinely less intuitive to debug than a straightforward bucket policy denial -- we ended up building a small internal runbook for common Lake Formation error patterns specifically because that friction was real and worth addressing directly rather than waving away.
commonMistakes: Re-argues the governance/security case rather than addressing the team's actual day-to-day workflow concerns
Proposes a broad rollout with no hands-on pilot the team could experience firsthand first
Describes the outcome only from the candidate's perspective, with no genuine voice from the team itself
Doesn't honestly acknowledge what the team still found harder about the new model
keyPoints: Investigates and addresses the team's actual current workflow and its real friction points
Identifies a specific, concrete pain point the new model solves, not just a theoretical risk
Proposes a hands-on pilot the team experiences directly rather than being told to trust
Includes genuine team-voiced evidence of adoption and an honest acknowledgment of remaining friction

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Depth of engagement with the team's actual workflow and concerns
Specificity of the pain point identified and addressed
Quality of the hands-on pilot approach
Genuineness and honesty of the described outcome

questions.title: Managing Scope Creep on a Cross-Team AWS Capstone-Style Platform Project
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you were leading a cross-team project to build a shared AWS data platform (combining ingestion, cataloging, warehousing, and orchestration end to end) and scope kept expanding as different teams added 'just one more requirement.' How did you get scope back under control without alienating the teams whose requests you had to say no to?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer names the actual pattern of scope creep specifically (which teams added what, and roughly how the original scope compared to where it had grown) rather than a vague 'scope kept growing,' and shows the candidate's diagnosis of why it happened -- often a project without a clearly documented, agreed initial scope that different stakeholders could point back to, which made every new addition feel reasonable in isolation with no visible cumulative effect. It should describe a concrete mechanism for getting scope back under control -- re-baselining and documenting the current committed scope explicitly, instituting a visible change-request process where a new ask has to be weighed against the committed timeline/resources rather than just added, and showing the cumulative cost of 'one more thing' back to the requesting stakeholders in concrete terms (this pushes the shared delivery date by two weeks) rather than a vague no. It should describe at least one specific instance of declining or deferring a request and how that was communicated -- showing the candidate protected the relationship by explaining the tradeoff honestly and, where reasonable, offering a path for the deferred request (a committed follow-up phase) rather than a flat, unexplained rejection. The close should include a concrete delivery outcome and whether the scope-control mechanism held for the rest of the project, not just for the one incident described.
questions.professionalAnswer: We were building a shared platform -- S3 ingestion, Glue cataloging, Redshift warehousing, Step Functions orchestration -- for four business teams, and by week six we'd accumulated requests that had grown the original three-sprint scope to something closer to six sprints, with each individual addition having seemed reasonable when it came in. The real problem was we'd never written down and circulated an explicit 'this is what we committed to' baseline, so every new ask landed in a vacuum with no visible cumulative cost attached to it. I went back and documented the original committed scope explicitly, shared it with all four teams, and set up a lightweight change-request process where any new ask got a specific, concrete answer: 'this adds approximately four days and pushes the shared delivery date by that much' rather than a vague 'we'll see.' The hardest instance was the finance team wanting a Lake Formation column-level permission model added mid-project for a compliance requirement they said had just come up -- which was a legitimate need, not a frivolous one, but accepting it as-is would have pushed delivery for all four teams by three weeks. Instead of a flat no, I proposed deferring their specific requirement to a committed, scheduled phase two that started immediately after the main platform shipped, with a firm date, rather than folding it into the current scope and making every other team's delivery slip for a need that was specific to finance. They weren't thrilled, but having a real date for their requirement, not an indefinite 'later,' kept the relationship fine, and the other three teams respected that their timeline wasn't being silently sacrificed for someone else's addition. We shipped the core platform on the re-baselined schedule, and the change-request process held for the rest of the project -- two more requests came in afterward, and both went through the same explicit cost conversation instead of just getting absorbed.
commonMistakes: Describes scope creep vaguely without naming the specific pattern or its cumulative cost
No concrete mechanism described for getting scope back under control, just 'we said no more changes'
Declines a request with a flat, unexplained no rather than an honest tradeoff conversation and alternative
No evidence the scope-control mechanism held beyond the one described instance
keyPoints: Names the specific scope creep pattern and diagnoses why it happened
Describes a concrete mechanism (baseline, change-request process, cumulative cost visibility) for controlling it
Describes a specific instance of declining/deferring a request with honest tradeoff communication
Shows the mechanism held for the remainder of the project, not just once

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Specificity of the scope creep pattern and diagnosis
Soundness of the scope-control mechanism introduced
Quality of handling a specific decline/deferral
Evidence the mechanism held going forward

questions.title: Delivering News of a Significant AWS Cost Overrun to a VP
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to tell a VP or senior leader that your AWS data platform had significantly overrun its budget, especially if it was at least partly a result of a decision you'd made or approved. How did you prepare for that conversation, and what was the actual reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer describes a genuine, meaningful overrun (with real numbers) rather than a minor variance, and shows the candidate going into the conversation with the actual root cause already diagnosed and a remediation plan already in motion, rather than going in to merely report the bad news and wait for direction -- a VP-level conversation about an overrun lands very differently when it comes with 'here's what happened, here's what I'm already doing about it, here's the revised number' versus 'something went wrong, what do we do.' If the candidate's own decision contributed to the overrun, the answer should show direct, specific ownership of that -- not hedging language that spreads responsibility vaguely across 'the team' or 'unforeseen circumstances' when the candidate's own choice was a real factor -- since VPs generally read evasive responsibility-spreading as a bigger trust problem than the dollar amount of the overrun itself. It should describe the actual reaction honestly, including if it was uncomfortable or if the VP pushed back hard, rather than a uniformly smooth 'they understood completely' story. The close should include what changed afterward -- in process, monitoring, or decision-making authority -- that reduces the chance of a similar surprise next time.
questions.professionalAnswer: Our EMR compute spend came in about 85% over budget for the quarter, and a meaningful chunk of that was a choice I'd made -- I'd approved a Spot Fleet configuration with insufficient instance type diversification to save a bit of setup time, and a sustained interruption wave on that pool had forced repeated, expensive recomputation over several weeks before anyone caught the pattern in the billing data. Before I went to my VP, I made sure I already had the root cause nailed down precisely and had already fixed the Spot diversification issue, so I wasn't walking in with just a number and a shrug. I opened the conversation by owning my part directly -- 'I made a configuration choice to save time that ended up costing us real money over several weeks, here's exactly what happened and here's what I've already changed' -- rather than describing it as a general team or process failure, because it genuinely was my call. She was not thrilled, and she asked pointed questions about why our billing alerts hadn't caught this sooner, which was a fair question I didn't have a fully satisfying answer for in the moment -- our alerting was threshold-based on absolute spend, not on a sudden rate-of-change, so a gradual weekly climb hadn't tripped anything until it was already significant. I said so plainly instead of deflecting. Coming out of that conversation, we rebuilt our cost alerting around week-over-week trend detection specifically, not just absolute thresholds, and I instituted a personal practice of reviewing Spot Fleet diversification settings against a checklist before approving any new fleet configuration, specifically because this was a preventable mistake I didn't want to make a second time.
commonMistakes: Describes a minor variance rather than a genuinely significant overrun
Spreads responsibility vaguely to 'the team' or 'unforeseen circumstances' when the candidate's own decision was a real factor
Goes into the conversation with only the bad news and no diagnosis or remediation plan already underway
Describes an unrealistically smooth reaction with no real discomfort or pushback
keyPoints: Describes a genuinely significant overrun with real numbers
Enters the conversation with root cause and remediation already in motion, not just the bad news
Shows direct, specific ownership where the candidate's own decision contributed
Gives an honest account of the reaction, including discomfort or pushback
Describes a concrete process change reducing recurrence risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Preparation quality (diagnosis and remediation already in motion)
Directness and specificity of ownership shown
Honesty of the described reaction
Concreteness of the resulting process change

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Engineer Who Keeps Under-Provisioning and Over-Running EMR Jobs
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you mentored a junior engineer who kept making the same category of mistake on EMR/Spark cost and sizing -- consistently under-provisioning clusters and then letting jobs run far longer (and more expensively) than necessary rather than fixing the sizing. How did you address a repeated pattern rather than just fixing it each time yourself?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer shows the candidate recognizing a repeated pattern rather than treating each instance as an isolated, independent mistake to quietly fix themselves -- the core coaching failure to avoid here is a senior engineer repeatedly swooping in to resize a struggling cluster without the junior engineer ever having to diagnose why their original sizing was wrong, which trains the junior engineer to expect rescue rather than building the actual diagnostic skill. It should describe a deliberate shift from fixing the symptom to teaching the diagnostic process -- having the junior engineer walk through Spark UI/CloudWatch metrics themselves to identify where a job was actually bottlenecked (executor memory, shuffle spill, skewed partitions) before any resize happens, with the mentor asking guiding questions rather than supplying the answer directly. It should address the real risk of being too hands-off while teaching -- a cost-sensitive production job isn't a place for unlimited learning-by-failure, so the answer should show the candidate setting appropriate guardrails (a non-production sandbox for the junior engineer to practice diagnosis and tuning, or a cost ceiling/alert on anything they're sizing solo) rather than either rescuing every time or simply letting costs run up indefinitely in the name of learning. The close should include evidence of the pattern actually breaking -- a specific instance where the junior engineer diagnosed and fixed a sizing issue independently, not just the mentor's own continued confidence that they'd improved.
questions.professionalAnswer: I noticed I'd resized the same junior engineer's EMR clusters mid-run about four times over two months, and each time I'd just fixed it directly because that was faster in the moment -- which I realized was actually the problem, not a kindness, because he was never building the muscle to diagnose it himself. So the next time his job was running long, I didn't touch the cluster. I pulled up the Spark UI with him and asked him to walk me through what he saw, rather than telling him what I saw -- and he found, on his own, that a handful of partitions were wildly skewed relative to the rest, which was actually the root cause behind several of his past 'just needs more nodes' fixes, since adding nodes never actually fixed a skew problem, it just bought a little more headroom before it became a problem again. I didn't let this play out on a production job with an unbounded budget, though -- I'd set him up with a sandboxed EMR environment with a hard cost alert specifically so he could practice this kind of diagnosis without risk to anything that actually mattered if he got it wrong a few times while learning. Over the next six weeks, he came to me twice with a sizing problem already diagnosed and a specific fix proposed, asking me to sanity-check his reasoning rather than asking me to just fix it, which was the actual signal the pattern had broken -- not that he stopped having sizing issues entirely, but that he'd become the one solving them.
commonMistakes: Describes repeatedly fixing the symptom directly without addressing why that doesn't build the junior engineer's own diagnostic skill
Doesn't describe guardrails for safely allowing the junior engineer to practice diagnosis without production cost risk
Supplies the diagnosis/answer directly rather than guiding the junior engineer to find it themselves
No concrete evidence of the pattern actually breaking, just the mentor's own assumption of improvement
keyPoints: Recognizes the repeated pattern and the risk of habitually rescuing rather than teaching
Shifts to a guided-diagnosis approach rather than supplying the answer directly
Sets appropriate guardrails (sandbox, cost alerts) for safe independent practice
Shows concrete evidence of the junior engineer diagnosing and fixing an issue independently afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognition of the repeated-rescue pattern and its coaching cost
Quality of the guided-diagnosis teaching approach
Soundness of guardrails for safe independent practice
Concreteness of evidence the pattern broke

questions.title: Disagreeing With Another Architect Over Redshift vs. Athena/Spectrum for a New Workload
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a peer architect about the right AWS service choice for a new workload (for example, loading data into Redshift versus querying it in place with Athena/Spectrum), and the disagreement wasn't easily resolved by one of you simply being technically wrong. How did you reach a decision, and how did you handle it if the final decision went against your original recommendation?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer shows a genuine disagreement where both positions had real merit -- not a strawman where the other architect was simply uninformed -- and describes the candidate working to understand the actual basis of the other person's recommendation (what assumption about query patterns, data freshness needs, or cost they were optimizing for) rather than only restating their own case more forcefully. It should describe a concrete way the disagreement was actually resolved -- ideally by identifying the specific, measurable factor the decision should hinge on (expected query frequency and latency requirements, data volume growth trajectory, cost at projected scale) and gathering real data or a small prototype/benchmark against that factor, rather than the decision being settled by seniority, a vote, or simply wearing the other person down. It should address, honestly, what happened if the final decision went against the candidate's original recommendation -- showing genuine support for the chosen direction going forward rather than quiet resentment, passive resistance, or saying 'I told you so' if problems later emerged, while still being honest about having held a different initial view. The close should include whether the outcome validated either position, and what the candidate learned about the actual tradeoff that they'd apply differently next time a similar choice comes up.
questions.professionalAnswer: A peer architect and I disagreed on a new analytics workload -- I wanted to load the curated data into Redshift, he wanted to query it in place with Athena/Spectrum straight off S3 to avoid the load pipeline and the Redshift storage cost. Both positions were genuinely reasonable: I was weighting the query latency and concurrency needs of the BI dashboards that would hit this data, he was weighting the cost and operational simplicity of not maintaining another load pipeline for data that wasn't being queried that frequently yet. Instead of just each restating our case, we agreed on the specific factor that should actually decide it -- expected query frequency and concurrent user count over the next six months -- and went and got real numbers from the product team planning to use the dashboards, rather than guessing. The real usage pattern turned out to be lower-frequency than I'd assumed, closer to his assumption than mine, so we went with Athena/Spectrum. I'll be honest that I thought he was underestimating how fast that usage would grow, but I didn't sit on that quietly -- I said it directly in the decision meeting, we agreed to revisit the choice if usage crossed a specific threshold within six months, and then I actually supported the Spectrum implementation fully rather than dragging my feet on something I'd lost the argument on. Usage did grow faster than his estimate within about four months, and we did revisit it and move that specific dataset into Redshift at that point -- which wasn't really a win for my original position, it was the triggered checkpoint we'd both agreed to working as designed. What I took from it: the right answer to a Redshift-vs-Spectrum disagreement usually isn't a one-time permanent choice, it's a decision with an explicit revisit trigger built in from the start, which is something I now propose by default in similar disagreements.
commonMistakes: Describes the other architect's position as simply wrong or uninformed rather than a genuinely reasonable alternative
Resolves the disagreement by seniority, persistence, or a vote rather than identifying a measurable deciding factor
Shows resentment or quiet resistance after the decision went against the candidate's original recommendation
No honest reflection on what was learned about the actual tradeoff
keyPoints: Presents a genuine disagreement where both positions had real merit
Identifies a specific, measurable factor to resolve the decision and gathers real data against it
Shows genuine support for the chosen direction, even when it wasn't the candidate's original recommendation
Reflects honestly on what was learned about the underlying tradeoff

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Fairness in representing both positions as genuinely reasonable
Soundness of the data-driven resolution method
Genuineness of support for the outcome, including when it went against the candidate
Quality of the reflection/lesson

questions.title: Building Cross-Team Consensus on a Shared AWS Tagging Standard
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to get multiple independent teams to agree on and actually adopt a shared tagging standard for cost attribution, when each team had already built their own ad hoc tagging habits that worked fine for their own purposes. How did you get real buy-in rather than a standard that looked good on paper but nobody actually followed?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer recognizes upfront that a tagging standard imposed top-down with no input from the teams who have to actually apply it tends to produce exactly the failure mode the question describes -- technically correct documentation that nobody follows in practice, because it didn't account for how each team's workflows actually create resources. It should describe the candidate involving the affected teams in designing the standard itself, surfacing each team's existing ad hoc conventions first and finding the overlap and genuine differences, rather than presenting a finished standard for feedback after the fact. It should describe how adoption was actually driven -- ideally a combination of making the new standard the easy, low-friction default (built into shared IaC modules/templates so tagging happens automatically rather than being a manual step anyone could skip) and demonstrating a concrete benefit back to each team specifically (their own team's cost visibility improving, not just an abstract platform-wide good), since teams adopt things faster when they see a direct benefit to themselves, not just compliance with a mandate. It should address a team that was genuinely resistant or slow to adopt, and how the candidate handled that without just escalating immediately -- understanding their specific blocker first. The close should include a measurable adoption outcome (percentage of resources tagged correctly, before and after) and whether the standard has held up as teams' usage evolved.
questions.professionalAnswer: I didn't start by writing the standard and asking for sign-off -- I started by pulling together leads from the five teams who'd each built their own tagging habits and asking them to show me what they were already doing and why, because I wanted to understand the real logic behind their existing conventions before telling them it needed to change. It turned out three of the five were already using very similar conventions with just different key names, which made the actual negotiation much smaller than I'd expected -- we weren't starting from scratch, we were mostly just aligning naming. The part that actually drove adoption, though, wasn't the agreement in the room, it was building the standard into our shared Terraform modules so that creating a new resource through the standard path just tagged it correctly by default, with no extra step anyone had to remember. One team was slower to adopt because a lot of their resources were still created outside those shared modules through an older, manual process, and rather than escalating that as non-compliance, I spent time understanding why they hadn't migrated to the shared modules yet, which turned out to be a real, legitimate gap in module coverage for their specific use case -- so I prioritized closing that gap instead of just pressuring them to tag manually in the meantime. Properly tagged resource coverage went from under 40% to around 92% over about ten weeks, and it's held steady since, mostly because the tagging isn't something anyone has to remember to do anymore, it's just what happens when they use the standard path.
commonMistakes: Designs the standard unilaterally and presents it for sign-off rather than involving teams in shaping it
Relies on policy/documentation alone rather than making the standard the low-friction default via tooling
Escalates a slow-adopting team's resistance immediately instead of understanding their specific blocker first
No measurable adoption outcome or evidence the standard held up over time
keyPoints: Involves affected teams in designing the standard rather than imposing it top-down
Makes the standard the low-friction default via shared tooling/IaC rather than relying on manual compliance
Demonstrates concrete, team-specific benefit to drive genuine adoption
Investigates a resistant team's real blocker before escalating
Gives a measurable, sustained adoption outcome

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Involves affected teams genuinely in shaping the standard
Makes adoption low-friction via tooling rather than policy alone
Handles a resistant team's real blocker thoughtfully
Gives a measurable, sustained adoption outcome
